7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Chapter 7 finishes two things. First, the call to holiness: since God has promised to live among his people and be their Father, they must cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit (7:1). Second, the story Paul broke off at 2:13. He had left Troas in anxiety and gone into Macedonia, where he found no rest: fighting outside, fear inside. Then Titus arrived with news from Corinth. The severe letter had hurt them, but the hurt had led to repentance. They had grieved, longed for Paul, and dealt with the offender.

So Paul explains the difference between two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret; worldly grief produces death. He lists what their godly grief produced: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and readiness to see justice done. Titus has been refreshed by them, Paul’s boasting about them has proved true, and he rejoices that he can have complete confidence in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 7 brings the long defence of Paul’s ministry (2:14–7:4) to a close and returns to the story of Titus. Verse 1 concludes the call to separation in chapter 6: since God has promised to dwell among us and be our Father, let us cleanse ourselves and pursue holiness. Then Paul asks again for open hearts (vv. 2–4). He tells how, in Macedonia, harassed and afraid, he was comforted by the arrival of Titus with news that the Corinthians had responded to his severe letter with grief, longing and zeal (vv. 5–7). He does not regret the letter, because their grief was godly grief, which leads to repentance and salvation, unlike worldly grief, which leads to death. He describes the marks of their repentance: earnestness, eagerness to put things right, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and justice (vv. 8–12). Titus’s joy and Paul’s confidence in them complete his comfort (vv. 13–16). The chapter is one of Scripture’s best descriptions of true repentance, and underneath every line of it is the God of all comfort, keeping the promise he made in chapter 1.

Since we have these promises, beloved. Everything hangs on the first three words. These promises are the ones just quoted at the end of chapter 6: I will dwell among them and walk among them, I will be their God, I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters (6:16–18). The command that follows is not the condition of the promises; it is the consequence of them. Get that order wrong and the Christian life becomes unbearable. Read as “cleanse yourself and then God will come to live in you”, this verse turns holiness into a probation with no visible end. Read as Paul wrote it, holiness is what a person does because the promises are already his and the house is already occupied.

Beloved. Notice the word dropped into the middle of a command. Paul is not haranguing them. It is one of only two places in this letter he calls them that (12:19), and it changes the temperature of everything around it. A command to holiness from someone who does not love you is a burden. The same command from a father who does is an invitation to become what you already are.

Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit. Two things are worth noticing. First, let us: Paul includes himself. There is no plateau of holiness from which an apostle issues instructions to people below him. Second, ourselves. “Cleanse” (katharizō) is something a Christian does, actively. That does not contradict the earlier chapters, where the verbs had God as their subject; both are true, and Scripture holds them together without embarrassment. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13).

Body and spirit. “Defilement” (molysmos) is a stain, the kind of pollution that clings. Corinth would have understood defilement of the body easily, in a city famous for it: sexual sin, the feasts in idol temples, drunkenness. The second is the one religious people forget. Defilement of the spirit is the sin that leaves no mark on the body at all: the settled contempt, the appetite for other people’s failures, the ambition that would step over someone, the private rehearsal of grievances, false worship held in the mind. A man can keep his body scrupulously clean and be filthy in a place nobody can see, and Paul refuses to let the two be separated. Holiness covers the whole person.

Bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God. “Bringing to completion” (epiteleō) means to finish, to carry through to the end. It is a process with a direction, which is honest about the pace. Nobody is finished. But a Christian ought to be able to name something he is further on with than he was five years ago, and if he cannot, the verb is worth thinking about. And notice the atmosphere it is done in: the fear of God. Not the terror of a God who might reject you; Paul has spent six chapters removing that. It is the awe of someone who has grasped who is living in the house. Nobody has to be told to be careful in a room they know is occupied by someone they love and revere.

Where Christians differ: who does the cleansing? Some say sanctification is entirely God’s work, with believers passive, waiting to be carried along; others speak as though it is entirely up to our effort. Verdict: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves, yet it is God who sanctifies by his Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate: we work out what God works in (Philippians 2:12–13; Westminster 13.1, 3). It is never complete in this life; perfect holiness comes at glorification, when we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s promises by cleansing ourselves. We already have the promises; holiness is our response. Nor does it mean that a Christian who still finds defilement in himself has never been cleansed. The blood of Christ has cleansed his guilt once for all (Hebrews 10:14); what he is doing now is clearing out of the house the things that do not belong in it.

What does cleansing myself actually look like? It looks like taking specific things out of your life, not making general resolutions. Name the defilement plainly before God and confess it (1 John 1:9). Then cut off its supply: the website, the habit, the friendship that always ends in gossip, the late evening alone with nothing to do. Put something in its place, because an empty house soon fills again (Matthew 12:43–45): Scripture read and memorised, prayer, the company of believers, work for others. Tell a trusted Christian friend if the sin is stubborn. And go on doing it. The verb is continuous because the work is.

Does this verse mean I must cut off my unbelieving friends? No. Paul has just been speaking of being unequally yoked (6:14), a binding partnership that pulls you away from Christ, such as marriage to an unbeliever or a venture that demands compromise. He said in his earlier letter that to avoid all contact with unbelievers you would have to leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10), and Jesus was called the friend of sinners. Keep your friendships and keep them for Christ’s sake. What you must cut off is whatever defiles, including any friendship in which you are being drawn into sin rather than drawing your friend toward the Saviour.

In a sentence. Since we have these promises, dear friends, let us purify ourselves from everything that contaminates body and spirit, perfecting holiness out of reverence for God.

On a Tuesday. Name one defilement of body and one of spirit in your life, the one people could see and the one they never could. Confess both to God by name. Then take one practical step today to clean out the first, and one quiet step to starve the second: a grudge you stop rehearsing, a comparison you refuse to make. Do it not to be accepted, but because you already are.

For worship. Here is the whole logic of the verse in one picture. The God who filled the tabernacle with a glory no one could stand in, and the temple so that the priests could not minister, has chosen to make his home in people like the Corinthians, and in us. He did not wait for the house to be clean before moving in; he moved in and began to clean it, paying for every stain with the blood of his Son. If God has come to live in you, the question is never whether you are permitted to keep the defilement. It is what on earth it is still doing in his house. And he will finish what he began: the Father who promised to be a father to you will present you holy and blameless before him, without one stain left.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks again for a place in their hearts, insisting he has wronged and exploited no one, and assuring them he says this in love, not accusation. He takes up the story from chapter 2: in Macedonia he had no rest, with conflict outside and fear inside, until God comforted him through Titus’s arrival and his news. The Corinthians had been grieved by the severe letter, and Paul briefly regretted sending it, but their grief led to repentance. He contrasts sorrow that turns to God and leads to salvation with worldly sorrow that leads to death, and lists the earnest, practical fruits their repentance produced. Titus was refreshed by them, Paul’s confidence in them proved justified, and he rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology: The distinction between godly grief and worldly grief is pastorally crucial. Worldly grief can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. But its focus is on the pain caused to oneself (loss of reputation, loss of relationships, loss of comfort) rather than on the offence against God. Judas displays worldly grief — he is distraught over what he has done, even returns the money, but cannot receive forgiveness; he destroys himself. Peter displays godly grief — the same tears, the same self-accusation, but directed toward the face of Jesus, resolved by Jesus’s restoration. The direction of the grief determines its outcome.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is confronted with evidence of long-term financial dishonesty. He weeps, expresses remorse, describes how devastated he is — by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never directly addresses the harm done to those he stole from, or the offence against God. His leadership team recognises, with the categories of this passage, that they are witnessing worldly grief — real grief, but pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance would ask different questions: not “what have I lost?” but “against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to make it right?”

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

Make room in your hearts for us. Paul picks up exactly where he left off at 6:13: widen your hearts, he said there, and now, make room. “Make room” (chōreō) means to give space, to make a place for. The subject never really changed; the paragraph about yokes was a necessary detour, and here is the appeal again. The Corinthians had let their affection for him shrink into a cramped little corner, and he asks for the room back.

We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. Three denials, and they are worth hearing as answers to charges actually being made. Wronged (adikeō): nobody has been treated unjustly by us. Corrupted (phtheirō): to ruin or spoil, perhaps pointing at the accusation that his teaching had led people astray, morally or doctrinally. Taken advantage (pleonekteō): to exploit, to cheat, the same verb used at 2:11 of Satan outwitting the church. This is the money charge, the suggestion that the collection for Jerusalem was a scheme, and he will have to answer it again at 12:17–18.

Three flat denials. Notice that he gives no explanation and produces no evidence. There is a kind of accusation that cannot be disproved and should not be dignified with a long defence, only with a plain contradiction and a life that goes on being what it is. Paul has already laid his life open to them (6:3–10). He is content to let that life answer.

I do not say this to condemn you. Immediately comes the sentence that shows what kind of man is speaking. He has just been forced to deny that he is a fraud, and his first concern is that they should not feel accused by his denial. Anyone who has been on the wrong end of a false rumour will recognise how rare that is. The natural motion, once you finally get to speak, is to make somebody pay for the months of silence. Paul closes that door before it opens.

For I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. Here is the reason he can afford to be generous. This is covenant language: the promise Ruth made to Naomi, that only death would part them, and the bond David and Jonathan swore before the LORD (Ruth 1:16–17; 1 Samuel 20:42). It is a pledge of unbreakable loyalty. It means there is no circumstance in which I stop being yours: not if you believe the rumours, not if you never apologise.

Dying first. Notice the order of the two verbs, because it is not the natural one. We would say live and die together; Paul puts dying first. He is not describing an association that would survive death if it came to that. He is describing one that has already been through it: a fellowship of people who died with Christ and now live in him (5:14–15), and who therefore cannot be parted by anything smaller than death. That is the standard for Christian relationships, and it is a rebuke to how easily most of them are abandoned. Churches are left over a decision about the music; friendships end over a comment; families divide over an estate and never recover. What Paul offers people who have been cool toward him for a year is a commitment with no exit clause in it at all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sinless. He knew himself to be the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). It means his conduct toward them had been honest, and that on these particular charges he had nothing to confess.

When I am falsely accused, should I defend myself? Sometimes, briefly and plainly, as Paul does here, especially when the accusation damages the gospel or other people rely on your trustworthiness. Say what is true, without heat and without counter-accusation, and then leave it. Do not spend your life chasing every rumour; you will never catch them all, and the effort will sour you. Let your conduct over years answer what words cannot (1 Peter 2:12, 15). Hand the matter to the Lord, who judges justly, as Christ did when he was reviled and did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). And watch your heart: aim to win the accuser back, not to defeat him.

In a sentence. Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, exploited no one. Paul does not say this to condemn you; he has said before that you have such a place in our hearts that we would live or die with you.

On a Tuesday. Think of one Christian relationship that has gone cool: the friend you stopped ringing, the family member you are polite to, the church member you avoid in the car park. Ask whether you have quietly written an exit clause into it. Then take one small step that says you have not: a message, an invitation, a prayer for them by name.

For worship. Paul could offer this kind of love because it had been offered to him first, by one who does not release anyone he has taken into his heart. Christ loved his own who were in the world and loved them to the end (John 13:1). He did not wait for his disciples to stop doubting him, or for Peter to stop denying him, before he bound himself to them. He died first, and then he lived, and those who are in him have died with him and now live with him, and nothing in all creation can separate them from his love (Romans 8:38–39). That is a heart with no exit clause, and it is open to us.

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.

I am acting with great boldness toward you. Four short statements, and they run in an order that is easy to miss. The first word is parrēsia again, met at 3:12: frankness, freedom of speech, the right to say everything. He is telling them there is nothing he is holding back, which is the natural companion of the wide-open heart of the previous chapter. A guarded heart produces guarded speech; an open one says what it means.

I have great pride in you. Literally, much boasting about you. This is a startling thing to say about the Corinthians. After all the trouble, the factions, the immorality, the cold year, Paul boasts of them. He is telling them how he speaks about them when they are not in the room, and it turns out he brags. Everyone who has heard second-hand that someone spoke well of them knows what that does to a heart.

I am filled with comfort. The word from chapter 1, the whole letter’s theme, and now stated as an accomplished fact. Paul, who despaired of life itself in chapter 1 (1:8), is filled. The God of all comfort has been as good as his name.

In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy. The last clause holds together two things most people think are alternatives. Not after the affliction, and not merely in spite of it: in it. “Overflowing” (hyperperisseuomai) means to superabound, to run over the top. The affliction has not been removed and is not being minimised; the news from Corinth has not made his circumstances one bit safer. Something else has been poured in until the container will not hold it.

Where joy comes from. Read the verse in context and the source is not mysterious. Titus arrived. He brought news that people Paul loved had turned the right way. That is what filled him: not a change in his health, safety, finances or reputation, but the spiritual good of other people. There is a searching diagnostic in that. Take an inventory of the last month and ask what actually lifted you and what actually sank you. For most of us the list is entirely circumstantial: money, health, weather, how things went at work, whether someone was pleasant. Paul’s list is other people’s repentance. A man whose joy depends on his own circumstances will be up and down for life, because circumstances are designed to move. A man whose joy is fastened to what God is doing in other people has tied it to something that tends in only one direction. That is why the affliction could not empty him. The things going wrong were all happening to Paul, and his joy was not being drawn from there.

What it does not mean. It does not mean affliction ended. It means joy can overflow even in it. Nor does it mean a Christian must hide his troubles behind a smile; in the very next verse Paul tells them about his fears.

Is it honest to say I am joyful when life is hard? Yes, if the joy is real and you do not pretend the hardship away. Christian joy is not a feeling that everything is fine; it is gladness in God and in his work that sits underneath the grief and is not destroyed by it. Paul elsewhere calls himself sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (6:10), both at once. So you can say truthfully, this is very hard, and I am glad of Christ and of what he is doing. If you cannot feel joy at all just now, do not manufacture it. Ask God for it, look for what he is doing in others, and wait; joy is the Spirit’s fruit, not your performance.

In a sentence. Paul speaks to you with great frankness; he takes great pride in you. He is greatly encouraged; in all our troubles his joy knows no bounds.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone today that you are proud of them in the Lord, and be specific about what God has done in them. Then, this week, make a short list of things that have lifted you. If none of them is what God is doing in another person, start praying for someone by name and watching for the answer.

For worship. The joy that ran over in Macedonia came from the same fountain as every other good thing in this letter. The Father of mercies does not merely remove our troubles; he fills us in the middle of them, and fills us with the very thing he delights in most, the turning of sinners back to himself. There is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), and Paul, in a Macedonian lodging with fighting outside and fear inside, was let in on that joy. So are we, whenever we rejoice in what God rejoices in. Our circumstances will rise and fall, but the Lord who gathers his people is not going backwards.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest. Paul goes back and picks up the story he broke off at 2:13. He had left Troas, unable to preach for anxiety at not finding Titus, and crossed to Macedonia to find him. Now he tells us what that was like. “Bodies” is literally flesh: his whole human self, frail and exposed. “No rest” is the word he used at 2:13 of his spirit: no relief, no loosening. Now it is the body too. He was not sleeping.

But we were afflicted at every turn, fighting without and fear within. Two directions, and the second is the remarkable one. Fighting without we expect: opposition, hostility, perhaps persecution in Macedonia, conflict wherever he went. Fear within is an apostle admitting, in a public letter to a church that already thinks him weak, that he was frightened: anxious for the Corinthians, and very likely for Titus’s safety on the roads with a sum of money. He does not qualify it. He does not say he wrestled the fear down or that it was brief. He lists it beside the external conflicts as simply part of the account. Any Christian who has believed that fear is incompatible with faith should read this verse slowly. The man who wrote that God gave us a spirit not of fear (2 Timothy 1:7) is the same man who says here that he had fears within, and the Bible puts both sentences in the canon without apology.

But God. Here is one of the great turns in Paul, two words on which whole lives have hinged (Ephesians 2:4). Everything before them is the human situation, honestly told. Everything after them is what God does with it.

Who comforts the downcast. Take the title he chooses, because it is chosen. It comes from Isaiah 49:13, where the LORD comforts his people and has compassion on his afflicted. The word is tapeinos: low, brought down, at the bottom, the ordinary Greek word for depressed or humiliated. It is the word Jesus used of himself: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). Of all the titles available to him, Paul reaches for the one that describes what God does for people who are on the floor. This is not a general statement about the divine nature. It is a man saying: I was down there, and this is what he is like when you are. God is especially near the downhearted (Psalm 34:18).

Comforted us by the coming of Titus. And notice how the comfort arrived. Not a vision. Not a voice. Not the third heaven, which Paul had known and which is not mentioned here. A friend walked in the door. That should be said plainly to anyone waiting for God to do something dramatic. The overwhelming majority of the comfort God gives his people arrives on two legs, with a face and a name. It looks like a visit, a meal left on a doorstep, a phone call from someone who did not know why they rang. Paul does not treat it as a lesser form of help. He calls it God comforting him, and the sentence has God as the subject and Titus as the instrument.

The journey somebody has to make. That has a consequence for anyone who finds it easier to pray for a suffering friend than to go and see him. Pray, certainly. But God has arranged the world so that the comfort of the downcast usually requires somebody to make the journey. Titus crossed a sea.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fear is always sin. Paul felt fear. Faith does not pretend fear away; it brings it to God. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3) is the prayer of a frightened man, not of a fearless one.

I struggle with anxiety or depression. Does that mean my faith is weak? Not necessarily. Paul was harassed, sleepless and afraid, and he was not walking in unbelief; Elijah asked to die, and the psalmists were often downcast. Anxiety and low mood have many causes: exhaustion, grief, illness, the chemistry of a body living in a fallen world, as well as sin and unbelief. Bring all of it to the God who comforts the downcast. Tell a trusted friend or your pastor, so that someone can be Titus to you. Use the ordinary means God gives, including rest, food, sleep, and a doctor or counsellor where needed; taking medication is not a failure of faith. And do not measure God’s nearness by how you feel. He is near to the brokenhearted.

In a sentence. For when we came into Macedonia, we had no rest, but were harassed at every turn: conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

On a Tuesday. Think of one person you know who is low just now. Pray for them, and then go, or ring, or write, or take a meal round today. You do not need to know what to say. Titus’s arrival was the comfort before he had said a word. And if you are the one who is downcast, let someone know. God’s comfort often waits for a door to be opened.

For worship. The God of the Bible has a particular address, and it is the low place. He dwells in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly (Isaiah 57:15). When his Son came, he came lowly in heart, and he went lower than any of us will ever go, into the darkness of Gethsemane and the cross, so that no downcast believer would ever find the bottom empty of him. The God who sent Titus across a sea sent his Son across a far greater distance. And he still comforts the downcast: not by explaining everything, but by coming, and by sending his people to come.
verseByVerse.note: Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.

And not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you. Follow the comfort as it moves, because this verse traces its whole route. God comforted the Corinthians. The Corinthians comforted Titus. Titus, comforted, came to Macedonia and comforted Paul. Three links, and the chain runs exactly as chapter 1 said it would: God comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction (1:4). Comfort received is comfort passed on, and the supply at the head of the line is God.

Not merely a messenger. Titus did not simply carry information. He had been changed by his stay in Corinth, and it was the state of the man arriving, as much as the news he brought, that lifted Paul. That is worth knowing about how encouragement actually works. People rarely encourage others by transmitting facts. They do it by being visibly people to whom something good has happened.

Your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me. Three words describing what Titus reported, and each is a mark of a church coming right. Your longing: they wanted to see Paul again. After a year of distance and rumour, the affection had come back on. Your mourning: this is the strong word, the grief you feel at a death. They were not merely embarrassed about how the situation had been handled; they grieved over the offence and over having hurt him. There is a great difference between a church that regrets an episode and one that mourns it, and the difference shows in whether anything changes. Your zeal for me: the root of our word zealous, heat, intensity. They were eager to defend him and put things right. Whatever coldness there had been was gone, and it had been replaced not by politeness but by warmth.

What restoration looks like. Take those three as a description of genuine restoration anywhere: in a marriage, between a parent and a grown child, in a friendship that went wrong. Not merely the end of hostilities. Longing, grief and warmth. If a reconciliation has produced nothing but a resumption of civil contact, it has not yet reached what Paul is describing.

So that I rejoiced still more. More than what? More than he had already rejoiced at the simple relief of Titus arriving safely. The news kept raising the level. Paul’s joy was greater even than his relief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all problems were solved. Chapters 10 to 13 show that some opposition remained. Paul rejoices in real progress without pretending it is the finished article.

What if I have no one to comfort me, or no one comforts me well? Then begin where the chain begins, with God himself, who comforts the downcast directly through his word and Spirit; the Psalms were written for exactly this. Then make yourself known. Most people are not comforted because nobody knows they need it. Ask for help plainly, even if it feels awkward, and give people the chance to be Titus to you. And look for someone to comfort yourself. It sounds backwards, but comfort often arrives on the return journey: the person you visit frequently sends you home lighter than you came.

In a sentence. and not only by his coming but also by the comfort you had given him. He told us about your longing for us, your deep sorrow, your eager concern for Paul, so that Paul’s joy was greater than ever.

On a Tuesday. Pass on good news about other believers this week: tell someone what God is doing in a person they love, or tell a pastor something good you have seen in his flock. It comforts and encourages more than you know. And if a relationship of yours has been patched up but is still cool, ask God for longing, grief and warmth, and be the first to show them.

For worship. Behind all of it stands the quiet arrangement that makes the chain possible. God chose not to be the only one who comforts. He gives the comfort, then puts it into people, then sends those people to each other, so that the consolation of an apostle in Macedonia depended on the state of a church in Achaia and the journey of a friend in between. He could have done it directly and instantly. He preferred to do it through his people, and in doing so gave every ordinary Christian a share in the work of the God of all comfort. What a Father, who will not keep even his consolations to himself, but makes his children carriers of them.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.

For even if I made you grieve with my letter. This is the severe letter, written out of much affliction and many tears (2:3–4), sent between 1 Corinthians and this one and carried by Titus. It is one of the most human sentences in the New Testament, and it is a great mercy that the Holy Spirit left it in.

I do not regret it, though I did regret it. Watch him change his mind twice inside a single line. The severe letter went off. Paul then spent the waiting weeks wishing he had not sent it. And now, knowing the outcome, he is glad he did. Consider who is writing. This is an apostle, describing a letter written for the good of a church, and he admits that after sending it he wished it back. He does not tidy this away. He does not present himself as a man of settled confidence who knew all along.

The stretch afterwards. Anyone who has ever had to say a hard thing knows this exact sequence. You agonise over whether to speak. You speak. And then comes the awful stretch afterwards: the message sent and unanswerable, the conversation you cannot take back, the silence in which you rehearse every word and become certain you were too harsh, or too soft, or should simply have left it alone. That stretch is in the Bible. Paul lived in it.

For I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while. Notice what resolved his regret. Not a better argument with himself, nor a stronger conviction that he had been right. The outcome resolved it. The regret ended when he saw what the letter had actually done. Which means that during the weeks of regret Paul was wrong, and the letter he wished unwritten was the right letter all along. That is worth holding on to, because the regret you feel after a hard conversation is not evidence about whether you should have had it. It is usually only evidence that you love the person and cannot see the end from here.

Only for a while. The last phrase is the pivot of the passage. The grief had a term on it. It was real, it was severe, and it was temporary, because it was grief that led somewhere. That is the difference between the wound of a friend and the wound of an enemy, and Proverbs said so long before: faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Proverbs 27:6). The friend’s wound hurts and heals. The flattery feels better and leaves the thing that was killing you exactly where it was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean inspiration removes all human emotion. Paul felt doubts. God’s word came through a real person, with real nerves, and God chose to let us see them. Nor does it mean the severe letter was a mistake that happened to work out. Paul’s regret was a feeling; his letter was right.

If an apostle regretted his letter, was the letter Scripture? We do not have the severe letter, and the church never received it as part of the New Testament. Not everything an apostle wrote was given to the church as Scripture; God preserved what he intended his people to have, and the canon he gave is complete and closed. Paul’s passing regret does not touch the reliability of what we do have. The inspired letter we are reading is the one telling us about the regret, and it tells us honestly, which is part of why we can trust it.

How do I know whether I should say the hard thing at all? Ask a few honest questions before you speak. Is it a real sin or harm, or only a difference of taste? Is it my place, because of my relationship or responsibility? Have I dealt with my own log first (Matthew 7:5)? Do I want this person’s good more than my own relief or vindication? Have I prayed, and if possible taken counsel? If the answers are yes, speak, gently and clearly, and then leave the outcome with God. Your feelings afterwards will not tell you whether you were right; only time and fruit will.

In a sentence. Even if Paul caused you sorrow by his letter, he does not regret it. Though he did regret it at first, he sees that the letter hurt you, but only for a little while,

On a Tuesday. If you are still carrying the regret of something you had to say, this verse gives you two things: permission to have felt it, since an apostle did, and the reminder that you are not yet in a position to judge. Paul could only write this sentence because Titus came back. Pray for the person, keep the door open, and wait for God’s timing.

For worship. Every faithful wound in Scripture comes from a heart that loves. The LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights (Proverbs 3:12), and his discipline, painful for the moment, yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Hebrews 12:11). Our Father never regrets a wound he gives his children, because he sees the end from the beginning and has already borne the deepest wound himself, in his Son. The grief he sends is always only for a while. The joy he brings out of it is for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.

As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. Here is one of the most practically important distinctions in Scripture, and everyone who has ever wondered whether their sorrow over sin was the real thing needs it. First, notice Paul’s care. He takes no pleasure in having hurt them. The grief was never the goal; it was the road. He rejoices in its fruit: repentance (metanoia), a change of mind that becomes a change of direction. Anyone who enjoys the discomfort he causes in the name of correction is not doing what Paul did.

For you felt a godly grief. Literally, grief according to God: sorrow shaped by his view of the matter, sorrow that God approves, that sees sin as God sees it. And so that you suffered no loss through us: the letter hurt, but did them only good.

For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret. The chain runs: godly grief, then repentance, then salvation. And it is never regretted. “Without regret” (ametamelētos) can be read with the repentance or with the salvation; either way the point is the same. Nobody who has ever come to Christ in genuine sorrow has looked back and wished he had not.

Whereas worldly grief produces death. The difference between the two kinds of grief is not intensity. Both hurt. Both produce tears. The difference is direction. Godly grief sees the sin as an offence against God first, and it moves toward him. The psalm every believer eventually prays is the model: against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Psalm 51:4). That is David, a man who had wrecked several lives, and he says against you only, not because the others did not matter, but because he had seen who the offended party ultimately is. Worldly grief is sorrow about consequences: regret, embarrassment, self-pity, the pain of being caught, without turning to God. It is real distress, and it is entirely about the self: what I have lost, how I am now seen, what happens to me next. It can be extremely convincing from the outside and even from the inside, and it leads to despair, bitterness and death.

Two men on the same night. Scripture gives us both kinds, and they were in the same story on the same night. Judas betrayed Christ, and then changed his mind, threw the money back into the temple, and said, I have sinned by betraying innocent blood; and he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3–5). Every visible mark of repentance is there: remorse, confession, restitution. And it ended in death, exactly as this verse says, because it never turned toward anyone. Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, went out and wept bitterly, and was restored over breakfast on a beach (Luke 22:62; John 21:15–19). The same night, a comparable failure, comparable remorse, and one man’s grief took him to Christ while the other’s took him to a rope.

Godly and worldly grief. Set them side by side. Godly grief is sorry for sin because it offends God; worldly grief is sorry for the consequences. Godly grief runs to God; worldly grief runs from him. Godly grief changes behaviour; worldly grief only feels bad. The Westminster Shorter Catechism defines repentance unto life as a saving grace whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, does, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience (Q. 87). Notice the mercy of God in Christ in the middle of that definition. Grief without hope of mercy never turns anyone; it only drives him into hiding.

A one-minute test. You can settle this about yourself quickly. When you are sorry for something, listen to the sentences in your head. If they are mostly about how this looks, what it will cost you and how you will get out of it, that is the sorrow of the world, and it will not save anyone. If they are about God, that you have grieved someone who loves you, that this is what you are and you need him to deal with it, that is godly grief, and it is already carrying you in the right direction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean repentance earns salvation. It is the fruit of grace and the way into salvation’s blessings. God grants repentance (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25); we do not pay for forgiveness with tears. Nor does it mean that a believer who has felt worldly grief has lost his salvation. Every Christian’s sorrow is mixed. The question is where it is taking you.

What if I do not feel sorry enough? Then you are in good company, because no one’s sorrow is ever as deep as his sin deserves, and we are not forgiven because of the depth of our grief but because of the death of Christ. Paul’s test is direction, not volume. Are you turning to God and away from the sin? Then go on turning. Ask God to show you your sin as he sees it, read the account of the cross slowly, and remember that tenderness grows as you walk with him. Some of the most genuine repentance is quiet and dry-eyed, and some of the loudest is only worldly grief. Do not wait to feel enough before you come.

What about the shame I keep feeling after I have confessed? Distinguish conviction from accusation. The Spirit convicts of a specific sin in order to lead you to Christ, and once you have confessed it he points you to the cross and says it is finished. The accuser keeps a vague cloud of shame hanging over you after the sin has been forgiven, to keep you from God. If the sin is confessed and, as far as possible, put right, then the lingering shame is not godly grief. Answer it with the promise: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

In a sentence. Yet now Paul is happy, not because you were made sorry, but because your sorrow led you to repentance. For you became sorrowful as God intended and so were not harmed in any way by us. Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.

On a Tuesday. The next time you are sorry for something, stop and listen to your inner sentences before you do anything else. If they are about yourself, turn them deliberately toward God: tell him what you did, against him, without excuses, and thank him for the cross. Then do one thing that turns from the sin. The grief that runs to God is the one that heals.

For worship. Judas and Peter both wept, and only one was restored, and the difference was where they went with their tears. But the deepest difference is not in Peter at all. It is in the Lord who had already prayed for him, that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), who looked at him across the courtyard, and who came looking for him on the shore and asked him three times, do you love me. Godly grief is never a ladder we climb to reach God. It is the sound of a sinner being found. The Saviour who turns us does not stand back to see whether our sorrow is adequate; he receives the turning and covers the sin with his own blood. No one has ever regretted coming to him.

parallels.desc: Peter’s tears and Judas’s remorse

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.

For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you. Having defined godly grief, Paul now shows what it looked like when it landed. This is the most concrete description of repentance anywhere in the New Testament: seven marks, and they can be laid against a life. Earnestness (spoudē) is literally speed, urgency, seriousness. Repentance that is real is in a hurry. It no longer shrugs, and it does not put the matter down to be dealt with when convenient, which is the surest sign that nothing has happened.

But also what eagerness to clear yourselves. The word is apologia, a defence. Not self-justification: they had just admitted they were wrong. It is the desire to put right what they were rightly blamed for, so that the charge no longer stands against them because the thing itself has been dealt with, and to show they did not approve of the wrong.

What indignation. Anger at the sin, at the situation, at themselves for tolerating it. Repentance without any heat in it is usually just embarrassment. A man who is genuinely done with something is angry about it.

What fear. A proper seriousness about God, whose name had been dishonoured in the whole affair, and perhaps also an awareness that the apostle might come with a rod (1 Corinthians 4:21).

What longing. For the restoration of what was broken, in this case for Paul himself. Sin isolates; real repentance wants back into the room.

What zeal. Heat again, but now positive: energy for what is right, for Paul, for God’s honour, where before there had been indifference.

What punishment! “Punishment” (ekdikēsis) means justice carried out, a wrong put right. They acted. The discipline was actually done: the punishment by the majority of 2:6, which Paul then told them was enough. This is the mark most often missing today, and its absence is why so much apparent repentance changes nothing. Nothing was done.

Lay the list against the usual article. We tend to be satisfied with the first minute of repentance: an apology, some evident distress, a request to move on. Paul’s list has urgency, anger, fear, longing, energy and action in it. The apology is not even mentioned. That gives an unusually practical test, and it works both ways. If you wonder whether your own repentance over something is real, walk the seven and ask which are present. And if you are on the other side, trying to judge whether someone who has wronged you has genuinely turned, this is a far better instrument than reading their tone of voice, because most of the seven are things that can be seen from outside.

At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter. “Innocent” (hagnos) means pure, clear. Paul is not saying they were never at fault. He is saying the matter is closed. By their response they showed they were not complicit in the wrong. That is what God does with a repentant person, and it is what a church must learn to do: not a probation, not a permanent asterisk, but a case fully and publicly shut.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they were never at fault. It means their repentance cleared them.

If someone has truly repented, must everything go back to how it was? Forgiveness, yes, fully and from the heart; the case is shut and must not be reopened in gossip or held over him. But forgiveness is not the same as restoring every position of trust at once. A treasurer who stole may be forgiven and still not handle the money again for a long while, and perhaps never; an elder who fell may be restored to fellowship long before he is restored to office (1 Timothy 3:2). Real repentance will accept those consequences without resentment; indeed eagerness to put things right is one of Paul’s marks. Where there has been abuse, protecting the vulnerable comes first: the matter must be reported to the authorities where the law requires it, and the abuser kept away from those he harmed. Forgiving him never means returning a victim to danger, and the church must never tolerate abuse under the name of grace.

In a sentence. See what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what concern, what readiness to see justice done. At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in this matter.

On a Tuesday. Take one sin you have recently repented of and walk it through the seven. Was there urgency? Have you put right what can be put right? Are you angry at it, or still fond of it? Is there a holy fear, a longing for restored fellowship, energy for the opposite good? And did you actually do anything? Where a mark is missing, ask God for it and take the step.

For worship. Only God can produce a list like this in a church like Corinth. The congregation that had shrugged at sin, quarrelled over leaders and gone cold on its founder was suddenly urgent, angry at evil, reverent, longing, zealous and active, and none of it was manufactured by a committee. It was the fruit of the Spirit working through a letter written in tears. And when it was done, God did what only he can do: he declared them clear. That is the gospel in miniature. The Judge who has every right to keep the file open closes it, because his Son has answered every charge in it, and he does not reopen what Christ has closed.

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.

So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong. Paul now tells them why he really wrote, and the answer is not what anyone would have guessed. Not mainly to punish the offender, though the man has been dealt with and forgiven (2:6–8).

Nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong. Not mainly to vindicate the one offended, and since that was very probably Paul himself, this means: not for my own sake. He is stating that the letter was not written to get himself vindicated, which was precisely what his critics were saying about it.

Who was the one who did the wrong? Some take him to be the man of 1 Corinthians 5, who had his father’s wife, with the father as the one who suffered the wrong. The more likely reading, as at 2:5, is that during the painful visit a member of the church had openly opposed and humiliated Paul himself, and the church had failed to stand with him, so that Paul is the one who suffered the wrong (2:5–11). Nothing in the application depends on the identification.

But in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God. Read the last part slowly, because two small phrases carry the whole verse. Revealed to you: not to Paul, not to the neighbouring churches. To themselves. And in the sight of God: with him as the one before whom the revealing takes place. The Corinthians did not know what they were. They had grown cold, listened to rumours and let their affection narrow into a cramped little space, and they would have said, if asked, that this was simply how things now stood. The severe letter did not create their earnestness. It brought it out where they could see it. The love was still there under the resentment, and it took a crisis to prove it to them. Sometimes we do not know our own hearts until they are tested.

How God uses tests. That is a genuinely important thing to know about how God works. He very often puts his people into a situation whose purpose is not to change them but to show them what he has already done in them. The trial arrives and you discover you did not let go, and the discovery is the point. Moses said as much about the desert years: God led Israel forty years in the wilderness that he might humble them, testing them to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2), and God, of course, already knew. It was Israel who needed to find out. That reframes the hardest seasons in a Christian life. You may never be told what a particular stretch of suffering accomplished for anyone else. It is entirely possible that a large part of what it was for was that you should find out what you actually believe, in the sight of God, where the finding-out counts.

What Paul assumed about them. Notice what he must have believed in order to write the sentence at all. He assumed the earnestness was there to be revealed. He never at any point believed that these people had stopped loving him. He believed the affection was buried and wrote a letter to dig it up, which is what a father does, and not what an offended colleague does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the wrong did not matter. It means Paul’s deepest concern was the church’s spiritual health, not his own reputation or the punishment for its own sake.

How do I know what is really in my heart? Partly by watching what comes out when you are tested. Pressure does not create what is in you; it reveals it. Pay attention to how you respond when you are crossed, when you lose something, when a believer is under attack and it would cost you to stand with him. Ask God to search you, as David did (Psalm 139:23–24), and invite honest friends to tell you what they see. And take comfort from this verse as well as warning: tests reveal grace as well as sin. You may find there is more of Christ’s work in you than you dared to think.

In a sentence. So even though Paul wrote to you, it was neither on account of the one who did the wrong nor on account of the injured party, but rather that before God you could see for yourselves how devoted to us you are.

On a Tuesday. Think of the hardest thing you have been through in the last few years and ask not only what it cost you, but what it showed you about yourself. What did you find you still loved, still believed, still clung to? Thank God for what he revealed. And when you correct someone, aim like Paul at their good before God, not at your own vindication.

For worship. The God who tests his people is the God who has already done the work he is testing. He does not send trials to find out whether he succeeded; he sends them so that we may see what he has done and give him the glory. He knows our hearts better than we do: the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). And the One who lays us open in his sight is the same One who has clothed us in his Son, so that being revealed before God is no longer a terror but, for his people, the discovery of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.

Therefore we are comforted. The word closes the circle opened in the first paragraph of the letter. The God of all comfort has done in Paul’s own case exactly what chapter 1 promised, and it took a year, a painful visit, a letter written in tears, and a friend crossing a sea. God’s comfort is rarely quick. It is always sure.

And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus. Something easy to hurry past. Paul’s own comfort is not the peak of his gladness. What lifted him higher was watching somebody else be happy. That is a rare and unmistakable mark of a man who has genuinely stopped living for himself and lives for the one who died and was raised for him (5:15). Most of us find it easier to weep with those who weep than to rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15), because another person’s gladness can feel like a comment on our own lack. Paul simply delights in his friend.

Because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. “Refreshed” (anapauō) means rested, given relief, the word Jesus used when he promised rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28). Titus had gone to Corinth carrying a letter that might have provoked a riot, expecting trouble, and he came away rested and warmed. A congregation can do this to the people who serve it, in either direction. There are churches that send their workers away refreshed and churches that send them away hollow, and the difference is almost never about size or resources.

For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. Then Paul admits something rather charming. Before Titus went, he had bragged about the Corinthians to him: told him they were a good people, that they would come right, perhaps to encourage a younger man setting out on a frightening errand. Then he had to wait to see whether he had made a fool of himself. He had talked them up when the evidence was thin. They proved him right.

But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true. Notice the logic. Paul’s truthfulness to them and his praise of them behind their backs are of a piece. His word is reliable, whether spoken to them or about them; it is the same yes he defended in chapter 1 (1:18–20). A man who tells you the hard truth to your face and speaks well of you elsewhere is doing the same thing twice. Both are honesty, and neither is flattery.

Believing the best goes first. There is practical wisdom here worth taking. Paul’s confidence went ahead of their performance, and it very probably helped produce it. Titus arrived expecting to find a church that would respond, treated them accordingly, and they responded. This is not manipulation; Paul genuinely believed it. But it is the opposite of how difficult people are usually handled. We approach the awkward member expecting the worst, communicate the expectation without saying a word, and are then proved right. Love believes all things and hopes all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). Somebody has to go first in believing the best. Paul did it here, at the risk of public embarrassment, because it had been done for him first: he was brought to the frightened apostles by Barnabas, who vouched for him when nobody else would (Acts 9:26–27).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul flattered them. He spoke the truth both ways. His praise was true, and so had been his rebukes.

What is the difference between encouragement and flattery? Encouragement is true, specific and for the other person’s good; flattery is exaggerated, vague and usually for the speaker’s benefit, to be liked or to get something. Encouragement points to what God is doing in someone (1 Thessalonians 1:2–3); flattery puffs up the person himself. Encouragement is said behind someone’s back as readily as to his face; flattery is mostly said to his face. So praise freely, but praise what is real, name it concretely, and give God the glory for it. And do not withhold true praise out of fear it will make someone proud. Paul was not afraid to boast of the Corinthians.

In a sentence. By all this we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were especially delighted to see how happy Titus was, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. Paul had boasted to him about you, and you have not embarrassed him. Just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting about you to Titus has proved true as well.

On a Tuesday. Speak well of other believers to others this week, truly and specifically, and live in a way that makes others’ good words about you true. Think of the person who serves your church most visibly and ask whether you send him home refreshed or drained. Then do one thing that refreshes him: a note, a thank you, a meal, an answered request.

For worship. Before the Corinthians had done anything to deserve it, Paul boasted about them. Before we had done anything at all, Christ did something far greater. He is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and he presents his people before the Father’s throne not as they are on their worst days but as they will be, holy and blameless and above reproach (Colossians 1:22). His boast about us will not be put to shame either, because he does not merely hope we will come right; he makes us come right. Every word he has spoken about his people will prove true.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

And his affection for you is even greater. The chapter ends in a place nobody could have predicted from chapter 2. “Affection” is splanchna again, the inward parts, the deep feelings of the heart: the very word used at 6:12, where the Corinthians’ affections had gone narrow. Titus’s are the opposite: enlarged, and growing. Something in that visit expanded the man.

As he remembers the obedience of you all. Not most of them. All. Whatever divisions had run through that congregation, on this they moved together. They obeyed the apostolic instructions they had been given.

How you received him with fear and trembling. The phrase is not about being frightened of Titus. It is Paul’s standard expression for a proper seriousness before God in a weighty moment; he uses it of working out your own salvation (Philippians 2:12) and of serving with a sincere heart as to Christ (Ephesians 6:5). They received Titus with reverence and humility, taking his message seriously as from God. They knew that what was happening in that room was not merely a difficult meeting with a visiting delegate. God was in it, and they behaved accordingly.

The right altitude. That is worth naming, because most church conflict is handled at exactly the wrong level. It is treated as a matter between people, to be managed with tact, patience and the right procedure, all of which are good and none of which reaches the actual height of it. The Corinthians handled theirs with fear and trembling, before God, and the outcome was not merely a settlement but a restored church, a refreshed messenger and an apostle overflowing with joy.

I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you. Then the last line, which ought to be read against everything that has gone before. “Complete confidence” is literally, I take courage in you in everything. This is the church of the factions, the lawsuits and the drunkenness at the Lord’s table. This is the congregation that sat still while its founder was publicly humiliated, compared him unfavourably with smoother men, and had gone cold on him for a year. And the last word of the chapter is confidence. It also prepares the way for what comes next: in chapters 8 and 9 he will ask this same church to give generously for the poor in Jerusalem.

Confidence in what? Nobody should read that as a verdict on how good they were. Paul is about to spend chapters 10 to 13 dealing with the opposition still active among them; he is not naive. His confidence is of the same kind as the unshaken hope of 1:7, resting not on their record but on what God does with people he has begun with. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thought them perfect. Chapters 10 to 13 show remaining concerns. But he rejoices in their present response, and he does not let what is still wrong spoil his gladness at what has come right.

Does this mean I must obey my church leaders without question? No. The Corinthians obeyed the apostolic word Titus brought, the teaching that is now in Scripture, and they received it as from God. Church leaders deserve respect, and we should gladly follow them as they lead us in God’s word (Hebrews 13:17). But no pastor or elder may bind your conscience beyond Scripture (Westminster 20.2), and leaders are themselves under the word and accountable. Fear and trembling is directed toward God. If a leader demands obedience to something Scripture does not teach, or uses his position to control or harm, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the church must deal with him.

How can I keep hoping for a church, or a person, that keeps letting me down? By resting your hope where Paul rested his: not on their track record but on God’s faithfulness to finish what he started. Pray for them specifically. Notice and name real progress, as Paul does, instead of only cataloguing failures. Keep speaking the truth where it is still needed, as he will in chapters 10 to 13. And remember how long God has been patient with you. Hope is not pretending things are fine; it is trusting that God has not given up, and so you will not.

In a sentence. And his affection for you is all the greater when he remembers that you were all obedient, receiving him with fear and trembling. Paul is glad he can have complete confidence in you.

On a Tuesday. Receive God’s word this Sunday as if God were speaking, because he is, and treat a hard conversation in your church or home this week as something that happens before him, not merely between people. And think of one difficult believer you have quietly written off. Pray for him by name, and tell God that you will hope for him, because God is not finished with him.

For worship. That is the only ground on which anyone has ever been able to hope for a difficult church, a difficult family, or himself. The God who did this in Corinth, who took a wrecked relationship, a humiliated apostle and a letter written in tears, and produced longing, mourning, zeal and complete confidence, has not changed his methods or lost his touch. He has never yet been handed a situation past mending. The Saviour who bled for the church loves her still, and he will present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27). Every church that has broken our hearts is a church he has not stopped washing.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.<sup>2</sup>Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one.<sup>3</sup>I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.<sup>4</sup>I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us.<sup>10</sup>For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.<sup>11</sup>For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.<sup>12</sup>So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore we are comforted.
