8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Chapters 8 and 9 are about money: the collection Paul was gathering from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Some background helps. The Jerusalem church had been poor for years. There was a famine under the emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28–30), many believers had lost work or family support for following Jesus, and the church had many widows (Acts 6:1). When Paul’s apostleship was recognised in Jerusalem, the leaders asked him to “remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief. It was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one body: the Gentiles, who had shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, were sharing material blessings in return (Romans 15:25–27). Corinth had started eagerly a year earlier (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), but the quarrel with Paul had stalled it.

In chapter 8 Paul encourages them to finish. He points to the poor, persecuted churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means and begged to take part, because they first gave themselves to the Lord. Above all he points to Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich. Giving should be willing, proportionate to what one has, and aimed at fairness between churches. Then Paul introduces the team who will collect the money, Titus and two trusted brothers, chosen so that the handling of the gift will be above suspicion before God and people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He describes the Macedonian churches, who in severe trials and deep poverty gave joyfully and beyond their means, even begging to be allowed to take part, because they had first given themselves to the Lord. He urges the Corinthians, who excel in so much, to excel in this generosity too. It is not a command; it is a test of genuine love, measured against the example of Christ, who was rich yet became poor for their sake so that they might become rich. They began a year ago; now they should finish, giving in proportion to what they have. The aim is not to burden them but fairness between churches, as with the manna in the wilderness, where no one had too much or too little.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is one of the key NT texts for the kenosis of the incarnation (alongside Phil. 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14). “Though he was rich” describes the pre-incarnate state of the Son — possessing all the resources of divine glory, honour, and power. “He became poor” describes the incarnation and more specifically the cross: the Son laid aside the exercise of divine prerogatives and took on the condition of creaturely poverty, ultimately the poverty of crucifixion and cursed death. “That you by his poverty might become rich” — the result is the enrichment of believers: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the inheritance of the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is considering its annual budget and the portion allocated to mission outside its own walls. One member argues that they should ensure their own facilities and staff are well-funded before giving generously abroad. This passage holds before him the Macedonian model: churches in deep poverty begging to give. And the Christological ground: the Son of God did not ensure his own comfort before giving to others. The board’s question is not merely financial but spiritual: does this budget reflect the grace described in v. 9?

verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.

Meaning first. Chapters 8 and 9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, which the Corinthians had begun a year earlier but not finished (1 Corinthians 16:1–4). These two chapters are the Bible’s fullest teaching on Christian giving. Chapter 8 makes three points. First, the example of the Macedonian churches, who, though desperately poor and afflicted, begged to give, beyond their means, because they first gave themselves to the Lord (vv. 1–5). Second, the supreme example and motive: the grace of the Lord Jesus, who though rich became poor so that we might become rich (vv. 6–9). Third, practical principles: finish what you started; giving is measured by willingness, not amount; and the goal is fairness, so that abundance meets need, as with the manna in the wilderness (vv. 10–15). Then Paul commends Titus and two trusted brothers who will handle the collection, so that everything is done honourably in the sight of God and people (vv. 16–24). Notice that Paul never uses the word money in these chapters; he calls the gift grace, fellowship, service, blessing and generosity. And at the centre of the whole appeal stands not a need but a Person: the rich Son of God who became poor.

We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia. Paul is about to ask the Corinthians for money, and he begins in a way no fundraiser would. He does not describe the need. He describes what God has been doing several hundred miles away. Macedonia is northern Greece, with churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. And notice the word he puts over the whole subject: the grace of God that has been given. Not the generosity of the Macedonians. Their giving is described as something God did in them. That word, charis, grace, will run through these two chapters like a thread, ten times in all (8:1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 16, 19; 9:8, 14, 15). Giving, in Paul’s mind, is not first a duty discharged. It is a grace received, and then passed on.

For in a severe test of affliction. Then comes the equation, and it is worth setting out as an equation because by every human reckoning it does not work. The Macedonian churches had been through it from the start. Read Acts and the letters and you find riots, a jailing, believers dragged before magistrates, a congregation Paul had to leave by night (Acts 16:19–24; 17:5–10; 1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14). They were under pressure, and it was not brief.

Their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty. The Greek is stronger than the English: poverty down to the depths, rock-bottom, the beggar’s level. Macedonia had been hard used by Rome ever since its conquest, and believers there had suffered for their faith on top of it. Affliction plus destitution: any reasonable person could predict the result. Nothing. No capacity, no surplus, nothing to spare, and every excuse in the world.

Have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part. And what came out was an abundance of joy and a wealth of generosity. Both are the language of overflow, something running over the top of the container, from people who by every measure had nothing to overflow with. “Generosity” is haplotēs: simplicity, single-heartedness, the open hand that gives without calculating or holding back. This is one of the plainest pieces of evidence in the New Testament that something other than human nature is at work in the church. Poverty makes people tight; that is not cynicism but observation, and it is a perfectly rational response to having little. Affliction makes people inward. Put the two together and you get a closed hand every time, unless something has got in underneath.

Grace, not character. That is why Paul calls it grace rather than character. He is not holding the Macedonians up as heroes to shame the Corinthians into competing. He is showing them what God does in people, and saying in effect: he is doing this over there, and he can do it here.

Waiting for the right season. There is a searching question in it for anyone who has ever waited for the right season to become generous. Most of us have a threshold in mind: when the mortgage is down, when the children are through school, when there is something spare. The Macedonians never reached it. They gave out of the depths, and the joy was not the reward for giving; the joy and the generosity overflowed together, out of the same well.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the poor can be truly generous. It means generosity comes from grace and joy, not from having plenty. The rich are commanded to be generous and ready to share too (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

Why were the believers in Jerusalem so poor? Several reasons came together. There had been a severe famine in the reign of Claudius, and the church in Antioch had already sent help (Acts 11:27–30). Many Jewish believers lost work, family support and standing when they confessed Jesus, and some had their property seized (Hebrews 10:34). The church also cared for a large number of widows (Acts 6:1). And the collection meant more than relief. It was a Gentile gift to the mother church of the Jews, a visible sign that Jew and Gentile were one body in Christ: if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings (Romans 15:26–27).

In a sentence. And now, brothers and sisters, we want you to know about the grace God has given the Macedonian churches. In the middle of a very severe trial, their overflowing joy and their extreme poverty welled up in rich generosity.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to be rich to be generous. Give out of joy in God, whatever you have. If you have been waiting for a threshold before you begin, name it honestly to God, and then begin below it this week, even with a small gift, as an act of trust.

For worship. The open hands in Macedonia were not the beginning of the story. Before any believer there gave a coin, God had given his Son, and with him the Spirit who turns hard hearts into springs. The same grace that saved the Philippian jailer at midnight was still at work in his church years later, making poor people glad and making glad people generous. The God who can do that in a city of affliction can do it anywhere. He is the fountain, and every overflow in his people is only his own fullness running over.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonian churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — were poor and persecuted.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—

For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means. Paul now describes the giving itself, and every phrase removes another of the usual explanations. According to their means: they gave proportionately, which is the normal biblical standard, and already more than most people do. And beyond their means: literally beyond power, past what they could actually afford. They did not calculate what was reasonable and give it. They went over, like the widow who put in two small coins, all she had to live on (Mark 12:41–44). Paul knows this is a large claim, so he inserts himself as a witness: as I can testify. He was there. He watched it happen and he is prepared to swear to it.

Of their own accord. Then the phrase that shuts the last door. “Of their own accord” (authairetoi) means self-chosen, voluntary. Nobody asked them. There was no appeal, no target, no pressure applied by an apostle who wanted the collection to succeed. In fact the pressure ran the other way, which is the astonishing part of the sentence.

Begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints. Read that slowly, because it is the exact reverse of every appeal for money you have ever heard. Paul is not begging them to give. They are begging him to be allowed to. He was evidently reluctant, since one does not take a collection from destitute people, and they pressed him until he agreed. And the word they used for what they were asking is charis again, which the ESV renders favour. They regarded being permitted to give as a privilege granted to them.

Taking part. The word for taking part is koinōnia: fellowship, partnership, having something in common. It is the same word used of the fellowship believers have with the Father and with his Son (1 John 1:3). And “relief” is diakonia, service, ministry. Money given to brothers they would never meet was, to these people, a way of being in fellowship with them, and a ministry in its own right.

Money leaving, or being let in. Set that beside the way giving is usually felt in a church, where the offering is the awkward part of the service and the annual appeal is something to be endured. Somewhere along the line we came to think of giving as money leaving. The Macedonians thought of it as being let in. And it is worth asking what makes a person want that. Not guilt, which produces a payment and then resentment. Not obligation, which produces a calculation. The only thing that produces begging to be allowed to give is having grasped what you have already been given, and Paul is a few verses away from naming it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should give irresponsibly, neglecting their families (1 Timothy 5:8). It means giving should be generous and joyful.

Does this mean Christians should give beyond what they can afford, even into debt? No. Paul reports what the Macedonians did; he does not command it: I say this not as a command (v. 8). The rule he gives is proportion: acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (v. 12); and I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened (v. 13). The Macedonians’ giving was a work of grace in them, and it is meant to stir us, not to shame anyone into borrowing or neglecting his family (1 Timothy 5:8). Sacrifice, yes, gladly; going without some comfort so that others may have bread is exactly what love does. But a gift paid for with a debt you cannot repay, or with your children’s needs, is not what God asks of you.

In a sentence. For Paul testifies that they gave as much as they were able, and even beyond their ability. Entirely on their own, they urgently pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the Lord’s people.

On a Tuesday. Notice your feelings the next time the offering comes round or an appeal arrives. Is it money leaving, or being let in? Ask God to change the feeling, and in the meantime give as one who believes it is a privilege, because it is.

For worship. Before the Macedonians begged to be allowed to give, Someone far greater had asked to give everything. The Son of God was not pressed into our service; he came of his own accord. No one takes my life from me, he said, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). He counted it joy to give, and endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Every glad giver in the church is a small likeness of him, and every privilege of sharing in his work is a gift from his hand.

parallels.desc: the widow gave out of her poverty

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.

And this, not as we expected. Here is the explanation, and it is the key to everything the two chapters say about money. Paul admits he was taken by surprise. He had hoped for something; what happened was of a different order. And when he goes looking for the reason, he does not find it in their circumstances or their temperament.

But they gave themselves first to the Lord. That is the whole thing. Before any money moved, they had handed over the people the money belonged to. The financial gift was not the transaction; it was the receipt. When the heart belongs to the Lord, the purse follows. Giving begins with consecration: present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God (Romans 12:1).

First. Notice the word. It is an order, not a coincidence. And the order explains why so much Christian teaching about money produces so little. We address the wallet directly, with better principles, clearer proportions, a stronger appeal, and it works for about a fortnight, because the wallet was never the problem. A man who has not given himself to God will find reasons not to give his money, and he will find good ones. A man who has given himself has already given everything else; what remains is bookkeeping.

A more searching test. That supplies a test more searching than any percentage. Do not ask first, am I giving enough? Ask, have I given myself? The first question can be answered with a calculation and leaves you exactly where you were. The second cannot be answered with money at all. And there is comfort in this order as well as challenge, because it means the person with almost nothing to give is not at a disadvantage. The Macedonians were destitute. Whatever they put in that bag would have looked unimpressive beside a Corinthian merchant’s contribution. That is not what God was measuring. He had already received the thing he was actually after.

And then by the will of God to us. A second surrender, and it is not an afterthought. Having given themselves to the Lord, they gave themselves to Paul: to the work, to the mission, to the church. The two go together and always have. There is no giving yourself to God in the abstract; it lands on people, and usually on the nearest inconvenient ones. And Paul calls even that the will of God. Their availability to a missionary enterprise whose results they would never see was not mere enthusiasm. It was obedience, and God arranged it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving money can replace giving yourself. God wants you first, and then your gifts. Nor does it mean that a person who has given himself to God need give nothing more; the Macedonians gave themselves and then gave beyond their means.

What does it mean to give myself to the Lord? It means acknowledging that you belong to him, body, time, money, gifts and future, because he bought you (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and telling him so. It happens decisively when you first trust Christ, and then it is renewed again and again, often at the points where something specific is being asked of you. In practice it sounds like a prayer: Lord, I am yours, and so is everything I hold; show me what to do with it. Then it shows itself in plain decisions: the budget, the diary, the use of your home, your willingness to serve where you are needed rather than where you are noticed.

In a sentence. And they went beyond what we expected: they gave themselves first of all to the Lord, and then, by the will of God, to us as well.

On a Tuesday. Before you decide what to give, give yourself again to the Lord. Pray it in words. Then open your bank statement and your diary, and ask honestly whether they look like the possessions of someone who belongs to Christ. Change one thing.

For worship. This is what it looks like when the gospel has actually landed in a person. He does not negotiate about what portion of himself God may have, because that was settled at the start, the day he understood that he is not his own, for he was bought with a price. And the price is the measure of the Buyer’s love. Christ did not give us a portion of himself; he gave himself for us, wholly, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession (Titus 2:14). The surrender he asks is only the answer to the surrender he made.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.

Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started. Having described the Macedonians, Paul turns to the practical arrangement. Titus, who had already begun the collection in Corinth, perhaps on an earlier visit, is being sent back to finish it. The verb urged is parakaleō once more, the word that has run through the whole letter as comfort, and here in its other sense: to appeal, to press someone. Even with a trusted colleague, Paul asks rather than orders.

So he should complete among you this act of grace. In the Greek it is simply this grace, the same word again. The English needs a noun to hang it on and supplies act, but the bare word is the point. The collection for the poor in Jerusalem is charis. God’s grace comes down into a church, and the same word describes it going out again as money to strangers. Grace is not a substance that stops when it reaches you. What God gives, he gives in order that it should keep moving, which is exactly what he said about comfort in chapter 1 and about reconciliation in chapter 5, and now about money.

Complete. Then the word that carries the practical weight of the verse. “Complete” (epiteleō) is the same verb as 7:1, bringing holiness to completion. Titus is to finish what he began. And the reason this is in the letter at all is that the Corinthians had started, enthusiastically, a year earlier, and stopped. There is nothing unusual about that and no need to be hard on them. It is the ordinary shape of religious enthusiasm. The appeal is made, the moment is genuine, the intention is real, and then the weeks pass, other things arrive, the sum that seemed straightforward in the meeting looks larger at the kitchen table, and the thing quietly lapses. Nobody decides against it.

A graveyard of good intentions. This is a good verse to stop at and be honest. What did you begin and not finish? A commitment made at a conference. A monthly amount you meant to set up. A person you said you would visit. A promise made at a graveside. Almost every Christian has a small graveyard of good intentions, and the reason they died is almost never a decision.

A person, not a sharper paragraph. Notice that Paul’s remedy is not a rebuke but a person. He sends Titus. He does not write a sharper paragraph and hope; he puts a man on a boat, because he understands that good intentions do not need more motivation, they need somebody to come and help finish them. That is worth knowing about how churches actually change: exhortation is cheap, and presence is what completes things.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Titus would pressure them. He would help them complete what they wanted to do.

Is it wrong for churches to ask for money or organise giving? No. Paul organised this collection carefully, gave instructions about setting money aside weekly (1 Corinthians 16:2), and sent men to gather it. Asking is right when it is honest about the need, puts Christ’s grace before the appeal, leaves people free to give willingly (9:7), and handles the money openly. What is wrong is manipulation: guilt, pressure, emotional stunts, promises that God will pay back a hundredfold if you give to this ministry, or appeals that hide where the money goes. Paul asks, explains and trusts. He never squeezes.

In a sentence. So we urged Titus, just as he had made a beginning earlier, to bring this act of grace on your part to completion.

On a Tuesday. Pick one unfinished good intention from your own graveyard and finish it this week. If it needs someone alongside you, ask a friend to be your Titus. And pray for those in your church who organise giving and practical care. Thank God for them, and tell them so.

For worship. The God we worship is the God who finishes. He finished the heavens and the earth and rested. His Son, who set his face to go to Jerusalem, did not stop halfway; on the cross he cried, It is finished (John 19:30). And the Spirit who began a good work in us will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). We are a people of half-built towers, and we belong to a Lord who has never left anything of his undone.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.

But as you excel in everything. Paul now names the Corinthian strengths, and he does it generously before he says what is missing. “Excel” (perisseuō) is a word for abundance and overflow. The Corinthians were richly gifted, not lacking in any gift (1 Corinthians 1:5–7). Whatever else was wrong in Corinth, this was a church with real gifts.

In faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you. Anyone who has read the first letter will recognise the list. These were the things the Corinthians prized: they were an articulate, gifted, energetic church that thought rather well of its own understanding. And Paul adds their recent earnestness, the eager repentance of 7:11. He does not sneer at any of it. He says they excel in these things, and he means it. Some manuscripts read your love for us rather than our love for you; the ESV notes this, and either way the bond between apostle and church is the point.

See that you excel in this act of grace also. Then the sentence turns. Generosity is added to the list, placed alongside faith, speech and knowledge as one of the graces a Christian is expected to grow in. That placement is quietly revolutionary, and it ought to change how a church thinks about maturity. We readily accept that a believer should grow in understanding, in prayer, in self-control, in love. We do not usually think of a person as immature in giving in the way we might think of him as immature in patience. Paul does. He treats generosity as a spiritual capacity that can be developed or left undeveloped, and he puts it in the same sentence as faith.

Advanced in everything but this. That raises an uncomfortable and useful question. It is possible to be genuinely advanced in several of these graces and entirely undeveloped in this one. A person can know his Bible thoroughly, speak well about it, be earnest, be warm toward the congregation, and give exactly what he gave ten years ago when he had considerably less. The other graces have grown and this one has not been touched. Notice the verb: see that you excel. It is an imperative with attention in it: look to this, make sure of it. Paul does not expect it to happen by drift, and the Corinthians are the evidence, since drift is precisely what had happened to their collection.

A rich church learning from a poor one. And notice one more thing, easily missed. He is asking a wealthy church to learn something from a destitute one. The Corinthians had every material advantage over Macedonia and were being told to catch up. Gift, eloquence and knowledge do not automatically produce an open hand; if anything they supply better arguments for keeping it shut. What produced it in Macedonia was not resources but grace, and grace is available on the same terms in a prosperous church as in a poor one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is more important than faith. It means it is part of a complete Christian life.

Is generosity a spiritual gift only some Christians have? Paul does list giving among the gifts in Romans 12:8, and some believers are clearly given an unusual capacity and joy in it, as some are given an unusual gift for mercy or teaching. But here he speaks of generosity as a grace every Christian should excel in, just as every Christian is to show mercy even though some have a special gift of it. So do not excuse yourself because you do not feel gifted. Grow in it the way you grow in any grace: by looking at Christ, by asking God for it, and by practising it until it becomes a joy.

In a sentence. But since you excel in everything, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness and in the love we have kindled in you, see that you also excel in this grace of giving.

On a Tuesday. If you are strong in knowledge and faith, ask: am I also strong in generosity? Compare what you give now with what you gave five years ago, alongside what you earn now and what you earned then. If the graces have grown and this one has not, take one deliberate step up this month.

For worship. Every gift the Corinthians boasted of had come from somewhere. What do you have that you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7)? Their faith, their eloquence, their knowledge, their love, were all poured out by the same open-handed God who gives to all generously and without reproach (James 1:5). He is not a God who excels in power and knowledge and is stingy in mercy. In him every perfection overflows together. A generous church is simply a church beginning to look like the Father it belongs to.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.

I say this not as a command. Paul stops and makes something explicit, and the fact that he bothers tells us how carefully he is handling this. He is an apostle. He could order it, and everyone reading knew he could. He declines. The reason is not delicacy about money; it is that a commanded gift would prove nothing and change nobody. He wants a certain kind of giving, and that kind cannot be produced by an instruction. Christian giving must be willing: not reluctantly or under compulsion (9:7).

How much? This is the natural place to answer the question every reader of these two chapters actually has, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a silence: is a Christian required to give a tenth? The honest answer is that the New Testament nowhere commands the tithe of believers, and Paul is the proof. Here he has two entire chapters on giving, the longest treatment of the subject in the New Testament, written to a church that had stalled and needed a clear standard, and he never names a figure. He had every opportunity and every reason to, and he did not. What he gives instead is harder rather than easier. He gives proportion (according to their means, v. 3), readiness (v. 12), cheerfulness (9:7) and one supreme example (v. 9). A fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten; a proportion has to be thought about again every time the circumstances change, and it will not let you stop at ten if you could give forty.

The tenth as a benchmark. None of which makes the tenth useless. Christians who treat it as a floor rather than a ceiling are not being legalistic; they are being sensible, and they have a great deal of Scripture behind the instinct, from Abraham and Jacob before the law onwards (Genesis 14:20; 28:22). But it is a benchmark, not a command, and it must never become the number that tells a rich man he has done enough or a poor man that he has failed.

But to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine. Here is the reason Paul refuses to command. “Prove” (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word: testing metal to see whether it is what it claims to be. And that is what money does. It is one of the most reliable tests of love there is, because it cannot be faked and it costs exactly what it costs. Anyone can say they care about the poor in Jerusalem. Very few things reveal what a person actually values as accurately as where the money goes when nobody is watching, which is why the Lord put it so bluntly: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21). He did not say the heart directs the treasure. He said the treasure shows where the heart already is. So the invitation here is not to be dutiful. It is to find out whether the love is genuine, and Paul is confident enough about them to let the test run. Genuine love gives (1 John 3:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is optional for Christians. It means it must be willing, not forced.

Should my giving go to my local church first? Usually, yes, a regular and substantial part of it. The local church is where you are fed, shepherded and cared for, and Scripture expects those who are taught to share all good things with the one who teaches (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). The weekly setting aside Paul taught was gathered through the churches (1 Corinthians 16:1–2). But this very collection shows that Christian giving also reaches beyond the local congregation, to needy believers elsewhere and to gospel work in other places. A wise pattern is faithful, planned giving to your church, with freedom and joy in giving beyond it as God opens your eyes.

In a sentence. Paul is not commanding you, but testing the sincerity of your love by comparing it with the earnestness of others.

On a Tuesday. Look at last month’s spending as an assayer would. If someone who did not know you read your bank statement, what would they conclude you love? Do not be crushed by the answer; let it lead you to Christ, and then plan your giving for next month deliberately, in proportion, before anything else is spent.

For worship. God has never needed to be commanded to give. Every gift he has given us was given freely, out of love that was genuine to its depths. In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him (1 John 4:9). His love passed every test, and it was proved where it cost most, at the cross. Our giving is not a test that wins his love. It is the glad evidence that his love has reached us.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul has been arguing about a collection. In one sentence he goes to the incarnation, and this is the ground everything else in two chapters has been standing on. You know the grace. He does not introduce it; they have it already, they have experienced it. The whole appeal turns on something they were told the day they believed. The supreme motive for Christian giving is not a need but a Saviour.

That though he was rich. The riches are not metaphorical. This is the Son before Bethlehem, the one who prays to his Father of the glory that I had with you before the world existed (John 17:5), who was in the form of God (Philippians 2:6). He possessed everything, needed nothing, was worshipped without interruption, and had never in eternity known a moment of want. All things were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16). He owned everything.

Yet for your sake he became poor. The verb is decisive and voluntary: he impoverished himself. “Became poor” (ptōcheuō) is built on the word for the beggar, which is not modest means. It is the man with nothing, dependent on what other people put in his hand. And the descent is traceable. He was laid in a manger, born to a family that could afford only the two birds the law allowed the poor to offer (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8). He worked with his hands. As a grown man he said that foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20). He was supported by the means of women who followed him (Luke 8:3). He rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room, and was buried in a borrowed grave. At the very end soldiers divided his clothing, which was all he had, and gambled for the one piece worth keeping (John 19:23–24). He died stripped, owning nothing at all.

The real poverty. And beneath the material poverty lies the deeper one. On the cross he was stripped of the thing that had never been taken from him in all eternity: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matthew 27:46)? That is poverty. That is destitution. The one who had always had the Father’s face bore the Father’s judgment on our sin, and went without the light so that we could stand in it.

So that you by his poverty might become rich. Not so that you might become comfortable. Rich. Forgiven, justified, adopted, indwelt by the Spirit, given a righteousness that is not our own, made heirs of everything, blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places (Ephesians 1:3, 18). All things are yours, he had already told this church (1 Corinthians 3:21). The exchange is exact and it runs in both directions: his poverty for our wealth, as at 5:21 his being made sin was for our becoming the righteousness of God.

Why Paul does not need to command. That is why Paul does not have to command anything. The argument is not merely give, because the Jerusalem church needs it, true as that is. It is: look at what was done for you, and then look at your bank account, and see whether the two can be held in the same mind.

Where Christians differ: what did the Son give up? Some, holding kenotic theories, teach that the Son gave up some of his divine attributes, such as omniscience or omnipotence, when he became man. Verdict: The Son did not stop being God or lose any divine attribute. He became poor by taking a human nature and the humble life and death of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine privileges for himself (Philippians 2:6–8). He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion, change, division or separation (Chalcedonian Definition; Westminster 8.2). His poverty was not a loss of deity but the addition of humanity and the humiliation he willingly bore in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s poverty promises believers material wealth. The riches are spiritual and eternal, as the prosperity gospel forgets. Paul himself, who wrote this verse, was often hungry, thirsty and poorly clothed (11:27), and called himself poor, yet making many rich (6:10).

If Christ became poor, is it wrong for a Christian to be wealthy? Not in itself. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and Scripture never treats having money as sin. But wealth is dangerous: it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom (Matthew 19:23), and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). So Paul tells the rich not to be haughty, not to set their hopes on uncertain riches but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). The question is not how much you have, but whether you hold it as Christ’s, with an open hand, and whether his poverty has made you rich toward others.

In a sentence. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich.

On a Tuesday. Before you next give, read this verse aloud slowly, and then read the account of the cross in one of the Gospels. Do not decide the amount until you have done both. Let the gift come from there.

For worship. End where the verse ends, without applying it. He was rich. He is the one by whom and for whom everything was made, and there was never anything he lacked. He looked at people who had nothing and could give him nothing, and he emptied himself out to the last coin and the last comfort and the last shred of the Father’s face, and he did it, the sentence says, for your sake. There is no accounting for that anywhere in heaven or earth except the word Paul uses for it: grace. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift (9:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.

And in this matter I give my judgment. After the summit of verse 9, Paul comes back to the practical business, and he handles it with great skill. He gives his judgement, not a command. He said in verse 8 he would not order this, and he keeps his word. What he offers is considered counsel from a man they have reason to trust.

This benefits you. A phrase easy to skate over. The advantage is theirs. Paul does not say here that the collection benefits Jerusalem, though obviously it does. He says the giving will do the Corinthians good. That is not sales talk; it is the settled New Testament view that a generous person gains most from his own generosity: it frees him from greed and grows his soul, and the Lord Jesus himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35). A closed hand damages the one it belongs to before it damages anyone else.

Who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. Then he does something worth watching, because it is one of the wisest pastoral moves in the letter. He reminds them what they themselves wanted. The Corinthians were the first to begin and the first to want to (1 Corinthians 16:1–2). Note the order: they did not merely begin the task, they wanted it. The enthusiasm was genuine and it was theirs. But they had stalled, very probably because of the troubles that fill chapters 1 to 7. Paul is not importing a burden from outside; he is handing them back something they laid down. That is a far better instrument than pressure, and it works because it is true. The most powerful motivation available to any of us is not somebody else’s expectation but our own earlier and better intention, recalled gently: you wanted this; you still do; finish it.

So now finish doing it as well. The whole weight of the verse is on completion. Good intentions must become action. And Paul then defines completion with two careful phrases.

So that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it. The desire and the deed are to be the same size. That is the standard, and it is uncomfortably precise: not that you should do great things, but that what you actually do should correspond to what you actually meant. Most of us live with a permanent gap there, and it is the quietest form of self-deception in the Christian life. We feel the intention and count it as though it were the act. We are moved by the appeal and file the feeling as a response. The intention is real; it simply never becomes anything, and after some years a person can have a rich interior life of good desires and very little to show.

Out of what you have. And here is the relief attached to the demand. Not out of what you wish you had, not out of what the Macedonians managed. Out of what is actually in your hand, according to your means and not beyond what you possess. That is the whole requirement, and it is within reach of everyone reading it today.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they had failed completely. It means they needed to follow through.

What if I promised a gift I can no longer afford? Then be honest, with God and with whoever you promised. Paul’s own rule is out of what you have, and circumstances genuinely change: a job is lost, an illness comes, a family need arises. Do not quietly let the promise lapse and hope nobody notices; that is the very drift Paul is correcting. Tell the person or church plainly what has changed, give what you now can, and keep the intention alive for when you are able again. Where a vow can still be kept at cost, keep it (Psalm 15:4). Where it cannot be kept without neglecting your family, God does not ask it.

In a sentence. Here is Paul’s judgement about what is best for you: last year you were the first not only to give but also to want to give. Now finish the work, so that your eager willingness may be matched by your completion of it, according to your means.

On a Tuesday. Is there a generous intention you have not followed through on? Write it down, with the date you first meant it. Then finish it this week, out of what you have. If it is too large now, do the part you can today.

For worship. God’s desire and God’s deed have never once been different sizes. Whatever he purposes, he performs; he says, My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose (Isaiah 46:10). He purposed to save a people, and he sent his Son; he promised a Spirit, and he poured him out. He has never filed a feeling as a response or left a promise lying in a graveyard of intentions. That is why our stalled resolutions need not end in despair. The God who keeps every word he speaks is able to work in us both to will and to work, and to bring our willing to its finish.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.

For if the readiness is there. This is the verse to hand to anyone who has ever felt that his giving is too small to matter. Three things are settled in one sentence. First, willingness comes first. “Readiness” (prothymia) is eagerness, a forward-leaning heart. It is the same order as verse 5, where they gave themselves before they gave anything else. God looks first at the heart, and without a willing heart the sum is beside the point in either direction.

It is acceptable. The word means well received, welcome. Not tolerated. Not graciously overlooked. Welcomed.

According to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. And there is the liberty. The measure is your actual resources: not the giving of the person beside you in the pew, whose circumstances you do not know; not what you could have given had life gone differently; not the figure in the appeal letter. What you have. Sit with how much that removes. A great deal of Christian unhappiness about money is really comparison, and it runs both ways. The person of modest means feels his contribution is negligible beside the large gift that paid for the roof, and quietly concludes that generosity is a rich man’s virtue. The person with more looks at the sacrificial giving of someone with less and cannot work out whether he is doing anything at all. This verse dismantles both, because it makes the measure personal and proportional rather than absolute.

The widow’s two coins. The Lord had already made the point in the most memorable way possible. He sat down opposite the temple treasury and watched people putting money in, large sums from the rich, and then a poor widow put in two small copper coins, the smallest in circulation. He called his disciples over to say that she out of her poverty had put in everything she had, all she had to live on (Mark 12:43–44). The largest gift given that day, by his accounting, was worth less than a penny. Which means the accounting in heaven is not the accounting in the ledger. There will be people at the end who are found to have given more than wealthy benefactors whose names are on buildings, and they will be as surprised as anyone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean willingness is enough without action. Paul has just said: finish it. It means God does not demand the impossible.

I have almost no money. What can I give? Give what you have, however small, gladly; this verse says it is welcomed. And remember that money is only one of the things God has put in your hand. Give your time, your skills, your home, your prayers, your presence with the lonely and the sick. Peter had no silver or gold, and gave what he had (Acts 3:6). The widow who prays faithfully for missionaries every night is investing in the same work as the rich man who funds them. God does not ask you for what you do not have; he asks you for a willing heart and what is actually in your hand.

In a sentence. For if the willingness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.

On a Tuesday. If your gift is small, give it this week without apology, and stop comparing. If your gift is large, ask whether it is large in proportion, or only large in number. Either way, check the readiness first: are you glad to give?

For worship. So if your gift is small, this verse says two things, and neither is a consolation prize. It is acceptable, genuinely welcomed by God and not merely permitted. And it is measured by a standard you can actually meet, which no one else’s giving can raise or lower. Nobody has ever been asked for what he does not have. That is the kindness of a God who sees the heart, who sat opposite the treasury and noticed two copper coins. He accepts the willing gift of the poor as gladly as the rich, because he is not made richer by any of it. He owns the cattle on a thousand hills. What he delights in is the heart that has been made like his own.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.

For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened. Paul now heads off a suspicion before it forms. He is not proposing that the Corinthians be squeezed so that Jerusalem can relax, or that they impoverish themselves for others’ comfort. Eased and burdened: one party comfortable at the other’s expense. That is not the arrangement, and he says so plainly, which tells us somebody in Corinth had probably said it was.

But that as a matter of fairness. The word he uses instead is isotēs: equality, fairness, an even balance. It occurs twice in the sentence, opening and closing it. The aim is that no believer lacks the necessities while others have plenty. Be careful here, because the word has been made to carry a great deal it will not bear. Paul is not proposing that all Christians should hold the same amount, nor that anyone should compel a transfer. Every element of this collection has been voluntary: of their own accord, not as a command, if the readiness is there. Whatever this is, it is not enforced.

Your abundance at the present time should supply their need. Look at the two things he attaches to it. Abundance is surplus, what is over and above need. And at the present time makes it a snapshot rather than a permanent classification. Corinth had more; Jerusalem had less. Neither was guaranteed to be true in five years.

So that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness. Circumstances change; one day the Corinthians may be in need, and others will help them. So the picture is not redistribution but circulation: a body in which resources move to wherever the lack currently is, in whichever direction that happens to be. The church is a family that shares. The aim is not that everyone should have the same but that no one should be in want.

The radical assumption. Notice what lies underneath, which is the genuinely radical part. Paul takes it for granted that a Gentile church in Greece is responsible for Jewish believers in Judea whom they have never met, will never meet, and who differ from them in language, diet, culture and temperament. There is no natural bond there at all. There is only the one thing they have in common, Christ, and Paul treats it as sufficient. That puts a question to any congregation with a surplus. It is easy to feel that the money raised here should stay here: the building needs work, the staff need paying, the local needs are visible and the distant ones are not. Paul’s categories do not let the question be settled locally. If the church is one body, a need in another part of it is not somebody else’s problem being brought to our attention. It is our need, currently being felt somewhere else.

Where Christians differ: Christian sharing and economics. Some use this passage to support enforced redistribution of wealth by the state. Others ignore it. Verdict: Paul is speaking of voluntary giving within the body of Christ, not compulsory state action (v. 8; 9:7). He does not call for absolute equality of possessions, but for generous sharing so that no believer lacks basic needs. Christians remain owners of their goods as stewards, but are called to deep generosity, especially to fellow believers (Acts 4:32–35; Galatians 6:10; 1 John 3:17). Christians may disagree on public policy, but they cannot neglect personal generosity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth is evil or that all Christians must have exactly the same. It means abundance carries responsibility.

Should I help unbelievers in need, or only fellow Christians? Both, with a particular care for believers. Paul’s rule is: as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). This collection was for the household of faith, and a church that neglects its own poor while giving elsewhere has its order wrong (1 Timothy 5:8, 16). But Jesus’ Samaritan helped a stranger, and God sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Christians feed the hungry and care for the vulnerable in their neighbourhood because their Father is kind to all, and such mercy often opens a door for the gospel.

In a sentence. Our desire is not that others might be relieved while you are hard pressed, but that there might be fairness. At the present time your plenty will supply what they need, so that in turn their plenty will supply what you need. The goal is fairness.

On a Tuesday. Look at your abundance, what is genuinely over and above your need and your family’s. Whose need could it meet? Ask your church whether any member is quietly going without, and whether there are believers elsewhere, persecuted or poor, you could help. Then share it, this month, not some day.

For worship. The one body Paul assumes is not a theory but a fact created by the cross. Christ has broken down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile and made one new man in place of two (Ephesians 2:14–15). So a Corinthian’s coins in a Jerusalem widow’s hand are a sermon about the blood that made them family. And the God who arranges our abundance and our need, in turn, is teaching his children to live as he does, from a fullness that is always moving toward the empty.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”

As it is written. Paul reaches for one line of Scripture to settle the whole argument, and it is a surprising choice: a sentence about breakfast in a desert. The quotation is from Exodus 16. Israel is a month out of Egypt, in a wilderness with no food, and God begins sending bread every morning. The instructions are specific: gather what you need for the day, an omer a person, and no more. And then the detail Paul quotes: when they measured it, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack (Exodus 16:18).

Stage it. The picture is what carries the point. Some men were strong and worked fast; some were old, or ill, or had small children slowing them down. They came back to the camp with visibly different amounts in their jars. And when it was measured out, everyone had exactly enough. The industrious man had no surplus to store and the slow man had no shortfall. Effort had made no difference to the outcome at all.

How God provides. Two things follow, and Paul leans on both. First, this is how God provides for his people: sufficiency for each, without regard to capacity. Nobody starved because he was weak, and nobody got ahead because he was quick. That was the arrangement in the wilderness, and Paul says the church is meant to look like it. The difference is only in the mechanism. In Exodus God did it directly with a miracle; in Corinth he does it through the offering. The surplus of the strong ends up meeting the need of the weak either way, and through generous sharing God’s provision reaches everyone.

Manna keeps badly. Second, and it is the sharper point, the man who gathered much never actually owned the surplus. It was not his to keep, and if he tried, as some did, it bred worms and stank by morning (Exodus 16:20). Manna could not be hoarded. It was given daily, for use, and it rotted the moment it was treated as property. That is a very old lesson and it has never stopped being needed. What you have beyond your need was not given to you to store. It is not a reward for having gathered faster; the whole story is designed to disprove that. It is manna, and manna keeps badly. Hold that beside the way most of us actually think about a surplus: as margin, as security, as evidence that things have gone well. Paul, quoting Moses, says the surplus in your jar this morning may have somebody else’s name on it, and that the God who arranged the imbalance did it deliberately, so that his people would become the means of each other’s supply.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there will be no differences in wealth. It means that in God’s family, no one should be left in need.

Is saving for the future, or for retirement, hoarding? Not necessarily. Scripture commends the ant that stores in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), Joseph who stored grain for the famine, and the person who provides for his household (1 Timothy 5:8); leaving an inheritance is called good (Proverbs 13:22). Hoarding is different. It is keeping more and more out of fear or greed, trusting the stockpile rather than God, while needs around you go unmet. Jesus’ rich fool built bigger barns and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). So save wisely and modestly for real responsibilities, give generously as you go, and ask regularly whether your savings serve love or have become your security.

In a sentence. As it is written: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little.”

On a Tuesday. Look at what you are storing: money, possessions, food, clothes, things in the loft. Ask what in it is real provision and what is fear. Give away one thing this week that you are keeping only in case. Thank God for his daily provision, and trust him enough to share rather than hoard.

For worship. The manna was never the point. The Lord Jesus said: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35). Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and died; he is the living bread that came down from heaven, and he gave his flesh for the life of the world. In him no one who gathers little goes without, and no one who gathers much has anything to boast of. Every believer has exactly the same portion: the whole of Christ. The God who fed a whole nation every morning for forty years has not changed, and he still gives his children their daily bread.
