verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for Titus’s eagerness to return to Corinth and introduces two companions: a brother well known among the churches for his gospel work and chosen by the churches to travel with the gift, and another brother proven in many tests. The arrangement is deliberate. Paul wants the handling of the money to be honourable not only before the Lord but in the eyes of people, so that no one can accuse him. He commends these representatives of the churches and asks the Corinthians to show them openly the love that Paul has boasted of.
verseByVerse.theology: The principle of handling ministry finances with transparent accountability applies directly to all Christian organisations. Paul, who could have simply trusted his own integrity, insists on multiple overseers and transparent processes — because the integrity of the ministry is at stake not only in God’s sight but in the sight of the watching world. Financial scandal in Christian ministry has consistently damaged the gospel’s credibility; Paul’s precaution (v. 20) is prophylactic wisdom.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission organisation implements a new policy requiring two-signature approval for all expenditures over a certain threshold, and annual independent financial audits reported to the whole organisation. Some staff feel this implies distrust. This passage gives the theological rationale: the precautions are not about distrust of individuals but about protecting the honour of the Lord and the integrity of the ministry in the sight of those who would use any irregularity to attack the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.

But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. The argument about money pauses, and Paul does something small and very characteristic: he thanks God for a person. And notice exactly what he thanks him for. Not that Titus agreed to go, but that God put into the heart of Titus the same care Paul had. He traces a colleague’s affection back past the colleague to its source. Good desires in our hearts come from God, who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

A habit worth having. That is worth pausing on, because it is a habit most of us do not have. When someone shows us real kindness we thank them, which is right. Paul thanks God, because he assumes that the love one Christian has for another did not originate in that Christian. Somebody put it there. Which has a practical use. Think of the person who has stood by you: the friend who kept turning up, the older believer who prayed for you for years, whoever it was that noticed. You have probably thanked them. Have you thanked God for the fact that they wanted to? That is not sentimentality; it is accuracy about where affection comes from.

For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord. Verse 17 is finely balanced. Both halves are true at once. Paul asked him, there was a genuine appeal, and Titus accepted it. And he was already going anyway, of his own accord, out of his own eagerness. The request did not create the willingness; it met it. God’s will and Titus’s own desire coincided.

Of his own accord. The phrase is the same one used of the Macedonians in verse 3, and its reappearance is not accidental. Everything in this chapter that God is doing, he is doing through people who chose it freely and would tell you it was their own idea. Both things are said in the same paragraph without embarrassment: God put it in his heart, and he is going of his own accord. That is the ordinary pattern of the Christian life, and it is a great relief to see it stated so plainly. You are not a passenger. Nothing in this passage suggests Titus was moved about like a piece on a board; he was eager, and the eagerness was his. And behind it, quietly, was Someone who had arranged it, which is why the paragraph opens with thanks rather than congratulation.

What Titus was eager about. Notice, finally, what it was. Not a preaching tour. He was volunteering to go and organise a collection in a church that had been difficult, and to handle other people’s money in a situation where he could easily be accused. That is the kind of enthusiasm only God puts in a heart.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Titus had no choice. God worked in his heart, and he freely chose. God’s sovereign work in us does not cancel our willing; it creates it.

How do I know whether a desire to serve comes from God? Test it by Scripture first: God never moves anyone to do what his word forbids. Then ask whether it fits the gifts and opportunities God has given you, whether it is aimed at others’ good and Christ’s glory rather than your own name, and whether mature believers who know you confirm it. Titus’s desire matched Paul’s appeal; inward desire and outward call agreed. You do not need a voice or a sign. A good desire, tested by the word and confirmed by the church, is very often God’s way of leading. Act on it, and thank him for it.

In a sentence. Thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same concern Paul has for you. For Titus not only welcomed our appeal, but he is coming to you with much enthusiasm and on his own initiative.

On a Tuesday. Thank God by name for one person whose love has carried you, and thank him that they wanted to. Then thank the person too. And think of one good desire God has put in your own heart that you have not acted on. Test it, and take the first step.

For worship. Every Titus in the church is a gift from the same hand. The Lord of the harvest sends out labourers into his harvest (Matthew 9:38), and he does it not by conscription but by giving them his own heart for his people. The care Titus felt for Corinth was a small share of the care of the Good Shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. When anyone loves us in Christ, it is Christ’s love reaching us through him, and the thanks belongs first to God.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.

With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. A second man joins the party, and Paul does not tell us his name. The guesses have been made for nineteen centuries: some early writers guessed Luke, because he was with Paul and wrote a Gospel; others Barnabas, Silas or Apollos. There is no way to decide, and the anonymity may well be deliberate. This is a letter about money that will be read aloud across the province; naming the man who is coming to collect it would make him a figure rather than a servant, and might look like Paul commending his own choice.

Famous for the gospel. What we are told about him is two things, and they are the two things that matter. First, he is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel: a man of real standing, known everywhere, whose reputation was made in gospel ministry and not in administration. And he is being sent to help carry a bag of money to Jerusalem, a journey of many weeks. There is a quiet rebuke to a certain kind of ministry ambition in that. Nobody is too senior for the practical work. One of the best-known preachers around the Aegean is spending months of his life as a courier and an auditor, because the money has to be handled properly and somebody trustworthy has to do it.

And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us. Then the crucial detail. “Appointed” (cheirotoneō) originally meant to stretch out the hand, to elect by show of hands. He was not chosen by Paul. The congregations themselves selected him as their representative, and he answers to them. Paul is building a structure here, and he is building it deliberately: several men, chosen by the givers, travelling with the gift. He who could have said with complete honesty that his own integrity was sufficient arranges things so that it does not have to be taken on trust.

For the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will. Then the aim of the whole exercise, and it lifts the accounting into another register. A collection for hungry believers, carefully audited and honestly delivered, is done for the glory of the Lord, and shows the eagerness of all involved. That is worth saying to everyone who has ever felt that the practical end of church life is the unspiritual end: the treasurer, the person who counts the offering, the one who checks the invoices and is never thanked. Paul puts that work and the glory of God in the same sentence, because a church whose money is handled honestly is telling the truth about its God, and one whose money is handled loosely is telling a lie about him with every receipt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean his name is important for us to know. God knows him; that is enough.

Does it matter if my service is never noticed or remembered? Not to God, and that is the only audience that finally counts. This brother was famous in his day and is nameless now, and his work still stands in the record of Scripture. Your Father sees in secret and will reward you (Matthew 6:4). Many of the most important people in your church are those you never hear about: the woman who prays, the man who fixes the boiler, the couple who have quietly helped the same struggling family for years. Serve for Christ’s glory, not for recognition, and trust that nothing done for him is forgotten (Hebrews 6:10).

In a sentence. And we are sending along with him the brother who is praised by all the churches for his service to the gospel. What is more, he was chosen by the churches to accompany us as we carry this gift, which we administer to honour the Lord himself and to show our eagerness to help.

On a Tuesday. Thank someone this week who does practical, unseen work in your church, and tell them it matters to the glory of God. If you are one of them, do it again this week as worship.

For worship. Most of God’s best workers are unknown to history, and he likes it that way, because it leaves the glory where it belongs. The Lord who knows the names of all the stars knows the name of this brother, and has written it in the book of life (Philippians 4:3). He who made himself of no reputation, and took the form of a servant, is not ashamed to be served by couriers and auditors. On the last day he will name every one of them, and the unnamed brother will hear his own name spoken by the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.note: The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.

We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us. Here is the reason for all the arrangements, stated flatly, and it is one of the most practically useful principles in the New Testament. The verb means to find fault, to bring a charge. Paul’s critics might accuse him of stealing from the collection, as some evidently did suggest that he was crafty and took them in by deceit (12:16–18). So he has independent, church-appointed men travel with the money. And notice the timing. He is taking precautions against an accusation that has not yet been made, about a sum of money that has not yet been collected. He is not responding to a scandal. He is arranging matters so that a scandal cannot be manufactured, which is the only time such arrangements can be made, since after the accusation they always look like a reaction.

For we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man. The principle comes from Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek Old Testament. Two audiences, and both are taken seriously. The first is obvious, and it is where Christians usually stop. God sees; my conscience is clear; he knows my motives. All true. And Paul says it is not enough. The second audience is the watching world, which cannot see motives and must judge by arrangements. Here is the point so many sincere people miss: it is not sufficient to be honest. Where other people’s money is concerned, you must be visibly, checkably honest, in a way that does not depend on anyone believing you.

When oversight feels like an insult. This cuts against a common and rather pious instinct. A man of genuine integrity finds oversight faintly insulting: the second signature, the audit, the receipts, the rule that he may not authorise his own expenses. It feels like being suspected. Paul, whose integrity nobody should have doubted, built the structure himself and volunteered for it, and he did it precisely because he was trustworthy. It was not about him. The reputation of a ministry is not the private property of the person carrying it. It belongs to the gospel. And few things in modern times have damaged the credibility of the church in ordinary people’s eyes as reliably as money: the ministry whose accounts nobody sees, the appeal that funded a lifestyle, the collapse that made the news and gave a great many people a reason never to listen again. Every one of those started with someone who did not think the precautions applied to him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean reputation matters more than integrity. Integrity comes first, and transparency shows it.

How should I choose a ministry or charity to give to? Look for what Paul built here. Is the money handled by more than one person, with independent oversight and accounts that are open to givers? Is the work faithful to the gospel and doing what it says it does? Are the leaders known, accountable to a church, and living modestly rather than lavishly? Does the appeal tell the truth, without pressure or promises of guaranteed return? Give first to what you know well, your own church and workers it sends, and then to others you have checked. A ministry that bristles at reasonable questions about money has answered them.

In a sentence. We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. For we are taking pains to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of people.

On a Tuesday. In handling money, at church or work, be transparent. Two people count the offering. Nobody handles a fund alone. The accounts are open to the members. The person who decides the spending is not the person who signs the payment. None of it implies distrust; all of it removes a stumbling block from the road (6:3). If you hold any money that is not your own, ask today whether someone else can see what you do with it.

For worship. Behind Paul’s care is the character of the God he served. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). He does nothing in a corner; his ways are open, his word is true, and his dealings with us can bear every scrutiny. The Lord Jesus could ask his enemies, Which one of you convicts me of sin (John 8:46)? and no one could. A church that handles money in the light is reflecting its Master, the only treasurer in history who never once took what was not his, and who gave away all that was.

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.

And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters. A third man, also unnamed, and the way Paul describes him is worth attention. He does not say the man is gifted or well known. He says he has been often tested and found earnest in many matters. That is a reputation built slowly, in a series of small situations, over years. Somebody kept giving him things to do and he kept doing them. That is how trust is actually acquired, and it is worth saying in a church culture that tends to be impressed by the newly arrived and the obviously able. The man Paul will trust with a large sum is the man who has been reliable in a lot of unremarkable matters, and the reliability was shown before the responsibility was given, not after. One who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10).

But who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. Titus went to Corinth and came back with a good report, and it has evidently made an impression on this man, who now believes in the Corinthians and wants to go himself. A church that comes right does not merely settle its own trouble; it energises people who have only heard about it.

As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. Paul introduces the three men formally, and the titles rise as he goes. “Partner” is koinōnos, the man who shares the enterprise; not an assistant but a colleague with a stake in it. “Fellow worker” is synergos, one who labours alongside.

And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches. The ESV notes that messengers is literally apostles: apostoloi, sent ones. They are men formally commissioned and sent by the churches as their delegates, carrying their authority. They are not apostles of Christ like the Twelve and Paul, who were sent by the risen Lord himself, but representatives sent on a mission.

The glory of Christ. Then the last phrase, dropped in without explanation, and it is the largest thing in the verse. Of these men, one unnamed, one described only as reliable, both currently employed as couriers of a charitable fund, Paul says that they are the glory of Christ. That is what he calls them. Not only that they bring glory to Christ, though they do. They are his glory. It is the same astonishing claim as chapter 3, where the Corinthians were a letter from Christ, and chapter 4, where the treasure is in jars of clay. Christ has arranged that his glory in this world should be visible in people: in ordinary, unnamed, tested, faithful people carrying out unglamorous work for churches. He is not ashamed of the arrangement. He chose it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these men held the apostolic office. The word is used in its general sense, sent ones. The apostles of Christ laid the foundation once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and there are none today; but every church still sends and receives trusted messengers.

How can an ordinary Christian be the glory of Christ? Because the glory of Christ is seen wherever his character is reproduced, and it is most clearly seen in faithfulness that nobody applauds. When a believer keeps his word, handles money honestly, serves without being noticed and loves a difficult church, people see something of the Lord who did all those things perfectly. We are being transformed into his image from one degree of glory to another (3:18). You do not have to be gifted or famous to display him. You have to be his, and faithful in what he gives you to do.

In a sentence. In addition, we are sending with them our brother who has often proved to us in many ways that he is zealous, and now even more so because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is Paul’s partner and co-worker among you; as for our brothers, they are representatives of the churches and an honour to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of a small, unremarkable responsibility you have been given, and do it faithfully this week as if it were the glory of Christ, because it is. If you lead in a church, look for the tested and reliable, not only the impressive, when you hand out trust.

For worship. Thank God for faithful co-workers in his kingdom. The Lord Jesus, who is the radiance of the glory of God (Hebrews 1:3), has chosen to let that glory shine through couriers, treasurers and nameless brothers. He does not borrow glory from them; he lends his glory to them. And on the day when he comes to be glorified in his saints and marvelled at among all who have believed (2 Thessalonians 1:10), the world will finally see what Paul saw in two men on a road to Corinth.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles” — men sent by the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.

So give proof before the churches of your love. The chapter ends with a single instruction, and after everything that has gone before it is almost startling in its directness. Give proof. The word means to demonstrate, to show the reality of a thing. Paul has spent twenty-three verses on grace, on the Macedonians, on Christ becoming poor, on readiness and proportion and transparency. And it comes down to this: when the three men arrive, put something in the bag. That is not a descent from the theological heights. It is where the theological heights were always going. This is a letter, not a lecture, and the love that has been discussed has to be shown to actual people arriving on an actual day.

Proof of your love. Back to verse 8, where the point of the exercise was to prove whether their love was genuine. Love that cannot be demonstrated has not yet been shown to exist. John put it as bluntly as it can be put: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth (1 John 3:17–18).

And of our boasting about you to these men. There it is again, the thing Paul has been risking all through these chapters. He has told the Macedonians that Corinth would come through (9:2 will say so explicitly). He told Titus they were a good people and was not put to shame (7:14). Now he tells them in writing that his reputation is attached to what they do next. He could have kept that quiet. Instead he says it out loud, which is either reckless or a deliberate act of trust, and given how carefully he has handled everything else in this chapter, it is plainly the second. He is telling them: I have vouched for you. That is a form of love, and it makes a demand precisely because it was given before it was earned.

Before the churches. The demonstration is public. Other congregations are watching, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. So the chapter closes where it opened, with churches looking at each other and being stirred to something better. It began with Macedonia’s example held up to Corinth; it ends with Corinth’s response held up to everyone. That is not manipulation. It is the ordinary way God has always spread generosity through his people, one congregation catching it from another, let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works (Hebrews 10:24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving for show. It means letting genuine love be seen.

Doesn’t Jesus tell us to give in secret? Yes, and both teachings stand. Jesus forbids giving in order to be seen and praised by others, sounding a trumpet before you like the hypocrites (Matthew 6:1–4). That is about motive: do not give to win applause. But the same Lord says, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father (Matthew 5:16). Paul is not asking the Corinthians to parade individual gifts; the collection was a church’s gift, and its proof was to be seen so that God would be thanked (9:12–13). So keep your own giving quiet, and let your church’s love be visible for God’s glory.

In a sentence. Therefore show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our pride in you, so that the churches can see it.

On a Tuesday. Let your love be visible in action, especially in welcoming and supporting those who serve. When visiting workers or missionaries come to your church, give them a meal, a bed, a gift and your attention. And if someone has vouched for you, live so that they are not put to shame.

For worship. Every church that has ever caught generosity from another has caught it, in the end, from a Lord who was rich and became poor for their sake. He gave proof of his love before the whole universe, not in word or talk but on a cross, in deed and in truth. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). And he too has vouched for us, before his Father and the holy angels, confessing as his own a people who had given him every reason to be ashamed. His boast will not be put to shame.

9.title: Sowing Generously: The Cheerful Giver
9.overview:
Paul continues on the collection for Jerusalem. He has boasted to the Macedonians that Corinth was ready a year ago, and their eagerness stirred the Macedonians to give. Now he is sending the brothers ahead so that the Corinthian gift is ready when he arrives with Macedonian companions, as a willing gift and not something extracted under pressure.

Then he gives the principles of Christian giving. A farmer who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make every grace overflow, so that his people always have enough and plenty left for every good work; he supplies seed to the sower and will multiply it, enriching them so that they can be generous in every way. And the result goes far beyond meeting needs in Jerusalem: it overflows in thanksgiving to God, proves the Gentiles’ obedience to the gospel, and binds Jewish believers to them in prayer and love. The chapter ends with praise for the gift behind every gift: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Sowing and Reaping; the Cheerful Giver; the Inexpressible Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he hardly needs to write about the collection, since he has boasted of Corinth’s readiness to the Macedonians and it has spurred them on. He is sending the brothers ahead so that the gift is ready when he arrives with Macedonian companions, and is a generous gift rather than something extracted. Then come the principles. Giving is like sowing: the harvest matches the sowing. Each should give what they have decided in their heart, willingly, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply everything needed and more, so that his people can be generous in every good work; he provides seed and will multiply it. The gift will meet needs in Jerusalem, but it will also overflow in thanks to God, prove the Corinthians’ faith, and draw the Jerusalem believers to pray for them. Paul ends by thanking God for his gift, too great for words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sowing-reaping principle in v. 6 must be held in tension with the warning against prosperity theology, and the passage itself supplies the correction three times over. Paul is not promising that generous financial giving will result in financial wealth. The reaping he describes is named in v. 10 as “the harvest of your righteousness” — moral integrity and fruitfulness in God’s sight. The supply God gives in that same verse is “seed to the sower and bread for food” — resources to live on and resources to give again — and it is the seed, not the bread, that he undertakes to multiply. Verse 11 then adds that the enriching is “to be generous in every way.” The giver is not made wealthy; he is kept supplied so that generosity can continue. The decisive counter-example is in the previous chapter: the man held up as the supreme giver at 8:9 became poor.

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9. The psalm is a portrait of the man who fears the LORD, and it places distributing freely and giving to the poor among his identifying marks, alongside steadiness and courage — generosity as a feature of godliness rather than an optional extra of temperament. The clause Paul is after is “his righteousness endures forever”: the money is gone and cannot be pointed to, and what it produced does not go anywhere.

“God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7) comes from the Greek Old Testament at Proverbs 22:8, which carries a line the Hebrew text does not — a blessing on the cheerful and generous man. Paul’s citation focuses the divine pleasure on the disposition of the giver: the motivation and the manner of giving are as important to God as the amount.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation uses a pledge campaign with carefully designed giving targets and social dynamics (recognising top givers, publishing goals) that effectively apply social pressure to giving. Many give generously as a result. But the pastor wonders whether the giving is cheerful or compelled. This passage challenges not the amount raised but the mechanism: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (v. 7). The goal is not merely generous giving but the formation of cheerful givers — people who give because they have been gripped by the inexpressible gift of God and cannot hold back.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 9 continues the appeal about the collection. Paul first explains why he is sending the brothers ahead: so that the gift the Corinthians promised will be ready when he arrives with Macedonians, and will be a willing gift, not something squeezed out (vv. 1–5). Then he gives the principles of generous giving: whoever sows generously reaps generously; each should give as he has decided, not reluctantly or under pressure, for God loves a cheerful giver; and God is able to make all grace abound so that his people always have enough for every good work (vv. 6–11). Finally, he shows the wider results of giving: it meets needs, it overflows in thanksgiving to God, it proves the reality of the Corinthians’ confession of the gospel, and it binds Jewish and Gentile believers together in prayer and love. And he ends with praise for God’s inexpressible gift, Christ himself (vv. 12–15). Two chapters of timetables and delegates finish in an exclamation of worship.

Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints. Paul has just spent a chapter on the collection, and he opens the next by saying there is no need to write about it. The touch is light and entirely deliberate. Superfluous means unnecessary, surplus to requirements. It is a courtesy, and everyone knew it, since he is about to write fourteen more verses on the subject. But the courtesy is not empty. He is telling them that he is not addressing a delinquent church. He is addressing people whose willingness he takes for granted and whose reputation he has already staked. “Ministry” is diakonia, service: the money is a service to the saints.

For I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia. Then the disclosure. He has been going round northern Greece telling the poorest churches in the region that Achaia was ready a year ago. Achaia was southern Greece, the province with Corinth as its capital; Macedonia was the north. And notice the remarkable circularity of what has been happening. In chapter 8 the Macedonian example was held up to stir Corinth into action. Now we learn that the Corinthian example stirred the Macedonians in the first place. Each church has been provoked by the other, and Paul has been carrying the news back and forth between them.

Not manipulation. It is worth saying why. He has not told either church anything untrue. The Corinthians really had begun eagerly; the Macedonians really did give beyond their means. He is simply refusing to let two congregations far apart remain ignorant of what God is doing in the other, and the result is that each catches something from the other.

And your zeal has stirred up most of them. The word is zeal: heat, intensity. And the verb is that it stirred up most of them. Enthusiasm turns out to be contagious across provinces. That is a reason for churches to talk to one another, and for the report from another congregation to be treated as more than a slot in the notices. A church quietly convinced that giving on any serious scale is unrealistic will go on believing it indefinitely if it never hears what a poorer church down the road has just done. The single most effective thing Paul does in these two chapters is carry news.

Somebody is watching. There is a quieter warning in it too. Your church’s giving, or your own, is not a private matter with no downstream effects. Somebody is watching, and what they see either enlarges what they think possible or confirms them in what they already assumed. The Corinthians had stirred up a whole province without knowing it, a year before this letter, and would have gone on not knowing, had Paul not told them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was manipulating them. He spoke honestly of both churches.

Is it healthy for churches to compare themselves with one another? It depends on what the comparison is for. Comparing in order to feel superior, or to compete for reputation, is pride, and Paul condemns it a chapter later (10:12). But telling one church what God is doing in another, so that both thank God and are stirred to love and good works, is exactly what Paul is doing here (Hebrews 10:24). The test is whether the comparison ends in praise of God and fresh obedience, or in boasting and envy. Hear reports of other churches gladly, pray for them, learn from them, and never use them as a weapon.

In a sentence. There is no need for Paul to write to you about this service to the Lord’s people. For he knows your eagerness to help, and he has been boasting about it to the Macedonians, telling them that since last year you in Achaia were ready to give; and your enthusiasm has stirred most of them to action.

On a Tuesday. Your generosity can inspire others. Let it be seen, humbly, for God’s glory. Pass on one good report this week of what God is doing in another church or another believer, and let it stir you as well as them.

For worship. Behind the news Paul carried between Macedonia and Achaia is the God who delights to make his works known. The heavens declare his glory, and the church does too, one congregation telling another of his grace. He is not a God who works in secret and keeps his kindness quiet; he means his people to see what he is doing and to catch fire from one another. Every report of grace is an invitation to praise the one who gives it, and the zeal that leapt from Corinth to Macedonia was the Spirit himself moving through his church.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth; Macedonia was to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.

But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter. Having said it was superfluous to write, Paul now says exactly why he is writing, and he is remarkably candid about it. The brothers are the three men of 8:16–24. So that our boasting about you may not prove empty: he has made a claim in public and he does not want to be found to have overstated it. That is a plain admission of self-interest, and its plainness is part of the honesty.

So that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Good intentions need preparation. Titus and the brothers are being sent in advance so that the money is collected before Paul arrives with a Macedonian delegation.

Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated, to say nothing of you, for being so confident. Look at the order of the concern. He names his own embarrassment first and theirs as an aside. He could have led with theirs, which would have applied more pressure; he does not. And the little parenthesis is generous rather than pointed, the sort of thing said quickly and moved past. It is honest pastoral motivation.

What he is avoiding. Consider the scene he is preventing. If nothing has been gathered when he walks in with visitors, there will be an appeal on the spot, in the room, with witnesses present, and money will be produced; of course it will. And every coin of it will have been given under social pressure, in front of an apostle, to avoid a humiliation. It would have looked like generosity and been nothing of the kind. So Paul builds the timetable specifically to remove the pressure he could most easily have used. He is an apostle with a Macedonian audience and a year-old promise; he holds every card, and he arranges not to play them.

The technique of the moment. Set that beside how appeals are often run. The emotional peak, the visiting speaker, the pledge cards handed round while the feeling is high, the totals announced from the front, the giving made visible: it works, in the sense that it produces money. Paul’s judgement is that it produces the wrong thing, and he says so in the next verse.

Belief and structure. There is also something here about believing in people and providing for them. Paul genuinely expects the Corinthians to come through; he has said so publicly. And he does not simply expect it and wait. He sends three men and a timetable, because good intentions need infrastructure, and the leader who believes the best about people and gives them nothing to act on has left the believing half undone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they should give to avoid shame. It means they should follow through on what they promised.

Is it wrong to make a pledge or promise to give? No. The Corinthians had promised this gift (v. 5), and Paul expected them to keep their word. A pledge freely made, after prayer and with the figures in front of you, can be a wise way to plan and to help a church plan. What is wrong is a pledge squeezed out under pressure, or one made in a moment of feeling without thought. Once you have freely promised, keep it if you can, as you would any promise (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). If circumstances truly change, say so honestly rather than letting it quietly lapse.

In a sentence. But Paul is sending the brothers so that our boasting about you in this matter will not prove hollow, but that you may be ready, as he said you would be. For if any Macedonians come with him and find you unprepared, we, not to mention you, would be ashamed of having been so confident.

On a Tuesday. If you lead in a church, check whether your ways of raising money depend on pressure in the room. Give people notice, time and privacy instead. And if you have made a commitment to give, look at it today and make sure it is ready.

For worship. Ask God to help you keep your commitments, including your commitments to give, and rest in the faithfulness of the one who has never left a promise unready. Our God has never needed an appeal on the spot to produce his gifts. He planned our salvation before the foundation of the world, prepared it through the centuries, and gave it in the fullness of time, exactly as he said he would. He holds every card and plays none of them to manipulate us. He woos, he waits, he gives notice, and he makes us willing in the day of his power (Psalm 110:3). His boasting about his people will never prove empty.

verseByVerse.quote: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.

So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you. Here is the reason for all the arranging, and it turns on two words held deliberately apart. The brothers are to go ahead and prepare, so that the gift you have promised is gathered in advance.

And arrange in advance for the gift you have promised. A willing gift is, in the Greek, a blessing: eulogia, the word that gives us eulogy, meaning a good word spoken, and by extension a benefit freely bestowed. That is what Paul wants the money to be: a blessing, given as blessings are given, a blessing to others.

So that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction. “Exaction” is pleonexia: greed, covetousness, the grasping that takes what is not freely offered, something extracted. It is a hard word, and Paul uses it of what the collection would become if it were squeezed out rather than given. The related verb turned up at 2:11 of Satan getting the better of someone, and at 7:2 of taking advantage. So the same sum of money, arriving in the same bag on the same day, is either a blessing or a shakedown, and the difference is not in the amount. It is in whether it was freely given. If it is collected at the last minute under pressure, it will feel extracted, and it will be.

How compulsion works. That should land on how churches actually raise money, because the mechanisms that produce compulsion are rarely crude. Nobody is threatened. But there is the giving made visible so that the level is known; the target announced with a thermometer on the wall; the appeal placed at the emotional peak of a meeting; the pledge card passed along a row where everyone can see who is filling one in; the quiet awareness that the treasurer knows. All of these work. All of them shift the reason a person gives from what is in his heart to what the room expects. Paul’s instinct is to build the structure that makes freedom possible: give people notice, give them time, let them decide at home, and arrange to be absent while they do it. That is what arrange in advance means here. He is not making it easier to give; he is making it possible to give freely.

What Paul assumes about God. Notice what lies behind all this. He is prepared to risk a smaller collection in order to have a genuine one. He evidently does not believe that God needs the money badly enough to accept it on any terms, which is exactly right, since the whole letter has been saying that the God in question owns everything and his Son became poor on purpose.

What it does not mean. It does not mean planned giving is less spiritual. Planning makes giving free and generous.

How do I actually plan my giving? Sit down, preferably with your husband or wife, with your income and commitments in front of you, and pray. Decide a proportion of what comes in that you will give regularly, first, before other spending, as the firstfruits rather than the leftovers (Proverbs 3:9). Set it up so that it happens without needing to be remembered. Keep a further amount aside for needs that arise during the year, so that you can respond freely when God puts someone in front of you. Review it whenever your income changes, or at least once a year, and ask whether the proportion should rise. Then give it gladly, and forget about it.

In a sentence. So Paul thought it necessary to urge the brothers to visit you in advance and finish the arrangements for the generous gift you promised. Then it will be ready as a generous gift, not as one grudgingly given.

On a Tuesday. Before you give next, know which sentence you are answering: I want to, or I would look bad if I did not. The second is not wicked, and God is not standing over anybody with a stopwatch. But Paul has gone to considerable trouble here to make sure the Corinthians could answer the first, and so can you. Plan your giving ahead, so that it is generous and willing, not last minute and reluctant.

For worship. The whole gospel is a blessing and never an exaction. God did not extract our salvation from himself reluctantly, under pressure of our need. He has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3), freely, gladly, according to the purpose of his will. And he has never squeezed anything out of us. He gives first, and keeps giving, until our hearts open of their own accord. A God who could command everything chose to be loved by willing hearts, and that is why the gift he wants from us is a blessing too.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. Now the principle, drawn from the one place everybody in the ancient world understood. It is a farming proverb, and Scripture uses it often: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer (Proverbs 11:24–25; 22:9; Galatians 6:7). A farmer who plants few seeds harvests little.

Stage it. A farmer walks out in autumn with a bag of seed and a decision to make, and the decision is genuinely painful, because the seed in that bag is food. He could eat it. His family can see it. And what he is being asked to do is throw it on the ground and cover it up, where it will do nobody any good for months. The more he keeps back to eat, the less goes into the ground, and the less comes up in the spring. Everyone who farms knows this, and it never stops being hard, because the eating is now and the harvest is later. Giving works the same way, Paul says. What you release is not lost; it is planted. And the size of what comes back corresponds to what went in.

And whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. “Bountifully” is literally with blessings, the same word as verse 5. Generous sowing brings a generous harvest. And the harvest is described in the verses that follow: God’s abundant grace, the means to keep giving, righteousness, thanksgiving to God, and the love and prayers of others (vv. 8–14).

Handle with care. This verse must be handled carefully, because it has been made the foundation of one of the ugliest distortions of Christianity there is. The prosperity teacher quotes it and stops: sow generously into this ministry and God will return it to you multiplied, and the more you give the wealthier you will become. Money is thereby extracted from poor people by a promise God has not made, using a verse from a passage whose entire concern is that giving must not be extracted. Three things in the passage itself take that reading apart, and none of them requires going outside the chapter. First, look at what Paul actually says the harvest is. Verse 10 calls it the harvest of your righteousness. Verse 11 says you are enriched to be generous. Verse 12 says the yield is thanksgivings to God. The crop, named three times, is righteousness, further generosity and worship. Second, the supply in verse 10 is seed to the sower and bread for food: enough to live on and enough to give again. That is provision for a farmer, not a fortune. Third, and most decisively, the one Paul has just held up as the supreme example of generosity in 8:9 became poor. If sowing bountifully guaranteed material return, the Lord Jesus Christ is the counter-example, and so is Paul, who knew hunger and thirst, often without food (11:27).

Where Christians differ: the prosperity gospel and seed faith. Some teach that if you give money to God, often to a particular ministry, he will return far more money to you, so that giving is an investment for personal wealth. Verdict: Paul does promise that God rewards generosity. But the harvest is mainly spiritual: grace, righteousness, thanksgiving, and the means to be generous again (vv. 8, 10–11). God supplies enough for every good work, not luxury. Giving in order to get is the opposite of the cheerful, self-forgetting generosity Paul describes. Christ became poor to make us rich spiritually (8:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never blesses materially. He supplies our needs (Philippians 4:19). But giving is not a scheme for wealth.

Will God reward me for giving? Yes, and you are allowed to want the reward. Jesus himself said your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4), and told us to lay up treasure in heaven. The rewards are real: joy now, a deeper likeness to Christ, the thanks of those helped, the knowledge that nothing given for him is wasted, and treasure kept for the age to come (Luke 12:33; 1 Timothy 6:18–19). What you must not do is treat God as an investment fund, giving a hundred so that he owes you a thousand. That is not sowing; it is gambling with God’s name on it. Give because he has given, and leave the harvest to him.

A friend of mine follows prosperity teaching. What should I say? Begin with what is true in it: God is generous, he does reward giving, and he cares about our needs. Then open the Bible together at this chapter and ask what the harvest is in verses 8 to 12. Look at 8:9 and ask why, if giving guarantees wealth, Jesus and Paul were poor. Read 1 Timothy 6:5–10, where Paul warns against those who imagine godliness is a means of gain. Be gentle; many who are drawn to this teaching are poor or desperate, and have been exploited. Point them to the riches that cannot be taken away, and help them practically if they have given away what they needed.

In a sentence. Remember this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.

On a Tuesday. The only question the verse puts is the farmer’s question, and it is a hard one every autumn: how much are you willing to put out of your own reach, on the word of God that the ground is not a hole but a field? Answer it this week with one specific gift.

For worship. Sow generously today, not to get, but because God has sown so generously in you. The greatest sowing in history was not of money but of a life. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). The Son of God was buried like seed in a garden tomb, and the harvest from that one grain is a multitude no one can number. Nothing he gave was lost. Nothing we give in his name will be lost either. The ground is a field because he made it one.

parallels.desc: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

Each one must give as he has decided in his heart. One verse, and it settles the manner, the method and the motive of Christian giving. Each one: not the wealthy, not only those who feel able. Everybody. There is no exemption here for the poor, which is why the Macedonians gave out of the depths. As he has decided: the verb (proaireō) means to purpose, to determine beforehand. It is a personal, prayerful, settled decision, made in advance, not a reaction, and no fixed amount is imposed. This is the strongest argument in Scripture for planned giving. It is a decision reached in private, with the figures in front of you, before any appeal is heard, and once made, it takes the question out of the offering plate and out of the emotional temperature of a meeting. Paul told this same church to do it weekly and in advance, so that there would be no collecting when he came (1 Corinthians 16:2).

Not reluctantly. Then the two things it must not be, and both are shrewdly chosen. Not reluctantly is literally not out of grief: not with a pang, not with a heavy heart. That is the giving that is genuinely done and quietly resented, and the resentment usually surfaces later as a complaint about how the money is spent.

Or under compulsion. Not because you had to. The pressure need not come from outside; most of it does not. It is the calculation of what is expected, what others will think, what a person in your position ought to be seen to do, or simple guilt.

For God loves a cheerful giver. And then the sentence itself. Paul had it from the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8, and the word behind cheerful is a delight: hilaros, the root of our word hilarious. It is not sober approval; it is something closer to laughter. God loves a giver whose giving is a pleasure to him. That is a genuinely startling thing to be told, because it means God is not primarily after the money. Every beast of the forest is his, the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10). What he loves is a particular kind of person: one for whom letting go has become a joy rather than a loss. He is himself the most cheerful giver of all.

Made by contemplation. That cannot be produced by trying. You cannot decide to find giving delightful, any more than you can decide to find a person attractive. It comes from somewhere else: from having grasped, somewhere below the level of argument, that you cannot out-give the one who has already given you everything, and that nothing you release was ever really at risk. So if giving is currently a duty you perform with a small internal wince, the answer is not to give more grimly. It is to go back and look again at 8:9 until the arithmetic changes. Cheerful givers are made by contemplation, not by resolve.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you should only give when you feel like it. It means ask God to make you glad to give.

I don’t feel cheerful about giving. Should I wait until I do? No. Give what you have decided, and ask God to change your heart as you do. Feelings often follow obedience rather than leading it, and many believers have found that gladness came after they began giving regularly, not before. But do not be content with grudging. Bring the reluctance to God honestly; it usually points to fear about the future or love of something else. Meditate on Christ’s giving. And if you are giving out of pressure or guilt that is not from God, a manipulative appeal or a demand nobody has the right to make, you are free to decline it and give where you can give gladly.

In a sentence. Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under pressure, for God loves a cheerful giver.

On a Tuesday. Pray before you give. Decide in your heart, at home, with the figures in front of you. Then give with a smile, and if the smile is not there yet, read 8:9 again and ask God for it.

For worship. God does not merely approve of cheerful givers; he is one. He gave the world light on the first day and called it good, gave Adam a garden with every tree pleasant to the sight, gave Israel a land flowing with milk and honey, and gave his Son with joy, the joy of a Father bringing many sons to glory. Christ endured the cross for the joy set before him. There is no reluctance anywhere in God’s giving, no wince, no grudge. When he makes us cheerful givers, he is only making us like himself, and he loves what he sees, because it is his own likeness.

parallels.desc: from every man whose heart moves him
the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.

And God is able to make all grace abound to you. Paul now supplies the reason a person can afford to give freely, and the sentence is built out of totality. Count the words: all grace, all sufficiency, all things, all times, every good work. Five in one line. He is piling them up on purpose. Begin where he begins: God is able. That is the ground of the whole thing. Not God will make you comfortable, but God is able. The question of capacity is settled, and it is his capacity, not yours. To make all grace abound: grace again, the word running through both chapters, and here it plainly includes the material, since the context is money; but it is not only material, and Paul’s vocabulary refuses to let it shrink to that. All grace means every kind of blessing, material and spiritual.

So that having all sufficiency in all things at all times. The key word is autarkeia, sufficiency, and it has a history worth knowing. It was a great word among the Stoic philosophers, and it meant self-sufficiency: the ideal of the wise man who has trained himself to need nothing from anyone, and is therefore untouchable. It was an admirable and rather cold aspiration, and it depended entirely on the strength of the individual. Paul takes the word and quietly turns it inside out. The Christian has autarkeia; he lacks nothing; and it does not come from within him at all. It is supplied. He is not self-sufficient; he is God-sufficient, and therefore has the freedom the Stoic wanted without the self-reliance the Stoic required. Paul says elsewhere that he learned this by experience in both directions: I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content (Philippians 4:11), written from prison by a man who had been both well fed and hungry. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6).

You may abound in every good work. And then the purpose clause, which is the part that gets left out when this verse is quoted on its own. Why does God supply all sufficiency at all times? So that you may abound in every good work. Not so that you may be secure. Not so that you may relax. The sufficiency is given to free the hands. God gives to us so that he can give through us. He keeps a giver supplied for the same reason a farmer is kept in seed: there is more sowing to do.

The margin. That turns the verse into a searching question about what you have. Everyone has some margin, however small: money, time, a spare room, a skill, years of retirement. The verse says that the margin was supplied, and it names the purpose it was supplied for. If it has been quietly reclassified as security, something has gone wrong in the accounting, because a God who gives seed and gets no crop has not been dealt with honestly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians will always be wealthy. It means they will have enough to do the good God calls them to.

What if I give generously and then find I do not have enough? First, notice what God promises: sufficiency for every good work he calls you to, not freedom from all hardship. Paul himself knew both plenty and hunger (Philippians 4:12), and was content in both because Christ strengthened him. Second, God supplies through many means, including the generosity of other believers; that is the very point of 8:14, and you may need to receive as gladly as you once gave. Third, be wise: giving does not mean ignoring debts or your family’s basic needs (1 Timothy 5:8). But many who have given in faith testify that God has not let them down. Tell him your need plainly, and trust him.

In a sentence. And God is able to bless you abundantly, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.

On a Tuesday. Name your margin: the money, time, room or skill you have beyond what you strictly need. Write down one good work it could serve this month, and do it. Trust that God will give you enough for every good work he calls you to.

For worship. God is able. Paul never tires of saying it: able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20), able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 24), able to save to the uttermost (Hebrews 7:25). His supply is never measured by our need but by his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19). The Stoic stood alone and called it strength. The Christian stands in the hand of an inexhaustible Father and calls it grace, and he has never yet run out.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”

As it is written. Paul reaches for a psalm, and the choice repays looking up. It is Psalm 112:9, and the whole psalm is a portrait of a particular kind of man: the one who fears the LORD and greatly delights in his commandments. It describes him as gracious, merciful and righteous, unafraid of bad news, steady when others panic, and right in the middle of the portrait, as one of the marks of the God-fearing man, is this: he has distributed freely, he has given to the poor. That is worth noticing before anything else. In the psalmist’s picture of a godly life, open-handedness is not an optional extra for those of a generous temperament. It is one of the identifying features, listed alongside faith and courage as part of the description.

He has distributed freely. The verb (skorpizō) is a scattering word, the same motion as the farmer in verse 6: arm out, seed flung wide. It is not careful, measured allocation. It is broadcast. The righteous scatter their goods generously.

His righteousness endures forever. Then the phrase Paul is really after. In the psalm it is the man’s own righteousness: his standing as a God-fearing man, his settled character shown in his giving, and specifically the fact that it does not fade. Its fruit is eternal. And the point Paul draws from it is the contrast running through this whole chapter. The money went out and is gone; nobody can now point to it. What it produced does not go anywhere. The righteousness endures.

What survives. Hold that against the fate of everything else a person accumulates. The savings will be spent by somebody. The house will belong to strangers. The estate will be divided and, within two generations, forgotten. Every pound kept is a pound that will eventually be lost, because that is the nature of what can be held. The only portion that survives is the portion given away, which is precisely what the Lord said when he told his disciples to lay up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew 6:20).

The portrait’s original. There is a further note sounding under the psalm. The psalm before it, Psalm 111, says the very same words of God: his righteousness endures forever (Psalm 111:3). The righteous man of Psalm 112 is a reflection of the righteous God of Psalm 111. And the description of the man who scatters freely and whose righteousness endures for ever is, in the end, the description of only one person perfectly. The whole psalm is a portrait of a life nobody has quite lived, except the one who gave to the poor to the point of having nothing, and whose righteousness endures for ever because it is the righteousness of God himself. Every generous believer is a small copy of him, and he is the original the psalm was reaching for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving makes us righteous before God. It means generosity is a mark of the righteous life. Our righteousness before God is Christ’s alone, received by faith (5:21); the generous life is the fruit of it.

Should I give money to people who beg on the street? There is no single rule, and Christians who love the poor differ. Give with open hands and open eyes. Sometimes cash helps; sometimes, where addiction is involved, it feeds the very thing that is destroying someone. Often the best gift is food, a hot drink, your time and your name, treating the person as someone made in God’s image. Supporting local churches and ministries that know the people and can help wisely is often the most lasting way to give. Whatever you decide, do not walk past with a hard heart. Look the person in the eye, and remember who became poor for you.

In a sentence. As it is written: “They have freely scattered their gifts to the poor; their righteousness endures for ever.”

On a Tuesday. Scatter your gifts generously to the poor this week. It has eternal value. Choose one person or cause among the poor and give, not by careful calculation alone, but with the scattering motion of the psalm.

For worship. Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, says the psalm, and the blessing it describes is a copy of the God he fears. The LORD is gracious and merciful; he has given food to those who fear him; his righteousness endures for ever. He scattered his kindness across the whole earth, sending rain on fields that never thanked him. And he gave his Son to the poor, to beggars like us, who had nothing to give back. His righteousness, credited to us in Christ, endures for ever, and no moth, rust or thief will ever touch it.

parallels.desc: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.

He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food. This is the verse that decides how verse 6 must be read, and it is the one the prosperity preacher never reaches. The words echo Isaiah 55:10, where the rain and snow water the earth, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, and so God’s word goes out and does not return empty. God is the source of all provision. Start with the two things he supplies, because Paul distinguishes them deliberately. Seed to the sower: what is given to be put back in the ground. Bread for food: what is given to be eaten. Every farmer knows the difference and keeps the two in separate sacks, because confusing them is ruinous in both directions. Eat the seed and there is no crop next year. Sow the bread and the family starves this winter.

A mercy in two directions. So God gives his people both, and the distinction is a mercy both ways. It means you are meant to eat. Nothing in this passage requires a Christian to give away everything he has and call the resulting destitution faith; God supplies bread for food, deliberately, and it is his provision, not a compromise. And it means some of what you have was never meant for consumption. It is seed, and seed kept in the sack does nothing at all.

Will supply and multiply your seed for sowing. Then the two things he promises to do. Supply and multiply your seed: not multiply your bread. The increase is on the sowing side of the ledger. God takes a generous person and makes him more able to give, which is exactly what verse 8 said and exactly what most of us would not have chosen if asked.

And increase the harvest of your righteousness. Then the crop is named, and it is the plainest statement in the chapter. The phrase comes from Hosea 10:12: sow for yourselves righteousness, reap steadfast love. Not the harvest of your prosperity, nor your comfort, your security or your standard of living. Righteousness: good works, a godly life and its eternal fruit, a life more conformed to God, more like the man of Psalm 112, more like the Lord who became poor.

The whole offer. So the promise attached to generous giving in this chapter is exactly this: God will keep you supplied, he will enlarge your capacity to give, and he will make you a more righteous man. That is the whole offer. It is enormously generous, and it is not what is advertised on certain kinds of religious television, and the difference has cost poor and desperate people a great deal of money.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God multiplies seed so that we can eat it all. Seed is for sowing.

How do I tell my seed from my bread? Bread is what you and your household genuinely need to live, work and fulfil your responsibilities: food, housing, clothing, transport, care for children and elderly parents, modest provision for the future. Seed is what is over and above that, given to you to sow. The line is not fixed, and godly people draw it differently, but the danger nearly always runs one way: we keep reclassifying seed as bread. A useful check is to ask whether your standard of living has risen with each increase in income while your giving stayed level. If so, some seed has gone into the bread sack. Decide the line in prayer, with your family, and review it regularly.

In a sentence. Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and increase your store of seed and will enlarge the harvest of your righteousness.

On a Tuesday. Take an honest look at one area of your spending this week and ask whether it is bread or seed. Move one thing from the bread sack back to the seed sack, and sow it.

For worship. Notice the tenderness in the picture as well as the challenge. God is described as he who supplies seed to the sower: the one who fills the bag before the man walks out to the field. Nobody in this arrangement is being asked to generate anything. The seed you scatter was put in your hand, the bread you eat was put on your table, and the harvest is grown by someone else entirely. The farmer’s only part is the throwing. Every seed, every loaf and every ear of righteousness in the harvest comes from the Father of lights, from whom every good and perfect gift comes down (James 1:17).

parallels.desc: seed to the sower and bread to the eater

verseByVerse.quote: You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.

You will be enriched in every way. The sentence has a hinge in the middle of it, and everything depends on reading past the hinge. Stop here and it sounds like a prosperity verse, half of one at least, and half is exactly how it is usually quoted. God will make you rich, but for a purpose.

To be generous in every way. That is the purpose, and it is the third time in four verses Paul has attached the same clause to the same promise: sufficiency so that you may abound in every good work (v. 8); seed multiplied for sowing (v. 10); enriched to be generous (v. 11). He will not let the promise stand on its own for a single sentence. God’s blessings are given to flow through us, not to stop with us.

A river, not a marsh. Take the picture behind it. A river is enriched by rainfall in the hills. It does not thereby become a lake. It becomes a river with more water going through it, and everything downstream is better for the rain that fell three counties away. Water that stops moving is not a richer river; it is a marsh, and it goes bad. That is the theology of Christian prosperity in one image, and it explains why the New Testament is so unembarrassed about God giving people more. There is nothing wrong with increase. The question is only ever whether it is passing through.

Where the increase went. That puts an honest question to anyone whose circumstances have improved over the years, and most people’s do, quietly, without any single moment of becoming better off. Look at what happened to the increase. Almost always it was absorbed: a slightly larger house, a better car, a standard of living that rose to meet the income without a decision ever being taken. And the giving stayed roughly where it was when the income was half what it is now. Nobody chose that. It happens by default, which is why it needs naming. The only reliable guard against it is the deciding of verse 7: settling the proportion in advance, and revisiting it whenever the circumstances change, so that increase is a matter of policy rather than drift.

Which through us will produce thanksgiving to God. Then the end of the sentence, and it is where the whole chapter has been heading. Follow the chain. God enriches the Corinthians. The Corinthians give. Paul and his companions carry it. Believers in Jerusalem receive it, and they thank God. What comes out at the far end is not merely full stomachs. It is thanksgiving, going back up to the God who started it. The money makes a complete circuit and returns to its source as worship. That is what your giving is actually doing, and most of it happens where you cannot see it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s purpose is our comfort. It means his purpose is generosity and thanksgiving.

Is it wrong for a Christian to enjoy nice things? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and gratitude for a good meal, a holiday or a beautiful home honours the giver. Jesus went to feasts and accepted costly perfume. The danger is not enjoyment but absorption: when every increase is spent on ourselves as a matter of course, when comfort becomes something we cannot give up, or when our hope quietly moves from God to our possessions. Enjoy God’s gifts with thanks, hold them loosely, and make sure the river is still flowing out as well as in.

In a sentence. You will be enriched in every way so that you can be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will result in thanksgiving to God.

On a Tuesday. Ask: what has God enriched me with, so that I can be generous with it? Compare your giving now with your giving when you earned least, and if it has not grown in proportion, set a new figure this week.

For worship. All giving in the end returns to its source as worship, and that is because all giving started there. From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory for ever (Romans 11:36). The Father enriches, the Son became poor to make the riches ours, the Spirit moves the hand to give, and the thanksgiving rises back to the triune God who began it. We are not the fountain, and we are not the sea. We are the riverbed, and what a privilege it is to be the place where his goodness passes through.

verseByVerse.quote: For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,

For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints. Paul now spells out what a charitable collection actually accomplishes, and the list runs further than anyone would expect. The word for service is leitourgia, the word for priestly service, from which we get liturgy. Giving is worship, offered to God. It is not only supplying needs; that much is obvious and real, since people in Judea were hungry and this money bought food. Paul never sneers at the practical. But he says it is the smaller half.

But is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. The verb is the overflow word again. The gift meets needs and multiplies praise. It does not stop when the need is met; it spills over into worship.

By their approval of this service. Literally, by the proof (dokimē) of this service. The gift proves the reality of the Corinthians’ faith. And verse 13 requires knowing what was actually at stake, because otherwise it reads as pious padding. The deepest fracture in the first-century church was between Jewish believers in Jerusalem and Gentile believers in cities like Corinth. The Jewish Christians had watched a gospel without circumcision spread among people who ate what they liked and had never kept the law, and many were not at all sure about it. There had been a council about it (Acts 15). There had been a confrontation between Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). The suspicion was mutual and it was serious.

They will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ. Now picture what arrives: a bag of money, gathered over a year by Greek believers who have never seen Jerusalem, carried hundreds of miles at real risk, for Jewish Christians they will never meet. And Paul says what it will produce. The gift is evidence. It proves that the confession these Gentiles make is not words: that the gospel has actually gone in and changed what they do with their money. Their generosity is obedience flowing from confessing the gospel. The Jerusalem believers, who might have doubted Paul’s Gentile converts, will look at it and conclude that God is genuinely at work among the nations, and they will praise him for it. Giving is evidence of genuine faith (James 2:15–17).

And the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others. “Contribution” is koinōnia again: fellowship, sharing. The gift expresses unity with all believers, not only those in Jerusalem.

What argument cannot do. So the collection does something no argument could do. Paul had made the case for Gentile inclusion at length and in person, and arguments do not dissolve suspicion.
