Sacrificial generosity does. It is very difficult to go on doubting the faith of people who have gone without so that you could eat. That is worth carrying into every division a church knows: between generations, between congregations, between believers who are wary of one another for reasons that are half real and half inherited. Suspicion is rarely argued away. It is dissolved by somebody being unmistakably and expensively kind, and Paul spent years of his life organising exactly that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving saves. It shows salvation.

Is giving really part of worship, and should the offering be part of the service? Yes. Paul calls it leitourgia, priestly service, and elsewhere calls a gift a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18). Do not do good and share what you have, says Hebrews, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God (Hebrews 13:16). Whether a church takes an offering during the service or gives by other means is a matter of wisdom, not principle. What matters is that giving is understood as an act of worship offered to God, not a fee for services or a slot between the songs. However you give, give as you pray: to him, with thanks.

In a sentence. This service you perform not only supplies the needs of the Lord’s people but also overflows in many expressions of thanks to God. Because of the proof this service gives, others will praise God for the obedience that accompanies your confession of the gospel of Christ, and for your generosity in sharing with them and with everyone else.

On a Tuesday. Think of a believer or group of Christians you find it hard to trust or understand: another tradition, another generation, another church in your town. Do something unmistakably kind for them this week, at some cost to yourself. Then let it be worship, offered to God.

For worship. Let your giving be worship, offered to God, overflowing in others’ thanksgiving, and see in it the miracle of the gospel. Christ has made Jew and Gentile one, reconciling us both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:16). The bag of Greek coins carried up to Jerusalem was a small, glittering proof that the wall had really come down. The God who once chose one nation has now gathered a people from every nation, and he binds them together not by argument but by love poured out. Every time believers who should be strangers become family, heaven sees the cross bearing fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.

While they long for you and pray for you. The last thing the money produces, and it is the loveliest. They long for you: the word is a strong one, yearning, an ache of affection. And it belongs to Jewish believers in Jerusalem, directed toward Greek strangers in Corinth. These are the two groups whose relationship had been the great unresolved strain in the early church, and Paul expects the outcome of a collection to be homesickness for one another. The collection builds bridges between Jewish and Gentile Christians. And pray for you: the people who received the money will spend themselves on the people who sent it. That is what happens when a gift is received rightly. It creates an obligation of love that can only discharge itself in prayer.

What a sum of money did. Follow what has now happened to a sum of money. It fed the hungry. It produced thanksgiving to God. It proved the reality of a gospel that had been doubted. It bound two suspicious communities together. And it set one group of people praying by name for another group they would never meet in this life. No accountant could show any of that on a statement. It is worth remembering when giving feels like a transaction, a standing order leaving an account on the same day each month with nothing visibly happening. Paul’s account of what money does in the kingdom is that most of its effects occur where the giver cannot see them and would not recognise them if he could.

Because of the surpassing grace of God upon you. Then the reason for their longing, and it is not what we would have written. Not because of your generosity, nor because of your kindness. The Jerusalem believers look at what the Corinthians have done and see straight past them to God. They do not end up admiring Corinth. They end up amazed at grace. That is the mark of everything genuinely Christian, and it is the test that separates it from philanthropy. Philanthropy leaves people impressed with the giver, which is why the names go on the buildings. Grace leaves people looking at God, and the giver is not diminished by it. He is simply out of the way, which is the position every jar of clay was designed to occupy (4:7). And notice the word surpassing: grace beyond measure, exceeding the bounds. The observers in Jerusalem were not looking at a well-run appeal. They were looking at something they could not account for on any human basis, and the only explanation big enough was God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prayer can be bought. It means generosity creates bonds of love and prayer.

How can I build real bonds with believers in another culture or country? Give to them, and then get to know them. Support a missionary or a church abroad, and ask for their news and prayer requests. Pray for them by name, regularly. Welcome international students and immigrant believers into your home. If you can, visit, to learn rather than to impress. Read about the persecuted church and write to prisoners for Christ. Receive from them too: their prayers, their example, their insight into Scripture. Love grows along the channels where gifts and prayers flow both ways, exactly as Paul hoped it would between Jerusalem and Corinth.

In a sentence. And in their prayers for you their hearts will go out to you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you.

On a Tuesday. Give to believers in another place or culture. It will bind you together in love and prayer. Choose one, ask how you can pray for them, and start this week.

For worship. The surpassing grace the Jerusalem believers saw in Corinth was the same grace that had found them both. It is the grace of a God who does not leave his children strangers to one another. Christ prays for all who will believe, that they may all be one, just as the Father is in him and he in the Father (John 17:21). When believers who have never met long for one another and pray for one another, that prayer of the Son is being answered. And the Lord who intercedes for his people at the Father’s right hand teaches them to intercede for each other, until the whole family is gathered and longs for nothing more.

verseByVerse.quote: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

Thanks be to God. Two chapters about money end in an exclamation. Paul has been organising a collection: timetables, delegates, audits, appeals, proportions, the risk to his own reputation. And at the end of it he does not summarise. He breaks off, as though he has looked up from the ledger and seen something.

For his inexpressible gift! The word is anekdiēgētos: indescribable, beyond telling, literally un-out-narratable. It is built from a verb meaning to describe a thing all the way through, and Paul negates it. This is a gift that cannot be narrated to the end. Not that it is vague; the opposite. It is so definite and so large that language runs out before the description does.

What the gift is. He has already told us, in the previous chapter, and the two chapters have been standing on it the whole time: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (8:9). The gift is Christ himself, God’s Son, given for us. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son (John 3:16). He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)? That makes this the proper end of everything Paul has said about generosity. He has given the Corinthians a great deal of instruction: decide in your heart, do it in advance, give proportionately, do not be pressured, finish what you started, keep the accounts clean. All of it is useful and none of it is the engine. The engine is that God gave his Son, and that no one has ever got to the end of describing it. All our giving is a small response to God’s infinite gift.

Stop and try. Begin anywhere. The Word who was with God and was God, born in a stable. The hands that made the world learning a trade. The one who had never been refused anything being refused a bed, a hearing, a friend. Follow it to the garden, and the whipping post, and the nails, and the darkness at noon, and the cry of a Son who had never been out of his Father’s sight. Then the morning, and the stone rolled away, and the wounds still in his hands so that they could be touched. Now add what it purchased: a debt cancelled that could never have been paid; enemies made sons and daughters; the Spirit of God taking up residence in ordinary people; a righteousness that is not ours credited to us as though it were; a resurrection body; a new heaven and a new earth; and, at the end of it, his face. Nobody has ever finished that sentence. The apostles did not, the church has been trying for two thousand years, and the people who see him will spend eternity discovering how much of it they had not yet understood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the collection is the inexpressible gift. The collection is a small echo of it.

How do I thank God for a gift I cannot even describe? Start where Paul does, with plain words: thanks be to God. You do not need eloquence; you need to look at Christ and say thank you, often and specifically. Name one part of the gift each day: his birth, his obedience, his cross, his rising, your forgiveness, your adoption, his Spirit in you, the face you will see. Sing it with the church; the hymns exist because one voice is not enough. Let it shape your life, so that your giving, your forgiving and your patience are thank yous too. And do not be troubled that your thanks always falls short. That is what inexpressible means, and eternity is long enough to go on trying.

In a sentence. Thanks be to God for his gift, too wonderful for words!

On a Tuesday. Before you plan anything else about your giving this week, stop and thank God for his inexpressible gift: Jesus. Say it aloud. Then let whatever you give flow from that thanks, and see whether it changes the amount.

For worship. Thanks be to God. There is nothing else to say about a gift like that, and Paul, who could argue for chapters, does not try. The Father gave the Son. The Son gave himself. The Spirit gives him to us, and opens our eyes to see him. Every other gift in these two chapters, the Macedonians’ coins, the Corinthians’ promise, Titus’s eagerness, the prayers of Jerusalem, flows from that one gift as streams from a spring. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12). Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints,<sup>2</sup>for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.<sup>3</sup>But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be.<sup>4</sup>Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.<sup>5</sup>So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.<sup>6</sup>The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.<sup>7</sup>Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.<sup>8</sup>And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.<sup>9</sup>As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”<sup>10</sup>He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.<sup>11</sup>You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.<sup>12</sup>For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God.<sup>13</sup>By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,<sup>14</sup>while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.<sup>15</sup>Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

10.title: Divine Weapons and Boasting in the Lord
10.overview:
With chapter 10 the tone changes sharply. Chapters 1–9 are warm and relieved; chapters 10–13 are a fierce defence against the visiting teachers Paul will call “super-apostles” and “false apostles”. Some scholars therefore think these chapters were a separate letter, either the earlier tearful letter (2:4) or a later one written after fresh bad news. No manuscript divides the letter, and Paul may simply turn here from the repentant majority to the minority still under the rivals’ influence. Either way, these chapters are Scripture and their meaning is clear.

The rivals mocked Paul: bold in letters but feeble in person, a poor speaker, an unimpressive man. Paul answers that he appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, but he is not powerless. His weapons are not worldly ones (rhetoric, manipulation, status), but divine power that demolishes strongholds of false reasoning and takes every thought captive to obey Christ. What he writes when absent he will do when present. He refuses to measure himself against others who commend themselves. He keeps to the field God assigned him, which reached as far as Corinth, and hopes to go beyond it. The only boast that counts is in the Lord, and the only commendation that counts is the Lord’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Weapons of Divine Warfare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tone sharpens as Paul answers rivals who mock him as timid in person and bold only on paper. He appeals to them with the gentleness of Christ, hoping he will not have to act firmly against those who accuse him of worldly motives. He does live as a weak human being, but he does not fight with worldly methods. His weapons have God’s power to demolish fortresses of the mind: arguments and proud ideas raised against the knowledge of God. He aims to bring every thought under Christ’s rule, and is prepared to discipline persistent disobedience once the church as a whole is obedient.
verseByVerse.theology: The “weapons of warfare” in v. 4 are the weapons of gospel ministry: the proclaimed word, prayer, the demonstration of transformed lives, the power of the Spirit. These are not powerful by worldly standards (rhetorical brilliance, social influence, political power) but divinely powerful for pulling down strongholds. This is the consistent NT theology of ministry: God chooses the weak and foolish things to shame the strong and wise (1 Cor. 1:27), precisely so that the power is unmistakably his. The church that abandons the means God has ordained in favour of worldly methods of influence has swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones.
verseByVerse.examples: A church in a university town hires a communications consultant to help them “win the argument” with the secular culture. The consultant advises them to lead with culturally acceptable values rather than with gospel claims. This passage challenges the strategy: taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ is the goal, but the weapons for achieving it are not strategic communication management — they are the divinely powerful weapons of the gospel, prayer, and the demonstration of transformed lives. The strongholds that prevent the knowledge of God are spiritual, and only spiritual weapons can pull them down.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!— I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!—I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.

Meaning first. Chapters 10 to 13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul. The tone changes sharply: from relief and warmth to warning and irony. These intruders, whom Paul will call super-apostles and false apostles, boasted of their credentials, eloquence and visions, and mocked Paul as weak in person and unimpressive in speech. Chapter 10 begins Paul’s answer. First, he appeals to them by the meekness of Christ, asking them not to force him to be severe when he comes. His warfare is spiritual, with divine weapons that demolish strongholds of proud thinking and take every thought captive to Christ (vv. 1–6). Second, he answers the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person: he will be the same in action when present as in writing when absent (vv. 7–11). Third, he refuses to compare himself with those who measure themselves by themselves. He boasts only within the field God assigned him, which includes Corinth, since he brought them the gospel first. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord, for only the Lord’s commendation counts (vv. 12–18). Underneath the whole chapter stands the meek and gentle Christ, whose weakness is the power of God.

A change of tone. Everyone who reads the letter notices it. For nine chapters Paul has been warm, relieved, confident in them. From this verse to the end he is fighting. Some have concluded that chapters 10 to 13 must be a separate letter stitched on. There is no manuscript evidence for it, and there is a simpler explanation: he has finished with the majority who have come right, and now turns to the minority who have not, and to the men who have been working on them.

I, Paul, myself entreat you. The pronouns pile up. It is emphatic and personal; some think Paul took the pen himself here. He is stepping forward in person, and after this the letter will be full of I where before it was largely we.

By the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Notice what he appeals by. Before a word of combat he names the character he intends to fight in. “Meekness” (prautēs) is the word of the Beatitudes and of the Lord’s own self-description: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). It is strength under control, humility that does not need to assert itself. “Gentleness” (epieikeia) is reasonableness, forbearance: the quality of a man who does not insist on the full severity of what he is entitled to, the word used of a ruler who has the right to press a charge and does not. That is a remarkable thing to put at the head of four chapters of self-defence, and it should govern how they are read. Whatever sharpness follows is meant to be heard in that key. Paul’s gentleness, which his opponents mocked as weakness, is Christlike.

I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away! Then the taunt, quoted in his own sentence with a note of exasperation. “Humble” is tapeinos, lowly, which they meant as servile, timid. They were saying he was brave on paper and small in the room: that he wrote what he did not dare say. It is an accusation with real force, and it lands somewhere near home for most of us. Almost everyone is bolder at a distance. The message says what the conversation would not. The complaint made in the car is not made in the meeting. The strong opinion typed at eleven at night would be softened considerably by a face on the other side of a table.

I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness. Paul’s answer is not to become fierce in person. It is to say that the gentleness they mistook for cowardice was deliberate, and that he would greatly prefer not to have to prove it. He is asking them to make the confrontation unnecessary. He would rather not have to be severe.

Against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh. Some accused Paul of acting by merely human motives and methods: self-interest, weakness, manipulation, the ordinary calculations of a man protecting his position. He will pick up their word in the next verse and turn it over.

Force with a hand on it. That is what strength under control looks like, and it is why he began where he did. Meekness is not the inability to be forceful. It is force with a hand on it, and the one who models it had more than twelve legions of angels at his disposal and stood silent before Pilate (Matthew 26:53; 27:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean meekness is weakness. Christ was meek and yet overturned the tables in the temple.

How can I be gentle without being a pushover? Gentleness is about how you use your strength, not whether you have convictions. Be clear about what is right and say it plainly; Paul never hides his view. But choose the gentlest means that will do the job, give people time and room to respond, and keep your temper on a lead. Hold your ground on truth and on protecting others, and yield freely on your own preferences and rights. A pushover gives way because he is afraid; a meek man gives way because he chooses to, and stands firm because he must. Ask, in each case: what would the Lord Jesus, who is both lamb and lion, do here?

In a sentence. By the humility and gentleness of Christ, Paul appeals to you, Paul who is said to be timid when face to face with you but bold toward you when away! He begs you that when he comes he may not have to be as bold as he expects to be toward some people who think that we live by the standards of this world.

On a Tuesday. Be gentle like Christ, and do not let others mistake your gentleness for weakness. Think of one person you have been bolder about at a distance than to their face: in a message, in a complaint to someone else. Either take it to them, gently and in person, or let it go.

For worship. The Christ by whose meekness Paul appeals is the King who came to Zion humble and mounted on a donkey (Matthew 21:5). He had every right to come in judgment, and he came in gentleness. He did not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Matthew 12:20). And his gentleness was never weakness: it held back the wrath of heaven while he bore it himself on the cross. The one who could have called down legions chose to be led like a lamb to the slaughter. That is the strength under control by which Paul begs, and it is the strength that saved us.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul.

parallels.desc: Moses was very meek

verseByVerse.quote: For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.

For though we walk in the flesh. They had accused him of walking according to the flesh, of operating by ordinary human motives and methods. He picks the word up and turns it over. Though we walk in the flesh: yes, in one sense. He is a man, in a body, with human weakness, a bad back and a temper to govern. He has never claimed otherwise; a few chapters ago he called himself a jar of clay (4:7).

We are not waging war according to the flesh. That is the different question. Living in a body is not the same as fighting by the body’s rules. He does not fight by worldly methods: manipulation, force, rhetoric, political power.

The fortress above the city. Now comes the picture that governs the rest of the chapter. Paul reaches for siege warfare, and his readers knew what he meant. Corinth sat beneath the Acrocorinth, a great rock rising well over a thousand feet above the city with a fortress on top of it. Every Corinthian looked up at it daily. A stronghold was not an idea to them; it was that.

For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh. Name what fleshly weapons would be in this fight: rhetoric, reputation, credentials, charm, political leverage, the ability to out-argue and out-manoeuvre. Precisely the arsenal Paul’s rivals carried, and precisely what he keeps refusing to pick up. His weapons are spiritual: the word of God, prayer, truth, righteousness and faith (6:7; Ephesians 6:13–18). The letter itself has named them: the open statement of the truth (4:2), a gospel about a crucified man, prayer, the visible transformation of ordinary lives, and a messenger who is manifestly not the source of the power.

But have divine power to destroy strongholds. The Greek says the weapons are powerful to God, or powerful by God: the power is his, lent to the weapons he ordained. Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels. Proverbs 21:22 speaks of a wise man who scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust. The strongholds here are explained in verse 5: proud arguments and ideas that resist God.

Where Christians differ: what are the strongholds? Some popular teaching takes strongholds to mean territorial demons over cities, to be bound by special prayer, or demonic footholds in a believer’s life to be cast out. Verdict: Paul defines the strongholds himself in verse 5: arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. The battle is for minds and hearts, fought with the truth of the gospel. Spiritual forces are real (Ephesians 6:12), but Scripture never teaches us to map or bind territorial spirits. Our weapons are the word, prayer and holy lives.

Does this passage license binding demons or breaking strongholds over cities? No. The strongholds Paul names in the next verse are arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God: false ideas, not demonic territories. The weapons are the truth of the gospel and prayer. Scripture does speak of spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12), but the believer’s part there is to stand, resist and pray, not to name and bind spirits over places. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7). If you want to see a city’s strongholds fall, preach the gospel in it, pray for it, and live holy lives among its people.

Do we actually believe it? The uncomfortable question this puts to the church is whether we actually believe it. It is a great deal easier to reach for the fleshly weapons, because they are visible and they work in the short term: the campaign, the polish, the political alignment, the personality who can hold a room. None is wicked in itself. But a church that has quietly swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones will find it has won some arguments and pulled down no strongholds at all. And the arithmetic runs the other way from what we expect. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27): a message about an executed provincial, carried by unimpressive people. That is not a handicap he graciously works around. It is the chosen instrument, and it has been levelling fortresses for two thousand years.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should use physical force to spread the faith. That is warfare according to the flesh.

Should Christians be involved in politics at all? Yes, as citizens, and many faithful believers serve God well in public life; Joseph and Daniel served pagan governments. Christians may vote, campaign for justice, protect the vulnerable and hold office, and they should do it honestly and with love for their neighbours. What this verse forbids is thinking that the kingdom of God advances by political power, or that the church’s mission is won by getting the right people elected. Laws can restrain evil; only the gospel changes hearts. Believers who differ over policy should not divide over it, and no party should be confused with Christ.

In a sentence. For though we live in the world, we do not wage war as the world does. The weapons we fight with are not the weapons of the world. On the contrary, they have divine power to demolish strongholds.

On a Tuesday. Look at the next difficulty you face in your church, your family or your witness, and ask which weapons you are reaching for. If the honest answer is charm, pressure, cleverness or influence, put them down and pick up prayer, the plain truth spoken in love, and patient holiness. Pray today for one stronghold of unbelief in your culture to be pulled down by the truth of the gospel.

For worship. The fortress on the Acrocorinth has long since fallen to ruins. The weapons Paul carried are still in use, and they are still breaking walls. That is because their power was never in them, but in the God who said, Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:6). He took the cross, the most shameful weapon of the empire, and made it the weapon by which principalities and powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The gospel of a crucified Saviour has outlasted every empire that despised it, and it will outlast ours.
verseByVerse.note: Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,

We destroy arguments. The siege continues, and now we are told what the fortress is made of. “Arguments” (logismoi) are reasonings, philosophies, the constructions the mind builds. The strongholds are intellectual and moral systems that resist God.

And every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God. “Lofty opinion” (hypsōma) is literally a high thing, raised up; the word is used of a rampart or tower, something built tall specifically to keep an enemy out. It is pride lifted up against God, like the tower of Babel, built with its top in the heavens to make a name (Genesis 11:4). And note carefully what these are raised against: the knowledge of God. This is not a description of ideas that happen to be mistaken. It is a description of intellectual structures whose function is to keep God at a distance. That explains something otherwise puzzling. Very often the reasons a person gives for not believing are genuinely held and also not the real reason. They are the wall, and the wall was built for a purpose.

And take every thought captive to obey Christ. Against these Paul uses two verbs, and both are military. He destroys: pulls down, demolishes. And he takes captive: aichmalōtizō, the word for marching a prisoner of war away at spearpoint. First the wall comes down, then the occupants are led out. Every thought captive: every one. There is no province of human thinking with a treaty exempting it. The Christian mind is not neutral; it bows to Christ in everything: science, art, ethics, politics, relationships.

Two applications. This verse is quoted constantly, and almost always about the private thought-life: the anxious spiral at three in the morning, the intrusive thought, the resentment rehearsed for the tenth time. That application is legitimate and it is needed; a Christian who lets his mind run wherever it likes is being formed by it. But it is worth seeing that it is a second application rather than the first. Paul is describing his public ministry: the demolition of ideas that stand against the knowledge of God.

The most ambitious programme of the mind. That makes this the most ambitious intellectual programme anyone has ever proposed, and the opposite of the anti-intellectualism it is sometimes made to serve. Paul is not telling people to stop thinking. He is saying that every field of human thought, history, law, art, medicine, economics, the way you read a novel or run a business, is territory Christ intends to hold, and that the Christian mind is not a smaller thing than the unbelieving mind but a conquered and therefore ordered one.

Where Christians differ: how should Christians argue for the faith? Some approaches to apologetics try to meet unbelievers on neutral ground, reasoning from shared premises toward God. Verdict: No thought is neutral; all thinking either submits to Christ or rebels against him. Christians should reason carefully and use evidence (Acts 17:2–3; 1 Peter 3:15), but from a standpoint of submission to God’s revelation, not as if human reason were the final judge. The aim is not merely to win arguments, but to bring every thought captive to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be anti-intellectual. It means the mind is to be used fully, and in obedience to Christ.

How do I take a thought captive in practice? First, notice the thought for what it is, rather than letting it run unexamined. Then test it against what is true: is it what God says about himself, about Christ and about me? Then replace it, deliberately, with what is true, as Paul says: whatever is true, whatever is honourable, think about these things (Philippians 4:8). Take it to God in prayer, and if it returns, do the same again. An unwanted thought is not itself sin; it becomes sin when it is welcomed and fed. And where anxious or intrusive thoughts will not go, a believer should not be ashamed to seek help from a pastor or a doctor.

I have serious doubts about the faith. Is that rebellion against Christ? Not in itself. Doubt is often a question looking for an answer, and Christ is patient with honest questions; he showed Thomas his hands (John 20:27). Bring your doubts into the light: read, ask, talk to a mature believer, look at the evidence for the resurrection, and keep praying, even if the prayer is, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). The lofty opinion Paul tears down is different: a mind that has decided in advance that God must not be allowed to speak. Watch for that in yourself. Ask whether your doubt wants an answer, or wants an exit.

The rampart in your own heart. And then there is the personal edge, which no one escapes. Take the strongholds seriously in your own case. Most of us have one: an area where we have quietly built a high wall and decorated it with reasons. The relationship we will not reconsider, the habit that has an argument attached to it, the part of Scripture we have found a way round. It is not that we have never thought about it. It is that all the thinking has gone into the rampart. Those come down the same way the public ones do, by the same weapons, and to the same Lord.

In a sentence. We demolish arguments and every proud idea that sets itself up against the knowledge of God, and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Notice the thoughts in your own mind that rebel against God: worry, pride, lust, bitterness. Take one captive today and bring it to Christ. Then ask which wall in your life is decorated with the most reasons, and bring that one to him too.

For worship. Every high thing will one day come down. The LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, and the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day (Isaiah 2:12, 17). But the Christ who takes thoughts captive is not a tyrant marching prisoners to a dungeon. He leads captivity captive and gives gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8). The mind he conquers is the mind he sets free, for in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). To be his prisoner is to be at last at home in the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.

Being ready to punish every disobedience. The siege image runs on into its last stage. “Punish” (ekdikeō) means to bring justice, to put a wrong right. In ancient warfare, when a city fell, there was a distinction between the population that submitted and the resistance that fought on. Paul is still inside that picture. The campaign in Corinth is nearly over; most of the city has come in. There remains a pocket that has not, and he says he is ready to deal with it: he is prepared to exercise church discipline against the rebels when he comes (13:2, 10).

When your obedience is complete. But look when. Not before. The order of the sentence is the whole point. First the church as a whole must fully return to obedience. Then Paul can deal with the remaining troublemakers, with the church on his side. He is deliberately waiting. He will not move against the resistance while the majority is still coming over, because action taken too early would force people to choose sides before they were ready and would drive the undecided into the wrong camp. He has done this all through the letter: he stayed away to spare them (1:23), he wrote instead of visiting (2:3), he let the severe letter do its work and waited months for news. Every time, he has given them room and time.

Patience with a plan. That is patience with a plan behind it, and it is not the same as avoidance. Avoidance hopes the problem will dissolve. Paul is quite clear that he intends to act, and says so in advance, which is itself a mercy: nobody in Corinth can claim to have been ambushed. There is real pastoral wisdom here for anyone with responsibility in a church or a family. The instinct when trouble appears is to move immediately and settle it, and the instinct is often wrong. Timing is not a detail; it is most of the skill. A confrontation that would have split a congregation in March can sometimes be handled almost quietly in September, once the body of people has become settled and the issue is no longer a contest between factions.

Obedience to whom. Notice the two words held together: disobedience and obedience, side by side in one line. Paul frames the whole affair not as loyalty to himself but as obedience to Christ. The Corinthians are not being asked to take his side. They are being asked to submit to the same Lord he is under, which is exactly what he said in 1:24, where he refused to lord it over their faith. That distinction keeps church discipline from becoming a power struggle, and it is the first thing lost when a leader begins to experience opposition as a personal injury. The question is never, are they with me? It is whether they are obeying Christ, and the man asking has to be under the same authority, or he has no business asking at all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wants to punish. He wants obedience. Discipline is a last resort. Nor does patience mean delay where someone is in danger; where there is abuse or a threat to the vulnerable, protection cannot wait for a better season.

Does church discipline still happen today, and what is it for? It should, though many churches neglect it. Jesus laid down the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then tell it to the church, and only if the person still refuses to listen, treat him as an outsider (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul applied it in Corinth (1 Corinthians 5). Its aims are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church, the protection of others and the honour of Christ, never revenge or the leaders’ pride. It is for serious, unrepented sin, handled slowly and humbly, with the door always open to return, as 2:6–8 shows. A church that never disciplines is not kinder; it simply leaves people to their sin.

In a sentence. And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, once your obedience is complete.

On a Tuesday. If you have authority in a home or a church and trouble is brewing, ask God for wisdom about timing before you act, and make sure the question you are asking is whether people are obeying Christ, not whether they are loyal to you. Pray for your church leaders as they guard the church, and ask God to make your own obedience complete.

For worship. The patience Paul shows with Corinth is a faint echo of the patience of God. He is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). And yet his patience is never indifference. He has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has appointed (Acts 17:31). Until that day the door stands open, and the same Lord who will punish every disobedience has already borne the punishment of every disobedience of his people on the cross. His justice and his mercy meet, and neither is ever late.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to look at the facts. He belongs to Christ as much as anyone, and his authority was given to build them up, not tear them down. Some say his letters are impressive but he is feeble in person and a poor speaker; they will find him the same in action as on paper. He will not join those who rate themselves by comparing themselves with each other. His boasting stays within the field God assigned him, which included Corinth, where he was first to bring the gospel. He does not claim credit for others’ work, and hopes their growth will free him to preach further afield. In the end only one boast counts, boasting in the Lord, and only one approval, the Lord’s.
verseByVerse.theology: The criterion of the Lord’s commendation (v. 18) is the basis of all genuine ministerial authority in the NT. The super-apostles derive their authority from letters of recommendation (3:1), impressive personal presence, rhetorical skill, and visions and revelations (12:1). Paul derives his from the divine call (Gal. 1:1), the fruit of his ministry (the transformed Corinthians — 3:2), and ultimately from the Lord’s own assessment. This does not make Paul self-certifying; it means his legitimacy is determined at the bar of heaven, not at the bar of human opinion.
verseByVerse.examples: A minister with a large platform cultivates an online presence that constantly showcases his ministry’s results — attendance figures, conversion stories, speaking engagements, endorsements from well-known figures. He tells himself he is building credibility for the gospel. This passage asks a harder question: is he building the gospel’s credibility or his own? The test is not whether he mentions God in his self-promotion but whether his confidence is ultimately in the Lord’s assessment or in the metrics of human comparison.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.

Look at what is before your eyes. The opening is blunt and slightly weary. It can be read as a command, look at the plain facts, or as a diagnosis: you look only at outward appearances. Given how much of this letter is about outward appearance against the heart (5:12), the second is probably in it, and the Corinthian church had made a habit of the mistake. Either way: face the facts.

If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s. The rival teachers evidently claimed to belong to Christ in some special way, perhaps through links with Jerusalem, perhaps through visions and revelations.

Let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. Here is a sentence with unexpected restraint in it. Paul’s reply is not, and they do not. He does not deny their claim; he simply says that whatever they are, he is too. Paul belongs to Christ just as much. That is a very controlled response from a man who could have said a great deal more, and it is the meekness of verse 1 in operation.

For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you. The parenthesis in the middle is one of the most important sentences in the New Testament about authority in the church. Three things are settled in a dozen words. The authority is real: Paul has apostolic authority from Christ and does not apologise for having it. It is given, not achieved or seized, which means it is held on someone else’s terms. And it has a stated purpose, with a stated limit: it is for construction, and it is not for demolition (13:10).

Not for destroying you. Read that against the verses just before, and the irony is deliberate. Paul has spent four verses on siege warfare, demolishing ramparts and taking prisoners. Now he says his authority is not for destroying. The demolition is aimed at the strongholds; it is never aimed at the people. He tears down arguments in order to build up the person who was living behind them.

A simple test. That supplies a test that any Christian in any position of responsibility can apply, and it is uncomfortably simple. After you have exercised authority, as an elder, a parent, an employer, a husband, is the other person more built up or less? Not, were you right? You may have been entirely right and still have used the truth as a wrecking ball. Authority given for building up cannot be used to destroy without ceasing to be the thing it was given as. That is the line, and a man who crosses it is no longer exercising the authority Christ gave; he is exercising something else and using Christ’s name for it. Authority that destroys people is abused authority.

I will not be ashamed. His claim will be vindicated. Paul is content to let the Lord who gave the authority judge how it was used.

What it does not mean. It does not mean authority never corrects. Correction is part of building up. A builder must sometimes take out rotten timber; the question is whether he is building a house or merely knocking one down.

What if a church leader is using his authority to destroy people? Then he has stepped outside the authority Christ gave, and it must not be tolerated. Do not stay silent out of misplaced loyalty. Speak to him if it is safe, and then to the other elders or the wider church or denomination, taking a witness (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Where there is abuse of any kind, protect the vulnerable first and report it to the proper authorities; spiritual authority never overrides the law or the safety of the weak. Leaders are to shepherd willingly, not domineering over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:2–3). If a church will not deal with it, you are free to leave and find a faithful one.

In a sentence. You are judging by appearances. If anyone is confident that they belong to Christ, they should consider again that we belong to Christ just as much as they do. So even if Paul boasts somewhat freely about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, he will not be ashamed of it.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time you used authority, over a child, an employee, a team, a class. Ask honestly whether the person was more built up or less afterwards. If less, go back and build. And pray for leaders in your church to use their authority to build up, never to destroy.

For worship. All the authority in heaven and on earth has been given to the Lord Jesus (Matthew 28:18), and he uses every ounce of it to build. I will build my church, he said (Matthew 16:18), and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. He tore down the dividing wall, he tore the veil of the temple, he tore apart the bars of death; and he did it all to build a house for God out of living stones. The one with all authority came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Every right use of authority in his church is a small picture of him.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”

I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. Paul does not want his letters seen as threats from a safe distance. Here he quotes his critics directly, and it is one of the cruellest things said about anyone in the New Testament that we have in the words of the people who said it. Take the insult apart, because it was carefully made.

For they say his letters are weighty and strong. That is a concession, and it is the setup. They grant the letters their force in order to make the contrast land harder. Even his critics admitted his letters were powerful, and they are still read today, in more languages than his enemies ever heard of.

But his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account. His bodily presence is weak: the word covers appearance and physical bearing. He was evidently unimpressive to look at: perhaps small, worn, possibly marked by the beatings, possibly by whatever the thorn in the flesh was. An early tradition outside the Bible, in a second-century writing, describes him as short, balding and bow-legged; it is late and cannot be verified, but it survived perhaps because nobody in the early church found it surprising. And his speech of no account: literally despised. Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory. In a Greek city, public speaking was the highest art and the crowd was expert. Paul was not what they were used to. He had told them so himself: he came not with lofty speech or wisdom, and in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:1–4; compare 11:6).

And it worked. So the charge is: he can write, but he cannot hold a room, and he does not look like anything. And it worked, because it was substantially true. Sit with what it must have been to hear that sentence read aloud in the church you founded. He does not answer it with a denial. There is no, that is unfair. He quotes it, and moves on to the one thing that matters, which is whether the authority is real.

For the unimpressive. There is something here for a great many Christians who will never be apostles. Some people are simply not impressive in the way a room rewards. The voice is wrong. The manner is awkward. They think of the right sentence in the car afterwards. They have watched someone with half their faithfulness be listened to twice as attentively, and they have concluded, quietly, that God can use other people. The most fruitful missionary in the history of the church was despised as a speaker and unimpressive in person, and it is recorded in Scripture in the exact words of the men who despised him. God did not correct their assessment. He simply went on using the man they had accurately described, because the treasure was never the jar (4:7), and the power was never going to be mistaken for personality.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not speak well. Acts shows him as a powerful speaker, before crowds, councils and kings. It means he refused the showy techniques the Corinthians admired.

Should churches not want gifted, attractive speakers? Gifts are good, and a preacher should work hard to speak clearly and well; Apollos was eloquent and was a blessing (Acts 18:24–28). The danger is making polish the measure. Choose and judge preachers first by faithfulness to Scripture, godliness of life and love for people (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 2 Timothy 4:2). A plain man who opens the Bible faithfully will feed a church for decades; a brilliant one who does not will starve it while it applauds. And listen to sermons for the word of God in them, not for the performance.

In a sentence. Paul does not want to seem to be trying to frighten you with my letters. For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but in person he is unimpressive and his speaking amounts to nothing.”

On a Tuesday. Do not judge Christian leaders by charisma or appearance. Judge them by faithfulness to Christ. And if you are one of the unimpressive ones, do the thing God has given you to do this week without waiting to become impressive first.

For worship. The Lord whom Paul served had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isaiah 53:2). He was despised and rejected by men, and they said of him, Is not this the carpenter? The glory of God came into the world in a body nobody would have picked out of a crowd, and finished his work on a cross where they mocked him as weak. And that weakness was the power of God for salvation. A God who saves the world through a despised Messiah and spreads his gospel through an unimpressive apostle is a God who will not share his glory with any personality. All of it is his.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory.

verseByVerse.quote: Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.

Let such a person understand. One sentence, and it disposes of the whole accusation. Let such a person understand: singular, and slightly cold. He has a particular individual in view, probably the ringleader of the opposition, and he addresses him without naming him, which is both a courtesy and a warning.

That what we say by letter when absent, we do when present. The charge was a gap between the written Paul and the present Paul. His answer is that there is no gap. What the letters say, the man does. The distance changes nothing. And notice that he does not promise to be more forceful in person than they expect. He promises consistency, which is a different and larger claim. The letters have been gentle as well as firm: he has begged, entreated, wept and appealed by the meekness of Christ. All of that will also be true in the room. He is not warning them that a harsher man is coming; he is telling them the same man is coming. When he comes, they will find him as firm in action as in writing, and as gentle.

Two people. The gap Paul is denying is the commonest failure of integrity there is, and modern life has industrialised it. Almost everyone is now two people: the one who writes and the one who is present. Things are typed that would never be said. A tone is taken at a keyboard that would collapse instantly if the other person were in the chair opposite. Whole reputations are built in a medium where the audience cannot see the man, and the people who live with him could tell you he is not that. And it runs the other way too, which is the more respectable version. There are people who are warm and agreeable in person and quietly devastating about the same person elsewhere: nothing untrue said, exactly, but a different man in each room.

Undividedness. Integrity is a word that means undividedness, wholeness. It is not chiefly about grand honesty in large matters; it is about being one person. And it is worth the cost, because a divided man can be trusted by nobody, including himself, while the man who is the same in the letter and in the room can be believed the first time, every time, which is the only foundation a ministry or a marriage has ever been built on.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul will be harsh. It means he will do what is necessary.

I have already written something I would never say to the person’s face. What now? Go back and put it right. If what you wrote was untrue, unkind or exaggerated, delete it where you can and apologise to the person directly, and to anyone else who read it, without excuses. If it was true but should have been said in person, go and say it in person, gently. If it was about someone rather than to them, stop the conversation it started. Then set yourself a rule for next time: write nothing about anyone that you would not be content for them to read with you sitting beside them. Confession and repair are the way back to being one person.

In a sentence. Such people should realise that what we are in our letters when we are absent, we will be in our actions when we are present.

On a Tuesday. The test is Paul’s, and it is simple enough to run tonight. Would you be content for the person you wrote about to read what you wrote? Would you say, to their face, the thing you said about them at the kitchen table? If the honest answer is no, the gap is real. Close it this week.

For worship. Only one person has ever been perfectly the same in every room. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). What he said to the crowds, he said to the Pharisees; what he was on the mountain of transfiguration, he was in the boat with the frightened disciples and on the cross with the dying thief. There was no gap in him between word and deed, public and private, promise and performance. The Word became flesh, and the flesh was exactly what the Word had said. He is the integrity we lack, and he gives it to those who trust him, making divided people whole.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.

Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. Paul now names what is actually wrong with his rivals, and it is not first their doctrine. It is their measuring system. He opens with heavy irony: he does not dare put himself in the same class as these men. Of course he does not dare. He is not qualified to compete with people who are that impressive, and everyone reading heard the smile in it.

But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another. Then the diagnosis, and it is exact. Follow the circle. They are the standard. They are the ruler and the thing being measured. Nothing external is ever allowed into the calculation, so the result is always satisfactory: a closed circle of mutual admiration.

They are without understanding. Paul’s verdict is blunt. Not merely proud, not merely mistaken: foolish. It is a senseless way to live, in the ordinary sense of the word, because it guarantees you will never learn anything true about yourself. The only true measure is God’s standard, not comparison with others.

How comparison works. This is where the passage stops being about first-century opponents, because comparison is the water most people swim in, and it is worse now than it has ever been. You do not compare yourself with everyone; you select. The comparison group is chosen, unconsciously, to produce a tolerable result: near enough to be relevant, and arranged so that you come out somewhere acceptable. And the effect is always one of two things, both ruinous. Either you come out ahead, and you are quietly pleased, and the pleasure is in being better than someone rather than in anything real. Or you come out behind, and something corrosive begins: the diminishment, the resentment of a person who has done you no harm, the sense that your own work does not count. Neither tells you a single true thing about yourself, because the measurement never touched the actual standard.

Where it bites now. It is worth naming where this bites hardest. A generation ago a person compared himself with the families in his street. He now compares himself, several times a day, with a curated selection of the most successful, most photogenic and most articulate people on earth, all presenting their edited version. Nobody has ever had to endure that before, and it is not surprising that so many people feel like failures at something they were never in a contest about.

What it does not mean. It does not mean learning from others is wrong. Paul tells believers to imitate him as he imitates Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). It means comparison is a false measure of spiritual worth.

How do I actually stop comparing myself with others? You cannot simply stop; you have to change the ruler. Measure yourself by Christ and his word, which humbles you and frees you at once. Remember that your field is assigned by God (vv. 13–14), so another person’s gifts and results are not a verdict on yours. When you notice comparison starting, turn it into prayer: thank God for the other person’s gifts, and ask him for faithfulness in your own task. Limit what feeds it, which for many people means less time scrolling through other people’s edited lives. And rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15); it is the surest cure for envy.

In a sentence. We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they are not wise.

On a Tuesday. Notice the next time you measure yourself against someone else, whether you come out ahead or behind. Stop, name it, and thank God for that person. Then ask what Christ is asking of you today, and do that.

For worship. The way out is not to try harder at the comparison. It is to change the ruler, which is what Paul does in the next six verses, and where he ends is the only place there is: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord. Beside the Lord Jesus, all our comparisons collapse. No one comes out ahead of him, and no one needs to, because he did not come to rank us but to save us. In him the ladder is taken away, and the only measure left is grace: the one who knew no sin made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

verseByVerse.quote: But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.

But we will not boast beyond limits. Having refused the comparison game, Paul says what he measures by instead. He keeps within bounds.

But will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us. The phrase rendered area of influence is a single Greek word, kanōn. It means a measuring rod, and then by extension the boundary marked out with one: the surveyor’s line, the allotted plot. It is the word from which we get canon, the fixed rule. So Paul’s picture is of a field with boundary markers in it, and the markers were not put there by him. God gave Paul a field of ministry: the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9). He did not choose the Gentile mission or select Corinth from a list of options. He was given a plot, and he intends to be assessed on that plot and nowhere else.

The size of your field. That single idea disposes of an enormous amount of Christian unhappiness, and it is worth being concrete about how. If God assigns the field, then the size of your field is not your achievement and not your failure. A man given four acres who works them well has done exactly what a man given four hundred has done, and the accounting at the end will be per acre. So the small congregation is not a lesser version of the large one. The Sunday school class of six is not a failed attempt at sixty. The years given to caring for one dependent relative are not a career that did not happen.

A restraint as well as a comfort. It works as a restraint too. A man who knows where his boundary markers are does not need to be involved in everything, does not have to have a view on every controversy, and is not obliged to feel guilty about every good work he is not doing. There is a kind of exhausted Christian who is failing at nine things because he was only ever given three.

To reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. Corinth is within that field. Paul is not claiming territory that is not his.

For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ. He was there before anybody. He came on from Athens, worked at a bench with Aquila and Priscilla to support himself, and stayed eighteen months, founding the church (Acts 18:1–11). The rival teachers came later, to a church already standing, and tried to take over his work. That is the difference between a man on his own ground and a man on someone else’s, and Paul is about to say plainly what he thinks of the second.

What it does not mean. It does not mean churches belong to their founders. They belong to Christ. But Paul had a God-given responsibility for them.

How do I know what field God has assigned me? Look at what he has already put in your hands. Your field is made of your relationships, your gifts, your responsibilities and your opportunities: the family you belong to, the church you are a member of, the work you do, the neighbours you have, the needs you can actually meet. Ask what you are uniquely placed to do that no one else is. Listen to mature believers who know you. Pay attention to open doors (1 Corinthians 16:9). Begin there, faithfully, rather than longing for someone else’s field. If God enlarges it later, he will make it plain; for now, the plot you are standing on is the one he gave you.

In a sentence. We, however, will not boast beyond proper limits, but will confine our boasting to the sphere of service God himself has assigned to us, a sphere that also includes you. We are not going too far in our boasting, as would be the case if we had not come to you, for we did get as far as you with the gospel of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Write down the three or four things God has plainly given you to do in this season. Then look at what you are anxious or guilty about, and cross off what is outside your field. Give your best this week to the plot you were actually given.

For worship. Thank God for the field of service he has assigned you, and work faithfully within it. The boundary lines have fallen for me in pleasant places, says the psalmist; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance (Psalm 16:6). The Lord of the harvest knows every field and every worker, and he measures by faithfulness, not by acreage. The Son himself kept to the field his Father gave him, the lost sheep of Israel, and at the end could say, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). He will say well done to every servant who did the same with his few acres.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.

We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. Now the charge is made explicit, and it is a serious one. Unlike the intruders, who took credit for Paul’s work, he will not boast of work done by others. They had come to a church somebody else planted and taken credit for it. The image is of a man moving a boundary stone in the night, an old and much-hated crime forbidden in the law (Deuteronomy 19:14), and standing in a field he did not clear, showing visitors round.

Not only a first-century problem. It happens whenever a man arrives at a work built over thirty years by someone tired and unfashionable, makes some improvements, and lets it be understood that things really began when he came. It happens in the way ministries describe their own history. It is rarely a lie; it is usually a matter of emphasis, and the person who did the clearing is dead or elsewhere and cannot say anything.

But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged. Then Paul’s own ambition, and it is worth watching how carefully it is framed. Notice the sequence. He does not ask for a larger field. He asks that their faith should grow, and expects that his own scope will be enlarged as a consequence, because a church that is spiritually strong releases its workers instead of absorbing them. As the Corinthians grow and settle down, Paul will be free to go further. So the growth he wants in himself is downstream of the growth he wants in them. That is the right way round, and it is very rarely how ambition is actually ordered. The usual shape is a man wanting a bigger platform and hoping his people will supply it.

So that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you. There is the aim. He wants Corinth strong so that he can leave. The Corinthians are not his destination; they are a base. And the phrase lands beyond is the sentence of a man who cannot stop looking at the horizon. He tells the Romans he means to go on to Spain, because he makes it his ambition to preach the gospel not where Christ has already been named, lest he build on someone else’s foundation (Romans 15:20–24, 28). Pioneer mission was his passion.

Without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence. That is the deepest difference between him and the men troubling this church. They travelled to places where the work was done and the church was gathered. He travelled to places where nobody had heard of Jesus at all. Both are moving; only one is advancing. And the test of any ministry ambition is finally that plain: does it want a share of what already exists, or does it want the gospel to reach somewhere it has not been?

What it does not mean. It does not mean only pioneer work matters. Others water what pioneers plant (1 Corinthians 3:6), and Paul is glad of Apollos. It means no one should take credit for another man’s planting.

What are the lands beyond for an ordinary Christian today? There are still thousands of people groups with little or no access to the gospel, and many neighbourhoods near you where hardly anyone knows a believer. You may not be called to go to Spain, but every Christian can help the gospel move outward. Pray regularly for unreached peoples by name. Give to missionaries and church plants going where Christ is not known. Welcome people from other nations who have come to your town. Consider whether God might send you. And begin with the lands beyond your own circle: the colleague, the neighbour, the family member who has never heard the gospel explained.

In a sentence. Neither do we go beyond our limits by boasting of work done by others. Our hope is that, as your faith continues to grow, our sphere of activity among you will greatly expand, so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. For we do not want to boast about work already done in someone else’s territory.

On a Tuesday. Do not take credit for others’ work. If you have inherited something good, in a church, a job or a family, name and thank the people who built it before you. And pray for the gospel to reach the regions beyond: choose one unreached people or one unbelieving neighbour and pray for them every day this week.

For worship. The horizon Paul could not stop looking at is the horizon of God’s own promise. In Abraham all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3). The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14). The risen Christ sends his church to all nations, and promises to be with us to the end of the age. And one day a great multitude that no one can number, from every nation, tribe, people and language, will stand before the throne and the Lamb (Revelation 7:9). The lands beyond are not an afterthought; they are the Father’s gift to his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain.

verseByVerse.quote: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord. The chapter ends where the whole argument has been going, and Paul settles it with a quotation he had already used in his first letter (1 Corinthians 1:31). It is from Jeremiah 9, and the original is worth having in full, because Paul expects his readers to hear it: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness in the earth (Jeremiah 9:23–24). All legitimate boasting is in what the Lord is and has done.

Move the object. Three things a human being can be proud of, brains, strength and money, and they are still the three. Every comparison anyone runs is finally a version of one of them. Jeremiah does not tell his readers to stop boasting. He tells them to move the object. That matters, because Scripture is not against boasting as such. Human beings are built to admire and to say so; the instinct is not the problem. The problem is that it keeps attaching itself to things that cannot bear the weight, and that will be gone in fifty years.

For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved. Then the last word on the subject. “Approved” (dokimos) is the assayer’s word again: tested and found genuine. Self-promotion proves nothing. And the point is about who is holding the scales. A man can commend himself brilliantly and be worthless; he can be despised as a speaker, unimpressive in person, dismissed by the very church he founded, and be approved.

But the one whom the Lord commends. Only the Lord’s verdict counts. It is the Lord who judges me, Paul told this church; then each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:4–5). That is either terrifying or the most liberating sentence in the chapter, depending on where your confidence has been sitting. If your sense of yourself rests on the assessment of the room, this verse takes it away, and there is nothing to be done about that. If it rests on his assessment, then every unfair verdict passed on you is provisional, and the review is scheduled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never speak of what God has done through them. Paul does. It means all the credit goes to the Lord.

Is it wrong to accept praise, or to list my achievements in a job application? No. Receive praise graciously with a simple thank you, and quietly give the glory to God in your heart; refusing all thanks can be its own kind of pride. Stating your experience truthfully on a CV is not boasting in the sinful sense; it is giving honest information. What Paul condemns is self-commendation as a way of life: seeking a reputation, inflating your record, needing others to be impressed, and measuring your worth by what people say. Tell the truth about what you have done, never exaggerate it, and keep reminding yourself who gave you every gift you have (1 Corinthians 4:7).

In a sentence. But, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week what you most want people to notice about you. Then deliberately turn the conversation, or your own thoughts, toward something God has done. Seek the Lord’s commendation above all, and boast in him today, out loud, to someone.

For worship. And here is the astonishing thing, the thing that makes this good news rather than merely a warning. The commendation Paul is waiting for has already been secured, and not by him. He is approved because he is in Christ, who was made sin for him (5:21), and the words he is waiting to hear will be spoken over people who know perfectly well they did not earn them. The Father has already said of his Son, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased, and in Christ that pleasure rests on us. There is nothing else in the universe that will still be worth boasting about when everything currently being compared has been forgotten, and the only opinion left standing will be his. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.

11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview:
In this chapter Paul does something he finds distasteful: he boasts. The rival teachers in Corinth commended themselves loudly, with their Jewish pedigree, eloquence, visions and fees, and the Corinthians were impressed. So Paul plays “the fool” for a while, borrowing their method to expose it. He fears the church is being seduced away from Christ, like Eve by the serpent, by teachers who bring a different Jesus, a different spirit and a different gospel. He defends his practice of preaching free of charge, which they took as a sign of inferiority, and unmasks the rivals as false apostles, servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness.

Then comes the “fool’s speech” proper. Paul matches their credentials, Hebrew, Israelite, descendant of Abraham, and then lists not his successes but his sufferings: floggings, beatings, a stoning, shipwrecks, dangers on every road, hunger, cold and the daily weight of care for all the churches. The climax is deliberately absurd: his greatest exploit was being lowered in a basket through a window to escape from Damascus. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness.
