verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with a little foolishness from him, because he loves them with God’s own jealousy: he promised them to Christ like a bride to her husband, and fears they are being led away from simple, pure devotion to Christ, as Eve was deceived by the serpent. They tolerate teachers who preach another Jesus and another gospel, yet Paul is in no way inferior to these so-called super-apostles, even if he is no polished speaker. Was it wrong of him to preach to them free of charge, taking support from other churches instead? He will keep refusing their money, to cut the ground from under those who want to claim equal status with him. These men are false apostles disguised as apostles of Christ, which is no surprise, since Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light; they will end as their deeds deserve.
verseByVerse.theology: The identification of false apostles as servants of Satan (v. 15) is one of Paul’s most severe theological statements. It raises the question of how to identify false apostles — since they come disguised as servants of righteousness. The test that Paul has been applying throughout the letter is: what is the content of the message? What is the character of the minister? Does the ministry bear the cruciform pattern of genuine apostolic suffering? Paul’s opponents fail all three tests: their message is a different gospel; their character is self-promotional; their lives show no evidence of the suffering that authentic ministry requires.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity, and supernatural experience — all framed in Christian language. The pastor is concerned but cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the categories: the test is not merely whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus is being presented, which spirit is being invoked, which gospel is being preached. The angel-of-light disguise means the most dangerous false teaching often looks impressively spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 11 is Paul’s fool’s speech. The super-apostles at Corinth boasted of their credentials, and the Corinthians were impressed. Paul hates boasting, but to rescue the church he plays the fool and boasts, in order to expose the emptiness of their boasting. First, he explains his motive: a godly jealousy, like a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Christ, and fears she will be seduced, as Eve was, by another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (vv. 1–6). Second, he answers their complaint that he refused payment: he did it out of love, to show the difference between himself and the false apostles, who are Satan’s servants disguised as servants of righteousness (vv. 7–15). Third, he boasts as a fool. He matches their pedigree: Hebrew, Israelite, offspring of Abraham. But as a servant of Christ he outdoes them, not in triumphs but in sufferings: imprisonments, beatings, lashings, stoning, shipwrecks, dangers of every kind, hunger, cold, and daily anxiety for the churches. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness, like the time he escaped Damascus in a basket (vv. 16–33). And underneath the whole bitter, brilliant chapter runs one conviction: the glory belongs to Christ, and the servant who looks least impressive may be the one who looks most like him.

I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Paul is about to do something he finds distasteful, and he apologises for it before he starts. “Foolishness” (aphrosynē) is his name for boasting about himself, which he will call speaking not as the Lord would (v. 17). He knows exactly how what follows will sound, and he asks them to put up with it.

Do bear with me! The second sentence is almost a plea. The Greek can also be read as a statement, you are already bearing with me, and either way the tone is the same: a father who would rather not raise his voice, asking his children to let him say something hard.

For I feel a divine jealousy for you. Then he explains why he is willing to look ridiculous, and the reason is not wounded pride. The Greek repeats the root for emphasis: literally, I am jealous for you with God’s own jealousy. That word needs handling, because jealousy is a vice in most of its ordinary uses and a divine attribute in Scripture. The difference is what is being defended. Envy wants what belongs to someone else. Jealousy of this kind guards what already belongs to you and is being taken. A husband who feels nothing when his wife is being drawn away does not love her more than a jealous man; he loves her less. God calls himself jealous for exactly that reason: the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14; 20:5). It is the language of a marriage, not of a tyrant, and Hosea heard God say it to an unfaithful people: I will betroth you to me for ever, in righteousness and in steadfast love (Hosea 2:19–20).

Since I betrothed you to one husband. Which is precisely the picture Paul now draws. Stage it, because a Jewish betrothal was not a modern engagement. It was legally binding, and only a divorce could end it, though the wedding and the home-coming came later. Between the two lay a period of waiting, and in that period somebody had a duty: to guard the bride’s purity until the day she was handed over. Paul, the church’s spiritual father, promised the Corinthians to Christ when they first believed, and he regards the promise as his responsibility until the wedding.

The friend of the bridegroom. There was a role in the proceedings that Paul is claiming here: the friend of the bridegroom, who helped arrange the match, watched over the bride through the betrothal, and finally presented her to the husband. John the Baptist described himself the same way and said his whole joy was to hear the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29). So Paul is not the husband. He is the man who brought the bride to him and who is answerable for her until the day arrives. That is why he is jealous. Something is happening to his charge on his watch.

To present you as a pure virgin to Christ. At Christ’s return, the wedding day, the church will be presented to him (Ephesians 5:27; Revelation 19:7–9). Notice what this makes of the church, and it is worth pausing on. This congregation, divided, suspicious, easily impressed by the wrong men, is a bride being kept for a wedding. Everything she is now is provisional. What she is being prepared for is the day she is presented, and Paul’s hope is fixed on how she will look then, not on how she looks this year. That is a truer way to see the church than most of us manage. It is not first a society for religious improvement or an institution with problems. It is a woman under an engagement, and the one she is engaged to intends to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle. He is coming for her, and he has never once changed his mind about the arrangement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wants the Corinthians’ loyalty to himself. The friend of the bridegroom who tries to win the bride for himself is the worst kind of traitor. Paul wants their loyalty to Christ, and he is prepared to be thought foolish, and even to lose their affection, to keep it there.

Is jealousy ever right for me? Yes, when it guards something that truly belongs to you and to God, and when it is aimed at the danger rather than at the person. A husband or wife may rightly be jealous for the marriage when a third person is drawing one of them away; a parent may rightly be jealous for a child being pulled toward something destructive; a pastor may be jealous for his people. But test it. Godly jealousy wants the other person’s good and faithfulness to Christ; sinful jealousy wants control, suspects without cause, and resents another’s good gifts. The first speaks openly and prays; the second spies, sulks and punishes. If yours looks like the second, it is not God’s jealousy, whatever it calls itself.

Is the church the bride, or am I? Both, in the right order. The bride in Scripture is the whole church, the one people Christ loved and gave himself for (Ephesians 5:25). You are not a separate bride in a crowd of brides; you belong to her, as one member of the body she is. That guards against two mistakes: a sentimental individualism that forgets the rest of the church, and a cold collectivism that forgets that Christ knows each of his own by name. What is true of the bride is true of you because you are in her, and the faithfulness Paul is anxious about is yours too.

In a sentence. Paul hopes you will put up with a little of his foolishness; yes, please put up with him! He is jealous for you with a godly jealousy. He promised you to one husband, to Christ, so that he might present you as a pure virgin to him.

On a Tuesday. You are betrothed to Christ, and the wedding has not happened yet. Ask what in your life at the moment is acting like a rival suitor: not necessarily anything wicked, but anything that is quietly asking for the place in your affections that belongs to him. Name it, and turn your heart back toward the one who is coming for you. And when you look at your own church, with its quarrels and its tired people, look at it the way Paul looks at Corinth: as a bride being got ready.

For worship. Christ is not a reluctant husband. He chose his bride while she was still unlovely, paid the bride-price with his own blood, and has bound himself to her with a promise that only he could break and he never will. The jealousy that burns in Paul is a spark from his. And on the day the friends of the bridegroom finally hand her over, she will be without spot or wrinkle, not because she kept herself so, but because he washed her, and he will look at her and be satisfied.
verseByVerse.note: In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband-to-be, and her purity was guarded until the wedding; Paul pictures himself in that guardian role.

parallels.desc: I will betroth you to me forever

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.

But I am afraid. The apostle who has been telling this church he has complete confidence in them now says he is frightened for them, and the two are not a contradiction. A father can be sure of a child and lie awake about him in the same week.

As the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning. Then the comparison, and once again Paul reaches back to Genesis 3. The serpent, whom Paul will soon name as Satan (v. 14; Revelation 12:9), deceived Eve with clever words that twisted God’s word. The word Paul uses for his method is panourgia: readiness to do anything, craftiness. It is the same word he used at 4:2 of the cunning he himself renounced. Deception of this order is not crude. It is patient, plausible, and it works with the grain of what the hearer already half wants to believe.

How the deception worked. Go back and look at it, because everyone remembers the fruit and forgets the method. The serpent did not arrive denying God. He arrived asking a question: did God actually say? He did not begin by contradicting; he began by opening a small gap between what God had said and what God had meant. Then he offered a better reading of God’s motives, that the prohibition was self-protective and that God was holding something back. By the time he flatly contradicted, saying you will not surely die, the ground had already been prepared. That is still the pattern. Error rarely begins with a denial. It begins with a question that makes the plain word sound naive.

Your thoughts will be led astray. “Led astray” (phtheirō) means corrupted, seduced, ruined. The danger is to the mind, and it comes through teaching. Paul is not first afraid that the Corinthians will be dragged into gross sin but that their way of thinking about Christ will be quietly bent, and everything else will follow from that.

From a sincere and pure devotion to Christ. Notice exactly what Paul is afraid of losing. Not their orthodoxy in the first instance, but their devotion. The word behind sincere is haplotēs, the singleness met at 1:12: simplicity, being one thing rather than two. The word behind pure is hagnotēs, chastity, the faithfulness of a betrothed bride. Some manuscripts omit and pure, as the ESV’s footnote notes; the meaning is not affected, because both words describe the same undivided heart. He is afraid they will become complicated. The danger is not only wrong ideas but a divided heart, adding something to Christ or quietly replacing him.

The love you had at first. That is a very precise fear and it is worth taking personally. The danger to a Christian is rarely that he will one day decide Christianity is false. It is that the simple attachment, the plain love of Christ that made everything else fall into place, gets crowded. Other loyalties arrive, and interests, and a growing sophistication about the faith that somehow leaves less warmth in it than there was at the beginning. Nobody renounces anything. The devotion simply stops being single. The Lord said the same thing to the church at Ephesus, which was doctrinally impeccable, hard-working and patient, and had one thing wrong with it: “you have abandoned the love you had at first” (Revelation 2:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean simple devotion means simplistic thinking. Paul is the most demanding thinker in the New Testament, and he is not asking anyone to stop studying. He means undivided loyalty: a mind that may grow as deep as it likes, so long as it stays fixed on one Lord.

Is Paul saying women are more easily deceived? Not here. In this verse Eve stands for the whole church, men and women alike, and the warning is addressed to every reader in Corinth, most of whose leaders were men. The point of the comparison is the method of deception and the bride’s danger, not the sex of the one deceived. Paul does draw on the order of creation and the fall when he speaks about teaching in the church (1 Timothy 2:13–14), and that passage has its own place, but it is never a licence to treat women as gullible. Adam, standing beside her, was not deceived and sinned anyway, and Scripture lays the fall at his door (Romans 5:12).

How do I keep my devotion simple? By keeping Christ himself at the centre of the means God gives, not merely the activities around him. Read the Gospels regularly, so that you know the Lord’s own face and voice and not only doctrines about him. Pray to him, not only about things. When you sit at the Lord’s Table, remember him rather than yourself. Watch what you allow to compete for the first and last thoughts of your day. And when you notice that the faith has become a complicated arrangement of opinions, projects and causes, go back to the cross and look at what he did there. Love is kept simple by looking at the one you love.

In a sentence. But Paul is afraid that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may somehow be led astray from your sincere and pure devotion to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Run an honest test. Not do I still believe it? You almost certainly do. Ask instead whether Christ is still simply and plainly the one you love most, or whether he has become one item in a complicated arrangement. And notice the questions that have been getting into your head lately: did God really mean that? Eve did not stop believing in God. She stopped being single-hearted toward him, and the fruit came afterwards.

For worship. The serpent’s whole strategy was to make God look stingy, and the gospel is God’s answer to that slander. The God who was accused of withholding the fruit did not withhold his own Son. The second Adam met the same tempter in a wilderness instead of a garden, hungry instead of filled, and answered every crafty question with the plain word of his Father. Where Eve was led astray, he stood; and he stands now for his bride, keeping her mind and heart until the day he presents her to himself, single and pure.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.

For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed. This is the most precise diagnosis of false teaching anywhere in Paul, and it repays being taken apart slowly. Three things can be counterfeited, and he names them in order: a Jesus, a Spirit, a gospel. Notice that in every case the counterfeit keeps the word. Nobody arrived in Corinth announcing a new deity. They preached Jesus. Same name, different person. The rivals seem to have preached a Jesus without the cross, perhaps a triumphant wonder-worker whose servants should be impressive, or a Jesus who required law-keeping.

Another and different. The Greek marks a distinction the English cannot quite carry. For another Jesus Paul uses allos, another of the same sort, a second one. For the spirit and the gospel he switches to heteros, different in kind, another species altogether. Whether he intends the full weight of the distinction is debated, but the drift is unmistakable: a substituted Jesus produces a different spirit, and a different spirit produces a message that is no longer the same kind of thing at all.

Or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received. Not a second Holy Spirit; there is only one. Paul means the spirit that animates a false gospel, a spirit of the world and ultimately of the devil, a spirit of pride, power and spectacle, which makes people bold in a different message and enslaves rather than frees (Romans 8:15; Galatians 1:6–7). The Holy Spirit produces humility and love and points away from himself to the crucified Christ. That is why John says, test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1).

Or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted. A message other than the gospel of grace through Christ crucified. Paul told the Galatians that even if an angel from heaven preached such a thing, he should be accursed (Galatians 1:6–9). A gospel is not a different gospel because it uses different words; it is a different gospel because it tells a different story about what is wrong with us and what God has done about it.

So how would you know? The name is unchanged, the vocabulary is unchanged, and the man preaching is impressive. This is the practical question the verse exists to answer, and the whole letter has been supplying the tests. Ask what this Jesus did. The real one was made sin for us and bore the wrath our sin deserved (5:21). A Jesus who is chiefly an example, a teacher, a life-coach or a source of personal power is a different Jesus, however warmly he is spoken of. Ask what this Jesus asks. The real one calls people to die to themselves and no longer live for themselves (5:15). A Jesus who asks nothing that costs anything has been substituted. Ask what the message does with the hearer’s sin. The genuine gospel names it and then deals with it at the cross; a message that never mentions it is not a gentler version of the gospel but a different one, because it leaves the hearer with his actual problem untouched. And ask what kind of ministers it produces: does the messenger bear the shape of the cross, or has he been made comfortable, admired and rich by the message he preaches?

You put up with it readily enough. Then the sting in the tail, and it is aimed at the Corinthians rather than the teachers. It is irony: you put up with them easily, so put up with me! But it is also the heart of the crisis. The tolerance is the danger. A church that would argue for an hour about the seating plan sat quietly while the identity of its Lord was adjusted.

Where Christians differ: another Jesus. Many groups use the name of Jesus while teaching a different person: a created being, a mere prophet, a spirit brother of Satan, a teacher of self-improvement. Verdict: The true Jesus is the one the apostles proclaimed: eternal Son of God, fully God and fully man, crucified for our sins, risen bodily, Lord of all. Any Jesus who differs from the apostolic Jesus is another Jesus, and any gospel that adds to or subtracts from grace through faith in him is another gospel (Galatians 1:8). Christians must test teachers by Scripture (1 John 4:1–3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every disagreement among Christians is a different gospel. It means the core identity and work of Christ are non-negotiable.

How do I tell a secondary disagreement from another gospel? Ask whether the difference changes who Christ is or how a sinner is put right with God. Believers who love the same Lord differ on the mode and subjects of baptism, on the details of the end times, on church government, on worship styles, and those differences matter, but they do not make another Jesus. Denying that Christ is fully God and fully man, denying his bodily resurrection, denying that his death paid for sin, or teaching that we are justified partly by our own works: these change the person or the gospel, and that is where Paul draws the line. A useful question is this: if the other person is right, would my hope before God be different? If not, it is a family disagreement; if so, it is a different gospel.

What if my church begins preaching another Jesus? Do not simply drift away in silence, and do not stay in silence either. First make sure you have understood correctly: listen carefully, read what is taught, and compare it honestly with Scripture. Then speak to the leaders privately and humbly, asking them to show you from the Bible why they teach what they teach. If the error is real and persistent and touches the person or work of Christ, you have a duty to protect yourself and your family, and you should find a faithful church where the apostolic Jesus is preached. Leave without bitterness, and keep praying for those you leave behind.

In a sentence. For if someone comes to you and preaches a Jesus other than the Jesus we preached, or if you receive a different spirit from the Spirit you received, or a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it easily enough.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear about Jesus by Scripture, whether from a pulpit, a podcast, a bestseller or a song. Is it the Jesus of the apostles? The abiding danger is not solved by suspicion. It is solved by knowing the real one well enough that the substitute does not sound right, which is how, as the old saying goes, bank clerks were trained to spot forgeries: not by studying counterfeits, but by handling the genuine note until anything else felt wrong in the hand. Spend more time with the Gospels than with commentary on them.

For worship. There is only one Jesus, and he cannot be improved on. Every counterfeit is a smaller Christ: a teacher without a cross, a wonder-worker without wounds, a helper without a throne. The real one is more than all of them together, the eternal Son who took our flesh, bore our curse, broke out of the grave and reigns. Nobody needs another Jesus, because this one is enough for every sinner and every century, and he has given the one Spirit to everyone who trusts him so that they may know his voice from a stranger’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.

Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. The word is Paul’s own coinage and it drips: hyperlian apostoloi, literally the extra-super apostles, the more-than-apostles. It is the tone of a man repeating a title other people use with a straight face.

Who were they? Not, on balance, the Jerusalem apostles. Paul has no quarrel with Peter and James here and would not speak of them like this. These are the newcomers in Corinth, almost certainly the same men he will call false apostles in verse 13, and the title is either their own or the impression they had created: men who claimed a status above Paul’s.

Even if I am unskilled in speaking. Then the concession, and it is remarkable that he makes it. The word is idiōtēs: a layman, an amateur, a man without professional training. It is where our word idiot comes from, though it did not mean that; it meant untrained. He is granting the charge of 10:10. He was not a trained orator, or he refused to use the orator’s tricks, and in a Greek city that was not a small thing. Public speaking was the prestige skill of the age, taught by paid professionals and judged by crowds who knew the technique. Against a man who had been taught to handle an audience, Paul evidently sounded ordinary. And he lets it stand. He does not claim hidden eloquence or plead that his letters prove otherwise.

I am not so in knowledge. He simply moves the contest to different ground. What knowledge? Not cleverness in general. He means knowledge of God and of the gospel, the mystery of Christ revealed to him (Ephesians 3:3–4), the thing he has spent ten chapters unfolding, from the new covenant to the great exchange. He is saying: I may not be able to hold a room the way they can, but I know what I am talking about, and they do not.

Two separate gifts. That distinction is worth carrying, because the church loses it about once a generation. The ability to speak well and the possession of something worth saying are two different gifts, and they do not always come together. When they do, it is a great mercy. But an audience cannot easily tell them apart, which is why an articulate man with a thin message will generally be preferred to a plain man with a deep one, and the preference is usually described as a preference for good communication.

Indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things. Then Paul adds the one claim he does make for his manner. Not impressive. Plain. His teaching among them had proved it: whatever he lacked in polish, nobody in Corinth could say they had failed to understand him. That is a better ambition for anyone who teaches, and a considerably harder one. Being admired is easier than being understood, and the two are frequently confused by everyone involved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean polished speaking is wrong. Apollos was eloquent, and Paul honoured him (Acts 18:24; 1 Corinthians 3:6). It means content matters more than style, and that a gift for words is a servant of the truth, never a substitute for it.

Should I choose a church for its preaching style? Choose it first for what is preached. Ask whether the sermons open the Bible and say what the passage says; whether Christ crucified and risen is at the centre; whether you are being fed, corrected and comforted by God’s word rather than entertained. Style is not nothing: a preacher should work hard to be clear, and a dull sermon is no virtue. But a plain man who handles the Scriptures faithfully will do your soul more good over ten years than a brilliant speaker with little to say. If your pastor is not gifted as an orator, thank God for his faithfulness, and listen for the substance.

In a sentence. Paul does not think he is in the least inferior to those super-apostles. He may indeed be untrained as a speaker, but he does have knowledge. We have made this perfectly clear to you in every way.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last sermon or talk that impressed you, and ask what you can remember of its content. Then think of a plain sermon that genuinely changed something in you. The two may not be the same. And if you teach anyone, a class, a small group, your own children, aim to be understood rather than admired.

For worship. God has never needed the world’s eloquence. He spoke creation into being with a word and saved the world through a Word made flesh, who had no form or majesty that we should look at him. The Lord of glory chose fishermen and a tentmaker with a weak voice, so that our faith would rest not on the wisdom of men but on the power of God. Thank him for every plain preacher who has told you the truth about Christ, and for the Christ they told you about, whose own words were spirit and life.
verseByVerse.note: “Super-apostles” is Paul’s ironic name for the rival teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.

Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted? Now the strangest accusation in the letter. Paul is having to defend himself for not charging them money. The question is bitter and it is meant to be: he is quoting the shape of the complaint back at them. Somehow, working for nothing had been turned into evidence against him. Humbling myself means his manual labour: he worked with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), a lowly trade in Greek eyes, so that they might be lifted up by the gospel.

How Corinth read it. To see why this was a complaint, you have to understand how a Greek city thought. Teachers of standing were supported, by fees or by a wealthy patron who housed them and gained prestige from the association. Payment was the mark of worth. A man who worked with his hands to support himself was, by that reckoning, a tradesman rather than a professional, and manual labour carried real social contempt. Paul’s rivals took money, lived as guests of important people, and looked exactly like what a serious teacher was supposed to look like. So his refusal was not read as integrity. It was read two ways, both damaging: either he knew his teaching was not worth paying for, or, worse in that culture, he was refusing to enter the relationship of obligation that a gift creates, which is a way of holding people at arm’s length.

Because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? Was that a crime? (1 Corinthians 9:12–18). Notice the phrase God’s gospel. It was not his to sell. The message that cost God his Son was offered in Corinth without a price tag, and the messenger made sure his own conduct said the same thing.

I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you. The irony is heavy. “Robbed” (sylaō) is a military word: to plunder, to strip a defeated enemy. He is saying, with a straight face: yes, I took money; I took it from Macedonia, and spent it on you. It is a deliberate exaggeration. He did not steal; he accepted gifts from poorer churches so that he could serve the richer Corinthians free. And the Macedonians, we already know, were desperately poor (8:2).

A right he declined. There is a real principle underneath the irony, and Paul is careful about it elsewhere. He believed firmly that ministers should be supported. He argues it at length in the earlier letter and concludes that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14). He is not laying down a rule that ministry must be unpaid. He is describing a right he declined to use, in this city, for a reason. In a place where money bought influence and created obligation, taking it would have compromised the gospel he preached and given his rivals a way to claim equivalence. He removed the stumbling block (6:3) at real personal cost.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul stole. It means he accepted gifts that made his Corinthian ministry possible. Nor does it mean that a minister who is paid is less faithful than one who is not.

Should my pastor be paid? Yes. Scripture is clear that those who labour in preaching and teaching are worthy of their wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6), and a church that underpays its pastor while expecting all his time is not imitating Paul but disobeying Paul. Some ministers rightly work another job, by necessity or by choice, as Paul did in Corinth and as many church planters and pastors of small congregations do today; that is honourable, not second-class. The point of this passage is the motive and the effect: money must never buy influence over the message, and a minister must be willing to give up his rights when they would hinder the gospel.

In a sentence. Was it a sin for Paul to lower himself in order to lift you up by preaching the gospel of God to you free of charge? He robbed other churches by receiving support from them so as to serve you.

On a Tuesday. Ask what your giving buys, and whether anyone in your congregation could reasonably think that money has purchased influence over what is preached. Give generously and then let go of it. And ask the harder personal question: are you willing to be humbled, to do the lowly thing, the unpaid thing, the thing that will be misread, so that others may be lifted up? Paul was willing to sit up half the night cutting leather to make sure nobody could think he was selling Christ.

For worship. The Lord whom Paul served humbled himself so that we might be exalted, and did it free of charge. He who was rich became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (8:9). He took the form of a servant, worked with his hands in a carpenter’s shop, had nowhere to lay his head, and at the end was stripped of his only garment. Every free sermon Paul preached in Corinth was a small picture of that. The gospel is offered without money and without price because Someone else has paid it all.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.

And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone. He fills in the detail, and the detail matters. He was not comfortable. There were times in Corinth when he did not have enough. And still he did not ask. The word behind burden is a vivid one, katanarkaō: to be a dead weight, to numb something by pressing on it. He would not be that to them.

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. Where did the money come from? From Macedonia, and Philippi most likely. Silas and Timothy arrived from there while Paul was in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and the Philippians sent to him repeatedly, which he acknowledges warmly (Philippians 4:15–16). So the picture is this: the poorest churches in the region were funding the apostle’s work in the richest city he served, so that the rich church would not have to pay and could not say it had.

So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. He will continue the policy. Past, present and future are all in the sentence: he did not, he does not, he will not.

As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. Then the vow, and it is put under oath. He intends to go on refusing their money and he intends to go on saying so (1 Corinthians 9:15). That sounds stubborn until you see what it protects. If Paul once accepted support in Corinth, the whole distinction between himself and the men who had come for what they could get would collapse, and with it the one visible proof that he was not in this for anything. And notice the geography: in the regions of Achaia, not merely in Corinth. He is staking this across the whole province, in every congregation that will hear the letter read. A position taken that publicly cannot quietly be dropped later, which is presumably why he took it that publicly.

The cost of an unimpeachable position. There is a lesson here, and it is not a comfortable one. Paul’s policy did not make his life easier. It made him poorer, it made him tired, and it was used against him anyway. He kept it because the gospel’s credibility was worth more to him than his own comfort or his own reputation. Most decisions of that kind are invisible and unrewarded. The businessman who loses the contract rather than pay what everyone pays. The person who declines the gift because of what accepting it would quietly imply. The minister who will not let a major donor into the decision. None of these gets noticed, and several of them get misread as pride, as Paul’s was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean accepting support is wrong. Paul accepted it from others, gladly, and thanked them for it as a fragrant offering to God (Philippians 4:18).

Was Paul wrong to swear an oath, when Jesus said do not swear? No. The Lord was forbidding the casual oaths people used to make their ordinary words sound weightier, and the games of swearing by lesser things so that the oath did not really bind (Matthew 5:33–37). He was not forbidding every solemn appeal to God in a serious matter: God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13), and Jesus answered under oath at his trial (Matthew 26:63–64). Paul calls on the truth of Christ in him because his honesty is under attack and the gospel’s honour is at stake. Christians may take a lawful oath when the matter is weighty and the occasion requires it (Westminster 22.2), but their everyday yes should be simply yes.

Is it wrong to accept a gift that comes with strings? A gift given freely in love should be received with thanks, and refusing it out of pride is no virtue. But some gifts are not really gifts: they buy access, silence, influence or a favour later. Ask what accepting it would imply to the giver and to others, and whether it would make you less free to do what is right. If it would, decline it graciously and, where you can, explain why. Paul’s rule was simple: whatever would hinder the gospel, he would rather do without.

In a sentence. And when Paul was with you and needed something, he was not a burden to anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what he needed. He has kept himself from being a burden to you in any way, and will continue to do so. As surely as the truth of Christ is in him, nobody in Achaia will stop this boasting of his.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone who quietly supports gospel work at cost to themselves, the Macedonians of your world, and thank them, or join them. And ask whether there is a position you need to keep, at some cost, because the alternative would quietly compromise your witness. Keep it without fuss, and let God be the one who notices.

For worship. Behind the poor churches of Macedonia stands the God who supplies every need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. He has never been a burden to his people; he carries them. He fed Paul through the gifts of widows and labourers in Philippi, and he feeds his church still through the generosity of people who will never be thanked in public. The truth of Christ was in Paul, and the truth of Christ is that the Son of God came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

verseByVerse.quote: And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.

And why? Because I do not love you? He anticipates the obvious misreading and answers it before it can be spoken. Some said Paul refused their money because he did not care about them. That is what refusing a gift can look like from the outside, and in that culture it looked like it very strongly. To decline hospitality was to decline a relationship.

God knows I do! His answer is not an argument. It is a short sentence, with God as the witness, and nothing offered by way of proof. There are some things you cannot demonstrate to people who have decided otherwise, and the attempt to demonstrate them usually makes matters worse. He states it, calls God to witness it, and moves on.

When you have been misread. Anyone who has been misjudged by people they love will recognise the position. You can explain once. After that, explaining becomes its own kind of evidence against you, and the only thing left is to go on loving them and let God hold the record. Paul was doing all of it, the night work, the poverty, the humiliation of being thought worthless because he would not charge, for people who at that moment believed he did not love them.

And what I am doing I will continue to do. He will keep preaching free of charge. Not because he is stubborn, but because the reason has not gone away.

In order to undermine the claim. Here is the actual strategy. The rivals took payment and wanted parity. They wanted to be able to say: we operate on exactly the same terms as Paul, so judge us as you judge him. And the one thing that made the comparison impossible was the money. So long as Paul worked for nothing and they took payment, the difference was visible to everybody, and no amount of talking could close it. “Undermine” (ekkoptō) means to cut off, to cut the ground from under. That is what his empty purse did.

Evidence that cannot be copied. There is a principle in that worth carrying beyond first-century Corinth. When two accounts of a person are in circulation and words will not settle it, what settles it is a pattern of behaviour that would be irrational for a self-interested man to sustain. Paul’s poverty was an argument no rival could answer, because they could not copy it without becoming what they were pretending to be.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was being stubborn. He had a strategic reason, and love was underneath it.

What should I do when people I love think the worst of me? Say the truth once, plainly and without heat, as Paul does here. Then stop arguing. Commit your reputation to God, who knows, and go on doing good to the people who misjudge you, which over time is the only answer that persuades. Examine yourself honestly in case some of the criticism is true, and own that part. Do not withdraw your love to punish them, and do not keep a ledger of the injustice. The Lord who was misread more than anyone entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

In a sentence. Why? Because he does not love you? God knows he does! And he will keep on doing what he is doing in order to cut the ground from under those who want an opportunity to be considered equal with us in the things they boast about.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes love means refusing what is offered, so that the gospel is not compromised. And sometimes love means going on serving people who have decided you do not love them. Think of someone in that position in your life, and do one kind thing for them this week that asks nothing back.

For worship. God knows. It is the most comforting phrase in the paragraph. The God who searches the heart knew Paul’s love when Corinth doubted it, and he knows the love and the motives of his servants still, when no one else does. And his own love for us does not depend on our recognising it. He loved us while we thought him a hard master, while we were enemies, and he went on loving until the cross made it impossible to doubt. Christ was misread by everyone he came to save, and loved them to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

For such men are false apostles. The gloves come off. Paul has been ironic for twelve verses; here he simply says what these men are. Three descriptions, each worse than the last. False apostles, pseudapostoloi, a word that appears nowhere else in the New Testament and that Paul may have coined for the occasion. He names them plainly.

Deceitful workmen. “Deceitful” (dolioi) means crafty, treacherous, baiting a hook. They are workmen: skilled, busy, productive. The problem is not incompetence but craft. They work, but for themselves, by trickery, producing counterfeits.

Disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. The verb, metaschēmatizō, means to change one’s outward form, to put on an appearance, to masquerade. They look like apostles, but are not. Notice that Paul does not say they are sincere men who have gone wrong. That would be the charitable reading and Paul rejects it. These are people who are working a disguise.

And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. Then the explanation, and it is one of the most sobering sentences in the New Testament. Stop at no wonder. Paul is saying the church should not be surprised by this. It is the expected pattern, working exactly as it always has. And the pattern is not what most people imagine. The popular picture of evil is darkness, grotesquerie, something obviously repellent, which is precisely why the real thing gets through. Satan does not usually appear as obvious evil but as something beautiful, spiritual, enlightening. His most effective form is not the monster. It is the angel of light: the impressive, the luminous, the manifestly spiritual, the thing that looks better than what you already have. His most dangerous tactic is to imitate truth.

Discernment cannot run on instinct. If you are waiting to feel uneasy, you will be caught, because the whole point of the disguise is that it produces the opposite feeling. People do not follow false teachers reluctantly; they follow them enthusiastically, and describe the experience as the most spiritually alive they have ever been. So the test can never be how did it make me feel? It has to be the one Paul gave in verse 4: which Jesus, which Spirit, which gospel. Those are questions of content, and they can be answered by an ordinary Christian with a Bible, on a Tuesday, without any special sensitivity at all.

Nobody forges a worthless note. There is a mercy folded into the warning. The disguise exists because the genuine article is the only thing worth counterfeiting. That an enemy has gone to the trouble of imitating apostles of Christ is itself a backhanded testimony to what apostles of Christ actually carry. And the light he borrows to disguise himself is not his own, and never was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every teacher we disagree with is a false apostle. These men preached another Jesus and another gospel (v. 4). The label belongs to those who corrupt the person of Christ or the gospel itself, not to brothers who are mistaken about secondary things.

Does Satan really appear as an angel? The point here is disguise rather than visions: Satan’s usual angel of light is a teacher, a message, a movement that looks holy. But the warning also covers the spectacular. Paul told the Galatians that even an angel from heaven preaching another gospel is to be rejected (Galatians 1:8). So a vision, a voice, a dream or a miracle proves nothing by itself. God’s revelation is complete in Scripture, and every claim to a new word from God must be tested by what he has already said, and refused if it adds to it or contradicts it. Christ’s sheep are not kept safe by experiences; they are kept by his voice in his word.

Can I call someone a false teacher without being harsh? Yes, and you should be careful to. Be sure of the facts, and judge the teaching by Scripture, not by rumour or by a clip taken out of context. Keep the label for what touches the gospel itself. Speak about the teaching more than the person’s motives, which only God sees fully. Warn those who are in danger, because love for them requires it. And pray for the teacher, because he too can be rescued. Paul is severe here because a church is being lost; he is never cruel, and he never enjoys it.

In a sentence. For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.

On a Tuesday. Think of the voices that most shape your faith at the moment, the authors, preachers, influencers and friends. Ask of each, not how inspiring they are, but which Jesus they present and what they do with the cross. Not everything that looks bright and spiritual is from God. Discernment is not suspicion of everything; it is familiarity with the true light.

For worship. Satan can only borrow light; Christ is the light. He is the true light that gives light to everyone, the radiance of the glory of God, the one in whom is no darkness at all. Every counterfeit is a dim reflection of his brightness, and every disguise will be stripped off on the day he appears. Until then he keeps his sheep, and no one can snatch them out of his hand. The angel of light is a liar; the Light of the world laid down his life.

verseByVerse.quote: So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.

So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. The logic completes. If the master appears as light, his servants will appear as righteousness. The disguise runs all the way down. Satan has his ministers, diakonoi, the same word Paul uses of himself and of true servants of Christ. They talk of righteousness, perhaps law-keeping, morality or holiness, but they are his.

Servants of righteousness. Note carefully what they are disguised as. Not as scholars, not as leaders, not as men of power. As servants of righteousness: that is, as morally serious people. This is the most effective camouflage there is in a religious community, because it is the last thing anyone thinks to question. A man who is visibly rigorous about right and wrong is granted enormous latitude, and rightly so most of the time, which is exactly what makes the disguise worth wearing.

Severity that looks like holiness. It is worth being honest about how the counterfeit usually presents. It is very often more demanding than the genuine article, not less. The Judaizers in Galatia wanted more law, not less. The false teachers of Colossae wanted more self-denial. There is a kind of severity that looks like holiness and is actually a bid for control, and Paul had seen enough of it to name it: such rules have an appearance of wisdom in self-made religion and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:23).

Their end will correspond to their deeds. Then the last sentence, and Paul does not enlarge on it. Two things are in it. First, there is an end, telos: final judgment. The disguise is temporary; it works now and it does not work then. Everything about these men that is currently persuasive has a date attached to it (Philippians 3:19; 2 Peter 2:1–3). Second, the correspondence is to deeds, not appearances. What is judged is what was actually done, not what it looked like, which is the exact reversal of the Corinthian situation, where appearance was carrying everything.

The restraint. He says it in one line and stops, and the restraint is deliberate. He does not gloat over it, speculate about it, or use it as a threat. He simply notes that the accounts will be settled somewhere he is not required to settle them. And that is what frees a man to speak plainly and then let the matter go. Paul names these people for what they are, because the church is in danger and somebody has to. He does not have to destroy them, and he does not try. The Judge of all the earth will do right, and he can be left to it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they knew they were Satan’s servants. Deceivers can be deceived (2 Timothy 3:13). But they are accountable.

Can a false teacher repent and be saved? Yes. While a man lives, the door of repentance is open, and Paul himself is the proof: the fiercest enemy of the gospel became its greatest preacher. He tells Timothy to correct opponents with gentleness, in the hope that God may grant them repentance and they may escape from the snare of the devil (2 Timothy 2:25–26). So we warn against the teaching firmly, and we pray for the teacher sincerely. What we may not do is pretend the danger is small, or assume that a man who dies still leading others astray will be excused.

Should I listen to false teachers to understand them? Most Christians do not need to, and many should not. If you are not responsible for answering a teaching, there is little gain in feeding on it, and real danger, because the disguise is designed to work. Pastors and those who must protect others may need to study it carefully, and should do so with prayer, with good guides and with their Bibles open. For everyone else, the best protection is to know the true gospel deeply and to stay close to a faithful church. You do not have to taste every dish to know which one is poisoned.

In a sentence. It is not surprising, then, if his servants also masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will be what their actions deserve.

On a Tuesday. Look past the outward appearance of teachers, including the appearance of strictness. Test their message and their fruit (Matthew 7:15–20). And if you have been hurt by a leader who used righteousness as a weapon, take comfort: their end will correspond to their deeds, and you do not have to arrange it.

For worship. There is a true Servant of righteousness, and he is not in disguise. Christ is the Righteous One, who fulfilled all righteousness and then gave it away: he became sin for us so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (5:21). The false servants use righteousness to bind people; the true one uses it to clothe them. And because the Judge of all the earth will do right, his people can leave every unsettled account in his hands and rest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — The Fool’s Boast and the Catalogue of Sufferings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says again that he is not really a fool, but if they insist on thinking so, they can let him boast a little like one. He admits that this kind of boasting is not how the Lord would speak; it is the way of the flesh, which the rivals practise. The Corinthians, so wise in their own eyes, happily put up with fools, and even with leaders who enslave, exploit, take advantage, act superior and slap them in the face. Paul confesses, ironically, that he was too weak for that. Then he matches the rivals’ claims: like them he is a Hebrew, an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, and as a servant of Christ he outdoes them, in labours, imprisonments, beatings and near-deaths. He lists floggings in the synagogues, Roman beatings, a stoning, three shipwrecks and a night and day adrift, and every kind of danger on his travels, along with toil, sleeplessness, hunger, thirst, cold and exposure. On top of all that comes the daily pressure of concern for all the churches; he feels every believer’s weakness and burns over every one who is made to stumble. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness, and he swears before God that he is telling the truth. He ends with an anti-climax: at Damascus, when the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city to arrest him, he escaped by being let down through a window in a basket.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of sufferings is Paul’s primary credential. In his opponents’ world, apostolic legitimacy was demonstrated by impressive spiritual experiences (visions, tongues, miraculous signs) and social credibility (letters of recommendation, personal charisma, philosophical sophistication). Paul’s credential is precisely the opposite: a body broken by service, a life spent in the pattern of the cross. This is not masochism; it is the coherence of messenger and message. The one who preaches a crucified Christ must bear in his body the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A church’s senior pastor has served for 25 years in a difficult context: modest attendance, a neighbourhood in decline, countless crises with little visible breakthrough. When a search committee from a larger church comes to interview him, they ask about his “greatest ministry successes.” He does not know what to say. This passage suggests a different category: the 25-year record of faithfulness in hardship, the daily anxiety for the congregation, the pattern of showing up — this is the apostolic credential. The question “what have you built?” is not the only or even the primary question.

verseByVerse.quote: I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

I repeat, let no one think me foolish. Three verses of throat-clearing before the fool’s speech proper, and the hesitation is the point. Paul is not really a fool; he is playing a part, and he wants everyone to know it is a part.

But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting in order to expose it, and he calls it what it is: foolishness. In ancient drama the fool was the character who could say what others could not, and Paul takes up the role deliberately. If the Corinthians insist on weighing men by their boasts, he will give them a boast to weigh, and they will not like what is in it.

What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. He says it as plainly as it can be said. This is Paul telling us that what follows is not how a Christian should ordinarily talk. Our Lord did not go about listing his qualifications. Boasting about oneself is not Christlike, and Paul does it under protest. That candour is worth noticing for what it says about Scripture. Paul is inspired here, and what he is inspired to record is that he is about to do something he regards as beneath the gospel. The Bible is not a collection of model speeches; it is God’s word given through real men in real situations, and here it preserves an apostle telling us he is arguing in the world’s way on purpose.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. According to the flesh means about worldly credentials and achievements, the things that impress the natural man. Then why do it? Because the alternative was worse. If Paul stayed silent while impressive men listed their credentials, the Corinthians would draw the obvious conclusion, and a church would be lost to a different gospel. So he enters a contest he despises, in order to win people out of it.

Answer a fool according to his folly. There is a genuine pastoral principle here and it is easily misapplied in both directions. Sometimes the only way to reach people is to meet them briefly on their own ground: to answer, as Proverbs puts it in one of its two facing maxims, a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes (Proverbs 26:5). Paul is doing that. What keeps it from becoming mere worldliness is that he says out loud what he is doing and why, so that nobody can mistake the tactic for the truth. The misapplication is the church that adopts the world’s methods for the world’s reasons and calls it strategy. The difference is visible in two places: whether the borrowing is acknowledged as a concession or presented as wisdom, and whether the man doing it is enjoying himself. Paul is plainly not enjoying himself.

Detonated from the inside. And watch what he does with the game once he has entered it. He is about to take the conventions of ancient self-praise, ancestry, achievements, hardships nobly borne, and fill them with floggings, shipwrecks, hunger, and an undignified escape in a basket. He does not win the contest. He blows it apart from the inside, which is a great deal more effective than refusing to play.

What it does not mean. It does not mean this passage is less inspired. Paul is deliberately using irony, under the Spirit’s guidance. Every word of the fool’s speech is true, and God meant it to be written; what Paul disowns is the manner of boasting, not the truth of what he says.

Is it ever right for me to talk about my achievements? Yes, when there is a real need and the aim is not your glory. A job application, a reference, a report to the people you are accountable to, a testimony of what God has done: all of these may require you to state plainly what you have done. Paul does it here to protect a church. The test is the motive and the manner. Are you saying it because someone needs to know, or because you need to be admired? Do you say it truthfully, without inflation, and give God the credit? And can you stop once the need is met? If you find you are always steering conversations toward your successes, that is the boasting Paul calls foolish.

In a sentence. Paul repeats: let no one take him for a fool. But if you do, then tolerate him just as you would a fool, so that he may do a little boasting. In this self-confident boasting he is not talking as the Lord would, but as a fool. Since many are boasting in the way the world does, he too will boast.

On a Tuesday. Notice the moments today when you feel the urge to let someone know how well you have done, how busy you are, how much you know. You need not obey it. And when you must speak of yourself, do it plainly, briefly, and with a sense of how little of it is really yours.

For worship. The only person who ever had the right to boast never did it for himself. Christ, who could have listed his credentials from eternity, the Word who was with God and was God, the maker of the stars, emptied himself and took the lowest place. He did not come to be served. The Father boasted of him instead: this is my beloved Son. And because he did not seek his own glory, every knee will one day bow to him, and every tongue confess him Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting to expose it, calling it foolishness.

verseByVerse.quote: For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.

For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! The irony turns savage here, and it is aimed squarely at the congregation. Paul is throwing their own self-image back at them. Corinth prided itself on discernment; the earlier letter is full of their confidence about knowledge and wisdom. You are so wise, he says, that you happily put up with fools. And these connoisseurs have been sitting contentedly under men Paul has just called servants of Satan. Then comes a list of five things they have put up with. Read them slowly, because Paul is not speaking in generalities; this is what was happening in that room.

For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you. Someone had taken control: over consciences, over decisions, over what could be questioned. The false apostles were enslaving them, governing their lives in a way Paul had refused to do (1:24).

Or devours you. The word is used of eating something up, and it is about money. These teachers were consuming the church’s resources, demanding payment and living on it. The Lord used the same word of the scribes who devour widows’ houses (Mark 12:40).

Or takes advantage of you. “Takes advantage” (lambanō) means takes, catches, as with bait: exploitation dressed up as ministry.

Or puts on airs. Literally, lifts himself up (epairō). The manner of a man who has let it be known that he is a considerable person, and that you are fortunate to have him.

Or strikes you in the face. And here the list may stop being metaphorical. It is quite possible that somebody had physically hit a member of that congregation, and the congregation had borne it. Or it may be a figure for public humiliation. Either way, it is abusive leadership. That is the whole indictment: a church that would not tolerate an apostle who worked with his hands, and did tolerate a man who slapped them.

Why people submit to it. It is worth asking why, because the pattern has never gone away and it is not obvious. Why do people submit to domineering leaders and resent gentle ones? Part of the answer is that confidence is easily mistaken for authority, and a man who behaves as if he has the right to treat you badly creates the impression that he must have it. Part of it is that being under a strong figure relieves the burden of thinking. And part of it is simply that harshness feels like seriousness, so a leader who is hard on people seems more committed to the truth than one who is gentle. Set the list beside 1:24, not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, and the two portraits could not be further apart. One of these men founded the church and refused its money; the others enslaved it, ate it, and struck it. The Corinthians could not tell which was the apostle.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians were stupid. It means they had been impressed by dominating personalities and mistook abuse for authority, which clever people do as easily as simple ones.

What does spiritual abuse look like? It is the use of spiritual authority to control, exploit or harm people. Its marks are often the five in this verse. Control: you may not question the leader, and doubting him is treated as doubting God. Exploitation: money, time or bodies are taken for the leader’s benefit. Manipulation: guilt, fear and shame are used to get compliance. Self-exaltation: the leader is beyond correction and surrounded by people who protect him. Humiliation: people are shamed in public, isolated or frightened. Physical harm or sexual misconduct is not spiritual abuse only; it is a crime. A godly leader can be firm, but he will always welcome questions, admit his faults, protect the weak, and point you to Christ rather than himself.

What should I do if I am being abused by a church leader? Tell someone you trust, outside his circle of influence, and do not carry it alone. If you are in danger, or a crime has been committed, go to the police; that is not disloyalty to the church but obedience to God, who appointed the authorities to protect the vulnerable (Romans 13:4). Bring it to the other elders, or to the wider body the church belongs to, and put what has happened in writing. You may need to leave, and it is not a sin to do so. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered up in the name of peace or forgiveness. Forgiveness does not require you to stay within reach of harm, and Christ is never honoured by a church that protects the wolf instead of the sheep.

Doesn’t the Bible tell me to submit to my leaders? Yes, to leaders who keep watch over your souls as those who will have to give an account (Hebrews 13:17). That submission is real, and a healthy church will gladly follow godly elders without needing everything explained. But it is not unlimited. Elders are commanded not to domineer over those in their charge but to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3). No leader may bind your conscience beyond the word of God (Westminster 20.2), command you to sin, or demand obedience that belongs to Christ alone. The more a leader insists on his own authority, the more carefully you should ask whether he is exercising Christ’s.

In a sentence. You gladly put up with fools since you are so wise! In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or puts on airs or slaps you in the face.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual abuse is real. If a leader controls, exploits or humiliates people, that is not Christlike authority. Seek help, and help others to find it. And think about the leaders you have found most impressive: was it the force of their personality, or their likeness to Christ?

For worship. The Lord of the church is the Good Shepherd, and the Good Shepherd is the opposite of the man in this verse. He does not enslave; he sets free. He does not devour; he feeds. He does not take advantage; he lays down his life. He does not lift himself up; he washed his disciples’ feet. He did not strike anyone in the face; he gave his own face to those who struck him and spat on him. Every bruised sheep can run to him, and he will carry it in his arms.

verseByVerse.quote: To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!
verseByVerse.commentary:
To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!

To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that! One line, and it is the sharpest sentence in the letter. The tone is impossible to miss. Paul has just listed five ways the Corinthians have been mistreated, and now, with mock contrition, he apologises for never having managed any of them. To my shame, I am sorry to say, we were too weak for that. Too weak to enslave you. Too weak to eat your money. Too feeble to hit anyone. The Corinthians had called Paul weak (10:10); he turns the charge around. If gentleness is weakness, he admits it. His weakness was Christlike gentleness.

Sarcasm in Scripture. It is sarcasm, and it is worth noting that Scripture contains it. Elijah used it on the prophets of Baal, suggesting that their god might be asleep and need waking (1 Kings 18:27); the Lord used something like it on the Pharisees more than once. It is a legitimate instrument, and like most sharp instruments it is safe only in particular hands and for particular purposes.

What makes it defensible here. Notice what makes Paul’s use of it right. It is not aimed at the weak; it is aimed at people in comfortable error who have stopped listening to plain speech. It is used to defend others rather than himself: the ones being enslaved and struck are the ones he is speaking for. And it comes after ten chapters of tenderness, so nobody could mistake it for his settled attitude. Sarcasm from a man who is habitually gentle is a shock; from a habitually sharp man it is just his manner, and it accomplishes nothing.

Real strength. Underneath the irony is a real definition of strength, and it is the thing the Corinthians had turned upside down. They had read Paul’s refusal to dominate as weakness. He is showing them what that judgment commits them to: if refusing to exploit people is weakness, then exploitation is strength, and the men who had been eating them alive were the strong ones. Say it out loud and the position collapses, which is exactly why he says it out loud. Real strength, in this letter, is the capacity to be wronged and not retaliate, to hold power and decline to use it, to be thought a fool rather than manipulate people into a better opinion. It is the strength of a Lord who could have called more than twelve legions of angels and did not open his mouth (Matthew 26:53; 27:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul regretted being gentle. The shame is mock shame. He would not trade his weakness for their strength for anything.

May I use sarcasm? Rarely, and with great care. Scripture shows it can serve the truth, but James warns how much damage the tongue can do (James 3:5–10), and Paul elsewhere says our speech should always be gracious (Colossians 4:6). Ask the questions Paul’s use passes. Am I defending someone else, or protecting my pride? Is it aimed at comfortable error, or at someone weak or hurting? Would the person know I love them? And is it my habit, or a rare exception? Never use it on your children, your spouse, or anyone who is struggling. If you are known for a sharp tongue, the safest course is to put it away entirely.

In a sentence. To Paul’s shame he admits that we were too weak for that!

On a Tuesday. Notice where you are tempted to treat gentleness as weakness, in a leader, a parent, a colleague, yourself. And ask where you are holding power over someone, at work, at home, in church, and whether you are using it to serve them or to get your way.

For worship. Thank God for leaders who are too weak to abuse, who serve gently like Christ, because they are copies of the original. The Lord Jesus was the strongest man who ever lived, and the gentlest. He had the power to destroy his enemies with a word and used it to heal the ear of a man who came to arrest him. He was crucified in weakness, and lives by the power of God (13:4). The weakness of God is stronger than men.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.

Are they Hebrews? The fool’s speech begins in earnest, and the rhythm is a drumbeat: three questions, three identical answers. So am I. The rivals were Jewish Christians who boasted of their pedigree, and each of the three words carries a different weight. Hebrews is the language and culture claim: not merely Jewish by birth but Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking, perhaps from Palestine, raised in the tradition rather than assimilated into the Greek world. Paul was entitled to it; he tells the Philippians he was a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), and Luke records him addressing a Jerusalem crowd in Aramaic to their evident surprise (Acts 21:40–22:2).

Are they Israelites? So am I. This is the covenant claim: members of the people God chose, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law (Romans 9:4; 11:1).

Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I. The promise claim: heirs of the man to whom God swore that in him all nations would be blessed. Paul matches them three times without elaborating, and the flatness of the repetition is doing the work. He is refusing to make a speech about it. Whatever they have, he has, and there is nothing more to say.

Why he does not dismantle it here. What is striking is what he does not do. Elsewhere, when the same credentials were being used to bind Gentile Christians to the law, he took them apart completely: he listed his own pedigree in full and then said that whatever gain he had he counted as loss for the sake of Christ, and counted it as rubbish (Philippians 3:7–8). He is capable of dismantling this whole category and has done it. He does not do it here because it is not the issue. The rivals are not, as far as we can tell, demanding circumcision; they are trading on prestige. So Paul simply refuses them the advantage and moves on to the ground where the real difference lies.

A contest that ends in a tie. And that is the shape of the whole passage. A contest of credentials always ends in a tie, because credentials are the sort of thing that can be matched. The Corinthians were weighing two sets of qualifications and were going to be persuaded by whoever had the better list. Paul is about to show them that the question was never what a man has been given, but what he has been willing to lose.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish ancestry gives spiritual superiority. Paul counts it as rubbish compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). He matches their boasts only to show they mean nothing. Nor does it mean the privileges of Israel were nothing in themselves; Paul calls them real gifts of God (Romans 9:4–5). They simply cannot be a ground of boasting before him.

Does my Christian upbringing count for anything? It counts as a gift, not as a credential. To be raised in a believing home, to have learned the Scriptures early, to have been prayed for by name: these are great mercies, like Timothy’s, who knew the sacred writings from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15). Thank God for them. But they do not make you a Christian, and they give you no standing above someone converted last month from a life of open sin. Each of us stands before God only in Christ. And if you came to faith with no background at all, you have lost nothing that matters: the newest believer is as fully a child of Abraham by faith as the oldest member (Galatians 3:7).

In a sentence. Are they Hebrews? So is Paul. Are they Israelites? So is he. Are they Abraham’s descendants? So is he.

On a Tuesday. Your background, whatever it is, does not make you better or worse before God. Christ is all. Notice the credentials you quietly rely on to feel secure, or to feel superior, your family, your education, your church, your years of service, and lay them down before him.

For worship. The true Hebrew of Hebrews, the true Israelite, the true offspring of Abraham, is Christ himself, the seed to whom the promises were made. Everything Israel was meant to be, he was. And he did not cling to his pedigree any more than to his equality with God; he spent it, to make Gentiles who had no pedigree at all into children of Abraham by faith. In him there is neither Jew nor Greek, and all the promises of God find their yes.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
