Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.

Are they servants of Christ? The fourth question breaks the pattern. The first three got so am I; this one gets I am a better one. Here Paul does not merely match them. They claim to serve Christ, and on that ground, the only ground that matters, he will not concede a tie.

I am a better one, I am talking like a madman. He immediately interrupts himself to say he has gone too far. “Madman” (paraphroneō) means to be out of one’s mind. The word is stronger than fool; he has moved from foolishness to raving. He can hear himself, and he is appalled. But he does not take it back, because it is true and the situation requires it. What he does instead is define what he means, and the definition is the turn the whole chapter has been building toward.

With far greater labours, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death. Stop and see what has just happened to the argument. Everyone in that room expected the sentence to continue with achievements: churches planted, miracles worked, revelations received, cities won. He had all of those and could have listed them. He lists what has been done to him. The surprise is that his proof is not success, but suffering. Labours: hard work, manual and pastoral. Imprisonments: at Philippi (Acts 16:23), and others not recorded. Beatings: countless. Near death: often (1:8–10). Four items, and each is an intensifier: far greater, far more, countless, often. He has lost count of the beatings. A man remembers the first few and stops numbering after that.

The measure of a servant. The word servant is diakonos, the ordinary word for someone who waits at table. And Paul’s claim is that the measure of such a man is not what he has accomplished but what he has absorbed. Anyone can serve while it is rewarding. The test is what is left when it costs. The marks of a true servant of Christ are the marks of the cross.

Measured by cost. Which puts a question to every assessment of Christian service that any of us makes, including of ourselves. We measure by output, because output can be counted and photographed. Paul measures by cost. On his accounting, the most useful servant in a congregation may well be someone with nothing whatever to show: who has kept turning up, kept forgiving, kept praying for a family member for thirty years, and has been quietly worn down by it.

The shape of the Master. And the accounting is not arbitrary. It is the shape of the Master. The Lord’s own ministry, measured by output at the moment it ended, looked like a failure: three years, a handful of followers, and every one of them gone by Friday morning. What he had was what had been done to him, and it saved the world.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns status. It means faithful service of a crucified Lord involves suffering. Pain in itself proves nothing; false teachers suffer too, and some people suffer for their own faults (1 Peter 4:15). What marks Paul out is suffering for Christ, in the course of serving him.

Should I seek out suffering to prove my faithfulness? No. Paul never went looking for beatings; he went looking for people to preach to, and the beatings came. Christians are not called to court persecution, to make themselves difficult in order to be opposed, or to treat hardship as a ladder to holiness. We are called to follow Christ wherever he leads, and to accept the cost when it comes rather than trimming the message to avoid it. If you are free from persecution, thank God for it and use the freedom well. The question is not how much you have suffered, but whether you would be willing to.

If my life is fairly easy, am I a lesser Christian? Not because it is easy. God appoints different measures of hardship to different servants, and it is not a competition (John 21:21–22). Many faithful believers live quiet lives without beatings or shipwrecks. But every Christian life has a cost somewhere: the sin you refuse, the opinion of others you give up, the time and money you give away, the patience you keep with a difficult person. Ask whether your faith is costing you anything at all. And use your ease for those whose life is not easy: pray for the persecuted church by name, and give to support it.

In a sentence. Are they servants of Christ? (Paul is out of his mind to talk like this.) He is more. He has worked much harder, been in prison more often, been flogged more severely, and been exposed to death again and again.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church whose service nobody sees: a carer, a faithful intercessor, someone who has stayed when it would have been easier to leave. Thank God for them, and tell them. And when you assess your own usefulness to God, stop measuring the output and offer him the cost.

For worship. Thank God for the sufferings of those who brought the gospel to the world, and above all for the Servant whose sufferings were the gospel. He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows; he was wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and with his wounds we are healed. Paul’s scars were the marks of his Master, and his Master’s scars are the price of our peace. The risen Christ still bears them, and will bear them for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;

Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Now the numbers, and they should be read slowly rather than skimmed as a list. This is the synagogue punishment. The law permitted forty strokes and no more (Deuteronomy 25:3); Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could never break the command. The victim was bound, stripped to the waist and struck with a strap; later Jewish law describes a third of the strokes on the chest and two thirds on the back. Men died of it. Five times: that is 195 strokes. And it is worth grasping what each one meant beyond the pain. This was the punishment a synagogue administered to its own. To receive it, Paul had to have submitted himself to the synagogue’s jurisdiction, walked in again, knowing what had happened the last four times, because his own people were there and he would not stop going to them first. He accepted their discipline rather than abandon them.

Three times I was beaten with rods. This is the Roman punishment, carried out by officials called lictors, and it was illegal to inflict it on a Roman citizen. Paul was one, and said so at Philippi, after the beating (Acts 16:22–23, 37). Acts records that occasion; the other two are nowhere else in the New Testament.

Once I was stoned. At Lystra. The crowd stoned him and dragged him out of the city supposing he was dead, and he got up and went back into the town (Acts 14:19–20).

Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea. None of these is the famous shipwreck of Acts 27, which had not happened yet. So there were at least four. And that short clause covers twenty-four hours in the open sea, clinging to wreckage, waiting.

What Acts leaves out. Notice how much of this the rest of the New Testament does not record. Acts gives us one beating with rods out of three and none of the five floggings. We have a book about Paul that leaves out most of what happened to him. Which is worth remembering when you read Christian biography, or measure your own life against what other people report. The account you have of anyone is partial, and the parts that were hardest are usually the parts left out. There are people in your church carrying things that would not appear in any summary of their lives, and the God who kept the real record has not mislaid a single stroke of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Acts is incomplete or wrong. Acts selects only some events, as every history does. Paul’s list shows how much more he endured, and the two accounts fit together without strain.

Why did God let this happen to his best servant? Because he was making Paul like his Son, and making the gospel visible through him. The Lord had said at the start that he would show Paul how much he must suffer for the sake of his name (Acts 9:16). The beatings were not God’s neglect but his appointment, and every one of them was limited: Paul was struck down but not destroyed, carried through each one until his work was done (4:8–10). Through his scars churches were planted, and through his letters written in chains we still read the gospel. God does not waste the suffering of his people. He does not always tell us why, but he always knows, and he never lets go.

In a sentence. Five times he received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times he was beaten with rods, once he was pelted with stones, three times he was shipwrecked, and he spent a night and a day in the open sea.

On a Tuesday. When you think the Christian life is hard, read this list. Then thank God for his sustaining grace, which is the same grace that carried Paul. And think of one person in your church whose hardship nobody has written down. Ask how they are, and listen.

For worship. He who kept Paul through 195 strokes was himself flogged by Roman soldiers and gave his back to the smiters. He who brought Paul up from the stones of Lystra was himself lifted up on a cross and laid in a tomb, and rose. He who held Paul through a night and a day in the deep is the Lord who walked on the sea and commands the wind and waves. Not one stroke, not one stone, not one wave was outside his hand, and he brought his servant safely home.
verseByVerse.note: The law allowed up to forty lashes; the synagogues gave thirty-nine to be sure of not exceeding it. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. The shipwrecks were before the one described in Acts 27.

parallels.desc: Paul stoned at Lystra
beaten with rods at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.

On frequent journeys. Paul travelled perhaps ten thousand miles in the course of his ministry, much of it on foot. Then the word danger eight times in a single sentence, hammered without a connective. It is the sound of a man reciting a life.

In danger from rivers, danger from robbers. The first two are the ordinary hazards of ancient travel, and they were not small. Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood, especially in the mountain passes of Asia Minor. The roads through those mountains were notorious for bandits, thinly policed or not at all, and a man carrying a collection for Jerusalem was worth stopping.

Danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles. Then the list turns human, and it covers everybody. Jewish opponents plotted against him (Acts 9:23; 20:3); Gentile mobs attacked him (Acts 16:19–22; 19:23–41). There was no group on earth among whom Paul was safe.

Danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea. Then geography, and it is total. The three places a person can be. He is saying there was nowhere.

Danger from false brothers. And then the last one, held to the end because it is the worst. Everything before this could be seen coming. A man knows to watch the river, the road, the mob. What cannot be guarded against is the person inside the fellowship who is not what he appears: who is in the meetings, who prays with you, and who is working against you (Galatians 2:4). Paul puts it last in a list that includes being stoned and left for dead. Anyone who has been betrayed by someone inside the church will not need this explained. It is a distinct species of wound, and it goes deeper than persecution because persecution comes from outside the family and this does not. The psalmist knew it: it was not an enemy who taunted him, which he could have borne, but his companion, his familiar friend, with whom he walked to the house of God (Psalm 55:12–14). And the Lord knew it, from a man who had eaten with him for three years.

In toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. Then the list turns from danger to the grinding daily conditions, and these are almost harder to admire because there is nothing dramatic in them. Toil. Sleepless nights. Hunger and thirst. Often without food may mean voluntary fasting, or simply going without. Cold and exposure means lacking clothing and shelter (4:11); years later, in a Roman prison, he would ask Timothy to bring the cloak he had left at Troas (2 Timothy 4:13). No single item here would make a story. This is simply what the life was like on an ordinary week: tired, hungry and cold. Most Christian faithfulness looks far more like this verse than like the floggings, and it is this sort that wears people out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must suffer like this. It means faithfulness may cost greatly, and that the ordinary wearing hardships of serving Christ are as truly suffering for him as the dramatic ones.

What should I do if someone in my church has hurt me? First, take it to the Lord honestly, as the psalmist did; he knows this wound from the inside. Then, if the person is a believer and the matter is serious, follow the path Jesus gave: go to him privately, and if he will not listen, take one or two others, and then the church (Matthew 18:15–17). If it involves abuse or a crime, go to the authorities and to other leaders at once. Forgive from the heart, which means giving up revenge, even if trust takes much longer to rebuild. And do not let one false brother persuade you that the whole family is false. Paul was betrayed, and he never left the church.

In a sentence. He has been constantly on the move. He has been in danger from rivers, from bandits, from his fellow Jews, from Gentiles; in danger in the city, in the country, at sea; and in danger from false believers. He has laboured and toiled and often gone without sleep; he has known hunger and thirst and often gone without food; he has been cold and without enough clothing.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for Christians who travel to dangerous places for the gospel, and for missionaries who are tired, cold and far from home. Ask God to protect them. And if your own faithfulness this week looks mostly like toil and sleepless nights, take heart: that is what the apostle’s life looked like too.

For worship. There is no road Paul walked that the Lord had not walked before him. Christ was in danger from his own people and from Gentiles; he was hungry in the wilderness, homeless in the city, asleep in a boat in the storm; he was betrayed by a familiar friend with a kiss. He knows every danger his servants face because he faced them first, and he has promised to be with them always, to the end of the age. No river, robber or false brother can separate them from his love.
verseByVerse.note: Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood; roads through the mountains were infested with robbers.

verseByVerse.quote: And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.

And, apart from other things. After the floggings, the stoning, the shipwrecks and the nights in the open, Paul says: and apart from all that, here is what actually weighs on me. Besides the outward sufferings there is an inward one.

There is the daily pressure on me. “Pressure” (epistasis) means something set upon a person, a crowd pressing in, a burden that bears down. And daily: this one does not stop when the ship reaches harbour or the bruises heal. It was there this morning.

Of my anxiety for all the churches. Then the word he chooses for what he carries: merimna, care, concern. It is exactly the word the Lord used when he said do not be anxious about your life (Matthew 6:25), and that Paul used when he told the Philippians not to be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6). And notice the reach of it: all the churches. Not the one he was in. Every congregation he had ever planted, scattered across four provinces, most of them out of contact, several of them in trouble he could do nothing about from where he was: churches being led astray, divided, persecuted.

Is this anxiety sin? It is worth answering carefully, because a great many faithful people are quietly condemned by the question. The anxiety Scripture forbids is the fretting of a person who does not believe he is provided for: worry about food and clothing and tomorrow, carried by someone who has forgotten he has a Father. What Paul describes here is not about himself at all. It is the weight of caring what becomes of other people. That is not a failure of faith; it is what love feels like when the people you love are at risk and out of reach. The two can be told apart, and the test is what the concern is about and where it goes. Is it fear for yourself, or care for someone else? And does it drive you to God, or round in circles? Paul’s went to God in prayer, and then to a boat: he crossed a sea because he could not bear not knowing (2:13; 7:5–7).

The hidden half of pastoral work. This is invisible by nature. Nobody sees it. It does not appear in any report. It is the elder awake at two in the morning over a family that is coming apart; the Sunday school teacher who cannot stop thinking about one particular child; the pastor who carries a dozen private sorrows that he may not discuss with anyone. There is no measure for it, and it is most of the job. Paul lists it as a suffering, alongside the whip and the sea, and he was right to. For Paul, this was as heavy as the beatings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul disobeyed the command not to be anxious (Philippians 4:6). This is the godly concern of love, which he brought to God in prayer.

Is my constant worry about my children godly care or sinful anxiety? Usually it is both, tangled together, and the way to untangle it is to pray it. Love for your children is good, and so is concern for their souls and their safety; that is what Paul felt for his churches. But when the concern becomes a sleepless loop of imagined disasters, a need to control every outcome, or a fear that God will not care for them as you would, it has crossed into the anxiety Jesus forbids. Turn each worry into a specific request, give thanks for what God has already done for them, do the next thing you actually can do, and then leave them in his hands, which are far safer than yours. He loves them more than you do.

In a sentence. Besides everything else, he faces daily the pressure of his concern for all the churches.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor and elders, who carry a daily burden of care for your church that you will mostly never see. Tell one of them this week that you are praying for them. And if you carry someone else’s trouble on your heart, carry it to God before you carry it anywhere else.

For worship. The Lord who said my sheep hear my voice, and I know them (John 10:27) carries every one of his churches still, without a night’s sleep lost and without losing one. Paul could only be in one city at a time; Christ walks among all the lampstands. Paul worried; Christ intercedes, and always lives to do it. The care that pressed on the apostle every day is held for ever in the heart of the Chief Shepherd, and he will present every one of his flock safe on the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? Two questions, and they explain where the daily pressure of the previous verse comes from. He is describing a man with no protective distance at all. When a believer somewhere is struggling, with doubt, with temptation, with a conscience troubled about food offered to idols, Paul does not counsel them from a position of strength. He goes down with them. He feels their weakness with them (1 Corinthians 9:22). He had told this church he would give up meat permanently rather than trip one weak brother (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? The second verb is stronger. “Indignant” (pyroō) is literally I burn, I am set on fire. When someone is tripped up into sin, especially by a false teacher, something in Paul catches fire: grief for the one who has fallen, and anger at whoever caused it.

Tenderness and heat. Hold the two together, because they are the anatomy of a pastor’s heart and they are not in tension. Tenderness toward the person who is struggling; heat toward whatever is causing the struggle. Get those the wrong way round, hard on the weak and relaxed about what is damaging them, and you have the exact inversion the Corinthians had achieved: tolerating men who devoured them and criticising the apostle who would not take their money. It is worth testing yourself on. Where does your anger actually go? Most of us find it easier to be irritated by the struggling person, the one who keeps failing, keeps asking, keeps needing, than by whatever is doing the damage. Paul’s reflexes ran the other way, and they were trained by watching how his Lord treated the crowds: he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36), and it was the shepherds who received the woes.

If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness. Then the sentence the whole fool’s speech has been climbing toward. The contest is over and Paul has changed the currency. Unlike the rivals, who boasted of strength, he will boast of the opposite, and not as a rhetorical trick. He means it, and chapter 12 will explain why: because weakness is where the power of Christ rests (12:9–10). This is the theology of the cross. The world counts what a man can do. God has arranged matters so that his power is displayed at exactly the point where a man can do nothing: in a clay pot, in a beaten apostle, in a crucified Messiah.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness is a virtue in itself. It means God’s strength is displayed in it. Laziness, cowardice and sin are weaknesses too, and Paul never boasts of those.

What does boasting in weakness look like in practice? It means being honest about your limits instead of hiding them, and pointing to Christ when good comes out of them. Admitting you are struggling, when the culture of your church rewards looking fine. Saying, when asked how you got through, that you did not, and God carried you. Telling your testimony with the failures left in. Accepting help rather than insisting on managing alone. Letting your children see you pray because you do not know what to do. It is not running yourself down for sympathy, and it is not false modesty. It is simply refusing to steal the credit for what God has done through a weak instrument.

In a sentence. Who is weak, and Paul does not feel weak? Who is led into sin, and he does not inwardly burn? If he must boast, he will boast of the things that show his weakness.

On a Tuesday. Think of the weakest believer you know, the one who keeps struggling, and ask whether you feel with them or merely about them. Then think of whatever is harming them, and ask whether you feel anything about that. And when someone praises you this week, find one honest way to give the glory to God.

For worship. Here is the reversal at the centre of this letter and of the gospel it serves. There has never been a moment when God needed anyone’s strength, and there has never been a weakness he could not fill. The Son of God took our weakness into himself, was tempted in every way as we are, and is not ashamed to sympathise with us. He burned with holy anger at those who caused little ones to stumble, and took the weak into his arms. Thank God that his strength shows in your weakness. Boast in that.

verseByVerse.quote: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. Paul swears an oath, and then tells a story about a basket. Take the oath first, because its placement is strange. He has just finished the catalogue, the floggings, the stoning, the shipwrecks, and he calls God as witness that none of it is invented, because the story he is about to tell is so humiliating. The whole passage is so far outside what anyone expects a man to boast about that it might be read as rhetoric. He is saying: this is not a device. It happened. And notice the title: the God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever. Even mid-oath, in the middle of the most bitter passage he ever wrote, the doxology comes out of him almost by reflex.

At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me. Then the story, and it is deliberately, almost comically, anticlimactic. This is his first escape as a Christian (Acts 9:23–25). Newly converted, preaching in the synagogues of Damascus that Jesus is the Son of God, he provoked a plot, and the gates were watched. Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he ruled from about 9 BC to AD 40, and his control of Damascus is one of the few fixed points for dating Paul’s early years (Galatians 1:17–18). Acts says that the Jews plotted to kill him; here it is the governor under Aretas who guards the city. The accounts fit together: Paul’s Jewish opponents could easily have enlisted the governor’s help, and both watched the gates.

But I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands. The disciples put him in a basket, the word suggests a large woven hamper of the kind used for provisions, and lowered him through a window in the wall at night, like a delivery. Consider it as the climax of a boast. The ancient convention had a place for the crowning honour, and Roman soldiers had one: the wall crown, given to the first man up the wall of a besieged city. Paul’s wall story is a man going the other way: first down the wall, in a basket, fleeing. That is the joke, and it is a serious one. He has taken the highest military honour available in his world and turned it inside out. This is what an apostle’s glory looks like: not first over the wall, but lowered out of a window in a hamper because otherwise he would be killed.

The pattern set at the start. And of all the incidents he could have chosen to end on, he chose the beginning, the very first thing that happened after Damascus. His Christian life began in humiliating weakness, and it set the pattern for everything that followed. The man who would carry the gospel across the empire left his first city as freight. That is his boast.

What it does not mean. It does not mean escape from danger is cowardice. Jesus told his followers to flee persecution when possible (Matthew 10:23).

When should a Christian flee danger, and when should he stay? Fleeing is often right. Jesus withdrew when his hour had not yet come, Paul left Damascus, Thessalonica and Berea when lives were at risk, and the early church scattered under persecution and spread the gospel as it went (Acts 8:1–4). It is wise to flee when staying would achieve nothing but harm, when others depend on you, or when the door is open elsewhere. It is right to stay when fleeing would mean denying Christ, abandoning those in your care, or running from a duty God has plainly given you. Paul later went to Jerusalem knowing chains awaited him (Acts 20:22–24). Pray, take counsel, and remember that faithfulness, not bravado, is what pleases the Lord.

In a sentence. The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is to be praised for ever, knows that Paul is not lying. In Damascus the governor under King Aretas had the city guarded in order to arrest him. But he was lowered in a basket from a window in the wall and slipped through his hands.

On a Tuesday. You do not have to be the hero of your story. Christ is. Think of the most humbling moment in your Christian life, the one you would leave out of your testimony, and thank God for what he did through it. Let him have the glory, even through your humbling moments.

For worship. Which is finally what this whole ridiculous, painful chapter has been for. Christ does not recruit the impressive, and he does not need them. He takes a man out of a window in a basket, and thirty years of floggings later the churches he planted are still standing, the empire that beat him is gone, and the name he preached is known in every country on earth. The glory was never Paul’s. It never had to be. It belongs to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, and to the Son who went down lower than any basket, into death itself, and came up again as Lord of all.
verseByVerse.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he died around AD 40.

Do bear with me!<sup>2</sup>For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.<sup>3</sup>But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.<sup>4</sup>For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.<sup>5</sup>Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles.<sup>6</sup>Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.<sup>7</sup>Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge?<sup>8</sup>I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.<sup>9</sup>And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way.<sup>10</sup>As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.<sup>11</sup>And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!<sup>12</sup>And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.<sup>13</sup>For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.<sup>14</sup>And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.<sup>15</sup>So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.<sup>16</sup>I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.<sup>17</sup>What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool.<sup>18</sup>Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.<sup>19</sup>For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves!<sup>20</sup>For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.<sup>21</sup>To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!<sup>22</sup>Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.<sup>23</sup>Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.<sup>24</sup>Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one.<sup>25</sup>Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;<sup>26</sup>on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers;<sup>27</sup>in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.<sup>28</sup>And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.<sup>29</sup>Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant?<sup>30</sup>If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.<sup>31</sup>The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.<sup>32</sup>At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me,<sup>33</sup>but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

12.title: The Thorn in the Flesh and Power in Weakness
12.overview:
The rivals in Corinth boasted of visions and revelations. Paul reluctantly matches them, and then turns the boast inside out. He tells, in the third person as if about someone else, of a man taken up into the third heaven, into paradise, fourteen years earlier, where he heard things no human may repeat. But he will not build his reputation on that. To keep him from pride after such revelations, he was given a “thorn in the flesh”, a messenger of Satan to torment him. Three times he begged the Lord to take it away. The Lord answered: my grace is enough for you, for my power is brought to completion in weakness. So Paul now gladly boasts of his weaknesses, because when he is weak, then he is strong.

The rest of the chapter returns to the relationship. Paul has been forced into this foolish boasting because the Corinthians failed to stand up for him, though the signs of an apostle were done among them. He is coming a third time, and still will not take their money: he wants them, not their possessions, and will gladly spend himself for them. He denies trickery through his co-workers, insists that everything he has said was for building them up, and confesses his fear that when he comes he will find quarrelling, immorality and unrepented sin, and will be humbled and grieved over them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Thorn in the Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he must go on boasting, though nothing is gained by it, and turns to visions and revelations from the Lord. He describes, as if speaking of another man, someone in Christ who fourteen years before was taken up into the third heaven, into paradise, whether in the body or not he does not know, and heard words too sacred for any human to speak. He will boast about that man, but about himself only of his weaknesses. If he did boast he would be telling the truth, but he holds back, so that no one rates him higher than what they see and hear from him. To keep him humble after such extraordinary revelations, he was given a painful thorn in his body, Satan’s messenger to beat him down. He pleaded with the Lord three times to remove it, and the Lord replied that his grace was sufficient and that his power reaches its full strength in weakness. So Paul will gladly boast of his weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on him. For Christ’s sake he accepts weakness, insults, hardship, persecution and distress, because when he is weak, then he is strong.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “power is made perfect in weakness” is the theological summit of the letter. The verb is from the word for a goal: brought to completion. Divine power achieves its intended perfection/completion in the context of human weakness. This is not simply a compensation for weakness (“when you can’t do it, God will”) but a statement about the natural habitat of divine power: it is when human resources are exhausted that the divine power is most purely displayed. The implication is not that Christians should cultivate weakness artificially but that they should not be surprised or ashamed when their weakness becomes the occasion for the display of a power that is clearly not theirs.

The three-fold prayer (v. 8) and the divine refusal is one of the clearest statements in the NT that God’s answer to prayer is sometimes “no, but here is something better.” Paul prayed earnestly, repeatedly, and specifically. The thorn was not removed. But what was given instead — a word of grace, an experience of Christ’s power — was worth more than the removal would have been. The “no” was a deeper “yes.”
verseByVerse.examples: A woman with a chronic pain condition has prayed for healing for years. She has been to healing services; she has been told that her lack of healing indicates insufficient faith. This passage speaks directly to her: the greatest apostle prayed three times for the removal of his thorn and was refused. The word he received instead was not a failure of faith but a revelation of grace. “My grace is sufficient for you” is not a consolation prize; it is a gift that the removal of the thorn would not have given him.

verseByVerse.quote: I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 12 continues Paul’s fool’s speech, now turning to the kind of thing the super-apostles most loved to boast of: visions and revelations. First, Paul tells, in the third person and with great reluctance, of being caught up to paradise fourteen years earlier and hearing things that cannot be told. But he will not boast of it (vv. 1–6). Second, to keep him from pride, he was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan. He pleaded three times for it to go, but the Lord answered: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. So Paul boasts of weakness, because when he is weak, then he is strong (vv. 7–10). This is the heart of the whole letter, and one of the most precious pages in the Bible for anyone carrying something that will not go away. Third, Paul ends the fool’s speech: the signs of an apostle were done among them; his only offence was not burdening them. He is coming a third time, seeking not their money but them, and gladly spending himself for their souls (vv. 11–18). Finally, he warns that he fears finding quarrelling, immorality and unrepentance when he arrives (vv. 19–21).

I must go on boasting. He is still apologising. Three times now he has stopped to say that what he is doing is foolish, and here he says it is also useless. I must go on: the word carries compulsion, it is necessary, I am obliged. Paul feels compelled because the Corinthians are being misled by the rivals’ boasts. Nobody would guess from the tone that he is about to describe the most extraordinary spiritual experience recorded of any Christian in the New Testament. And that reluctance is the first thing to notice, because it is the whole point of the passage. Paul is about to play his highest card, and he does it with visible distaste, having told us in advance that it proves nothing.

Though there is nothing to be gained by it. He does not mean the vision was worthless to him. He means it is worth nothing as an argument. It did not make him a better servant of Christ; the thorn that came with it did rather more, as he is about to explain. Boasting does no spiritual good, to the one who boasts or to those who hear.

I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord. Visions (optasiai) and revelations (apokalypseis) given by the Lord, or showing the Lord. Why raise them at all? Because his rivals almost certainly were. Everything about the way he introduces the subject suggests he is following their agenda rather than setting his own. In a religious culture fascinated by ecstatic experience, a man who could describe an encounter with the heavenly world had credentials nobody could check and everybody envied. So Paul produces one, and immediately disarms it.

Experiences cannot be checked. There is something here worth carrying into any age that prizes spiritual experience, and ours does as much as Corinth did. Experiences cannot be verified from outside. Nobody can check whether you heard from God in the night, and nobody can contradict you. Which means that in any contest of spirituality, the person willing to describe the most remarkable inner life wins, and there is no way to test the claim. Paul refuses to compete on that ground. His credentials in this letter have been things anybody could verify: a church that exists, a body with scars on it, an empty purse, a life spent in the open. He is about to add a vision, under protest, and then take it away again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul despised spiritual experiences. He had many (Acts 16:9; 18:9; 22:17–18). It means they are not the basis for authority.

Does God still give visions and revelations like these? Not in the way he gave them to Paul. Paul’s experience belonged to his apostleship, and Scripture is now complete: God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the faith has been once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God may still use dreams, impressions and providences in a believer’s life, and he certainly draws near to his people in deep experiences of his love. But no claimed vision carries authority over others, adds to Scripture, or binds anyone’s conscience. Every such claim must be tested by Scripture and set below it. If you have had a vivid experience, thank God for whatever good it did you, and build your life on his written word.

In a sentence. Paul must go on boasting. Although there is nothing to be gained, he will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Do not measure your faith, or anyone else’s, by spectacular experiences. Measure it by what can be seen: love, holiness, faithfulness to God’s word, patience under trial. If someone impresses you mainly by what they say has happened to them in private, look again at what can be seen in public.

For worship. Whatever happened to Paul fourteen years earlier, he had carried it for fourteen years without telling this church, and the only reason it appears in the Bible at all is that some impressive men in Corinth left him no choice. That is a great deal of humility to find in a man who had been to paradise, and it was not his own. It was the humility of the Lord who had been in the glory of the Father before the world existed and spoke of it only so that his disciples might believe, the Lord who could have dazzled the crowds with heaven and instead showed them his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—

I know a man in Christ. He tells it in the third person, and everybody has always known why. He keeps it up for four verses and then gives himself away in verse 7, when he explains that the thorn was given to keep me from becoming conceited. It is Paul. The distance is deliberate: a way of describing the experience without standing next to it and taking the credit, out of modesty and reluctance. In Christ simply means a believer. The first thing he says about the man who went to heaven is not that he was special but that he was in Christ, which is the only thing that would ever get anyone there.

Who fourteen years ago. Count back from the writing of this letter and it lands around AD 42, somewhere in the silent years after Damascus and before the first missionary journey: the long stretch in Tarsus, Syria and Cilicia that Acts passes over in a sentence (Galatians 1:21; Acts 9:30; 11:25–26). And he has said nothing about it since. Let that register. Fourteen years of silence about the most remarkable thing that ever happened to him. If it had been the making of his authority he would have led with it in every city. It appears once, under duress, in a passage he calls foolish. Those who constantly talk of their visions should note that.

Was caught up to the third heaven. “Caught up” (harpazō) is a strong passive verb: seized, snatched, the word used of believers caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). It happened to him. He did not achieve it by technique, discipline or preparation, which is worth saying in every generation that has produced a method for arranging such things. The third heaven means the dwelling place of God. Jewish writers of the period commonly spoke of the heavens in layers, some of them seven, and Paul uses the simpler scheme of his own world rather than teaching cosmology: the first heaven is the sky where the birds fly, the second the sky where the stars are, and the third the dwelling of God himself. He is saying he was taken all the way in.

Whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. Then the phrase he repeats twice, which is the most striking part. He was there and he cannot tell you the mechanics. Paul honestly does not know the mode of the experience, and he refuses to speculate. The one man in Scripture who could have written an authoritative account of the geography of heaven says twice that he does not know what happened to him.

And I know that this man was caught up into paradise. Verse 3 confirms it with a second name. Paradise (paradeisos) is a Persian word for a walled garden or park, used in the Greek Old Testament of Eden, and used by the Lord to the dying thief: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7). It is the same place as the third heaven, the presence of God. The garden that was lost at the beginning is the garden Christ opens at the end, and Paul has seen it.

Where Christians differ: visits to heaven today. Many popular books and speakers today claim detailed visits to heaven. Verdict: Paul, an apostle, was taken to paradise and was forbidden to describe what he heard (v. 4). He waited fourteen years to mention it, and then only to rebuke boasting. Claims today to have toured heaven and brought back detailed descriptions do not match Paul’s reticence, add to Scripture, and often contradict it. Scripture is sufficient to tell us what we need to know about heaven (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Westminster 1.6).

The contrast with modern accounts. Set Paul’s report beside the confident detail of most modern accounts of visits to the afterlife, and the contrast is instructive. The apostle’s report is short, reluctant, told about someone else by choice, and full of admitted ignorance. Theirs are long, eager, first person, and full of detail about colours, conversations and furniture. Certainty about the unseen world tends to be inversely proportional to how much of it a person has actually seen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s experience was imaginary. It was real, and he insists it was true (v. 6).

Was Paul dead, or did his soul leave his body? He does not know, and so we do not need to. He allows both possibilities, which tells us that a person can be with God apart from the body, as believers who die are now (5:8; Philippians 1:23), and also that God can take a living man into his presence as he pleases. What this passage does not teach is that Christians should seek out-of-body experiences, or that heaven can be reached by any technique. Paul was caught up; it was done to him. The ordinary way a believer enters paradise is by dying in the Lord, and that is enough.

What will heaven be like, if Paul could not describe it? Scripture tells us what matters most. It is the presence of God and of Christ; we will see his face (Revelation 22:4). There will be no more sin, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and at his return they will be raised bodily to live in a new heavens and new earth (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; 2 Peter 3:13). Beyond that, what we have is enough to make us long for it. Paul’s silence is not a hint that heaven is vague. It is a hint that it is greater than words.

In a sentence. Paul knows a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of the body he does not know; God knows. And he knows that this man, whether in the body or apart from the body he does not know, but God knows, was caught up to paradise.

On a Tuesday. When you read or hear a vivid account of someone’s trip to heaven, compare it with Paul’s: short, reluctant, humble, silent about the details. And when you think about heaven yourself, start from what is certain: Christ is there, and every believer will be with him.

For worship. Paradise is real, and believers will be there with Christ. The garden that was shut with a flaming sword was opened by the Son of God, who was himself shut out, crucified outside the city, so that a dying thief could hear the words, today you will be with me. Paul was snatched up to it once and came back with nothing he could say. One day every child of God will be caught up for good, and will not need to describe it, because they will be home.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks of himself in the third person. The “third heaven” means the highest heaven, the presence of God; fourteen years before this letter would be in the early 40s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—

And he heard things that cannot be told. Two things happened in paradise, and Paul reports only that they happened. The phrase is doubled for emphasis and the two halves are not the same. “Cannot be told” (arrēta) means unspeakable, beyond the capacity of language: things too holy for human words.

Which man may not utter. Not permitted, forbidden. So there are two reasons for the silence: some of it could not be put into words, and some of it was not allowed to be. That second reason is the more arresting. Paul was given something and told not to pass it on. Not every revelation was meant for publication. Whatever he heard was for him, and the church has never had it. That is a useful thing to know when someone claims a private revelation that must be received on their authority alone. God sometimes gives a person something meant for them only, and the mark of the genuine article here is that Paul never traded on it. He did not build a following on the strength of what he could not disclose. Fourteen years of not mentioning it is the most persuasive detail in the account.

The secret things. It tells us something about Scripture as well. God has not told us everything he could have told us. There are things about heaven, about providence, about the future, that were available and were withheld. The Bible is not a complete transcript of what God knows; it is what he judged his people needed. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29). A great deal of unhappiness comes from demanding the first half, and a great deal of peace comes from being content with the second.

On behalf of this man I will boast. Then verse 5, and here is the reason for the whole third-person device. He has split himself in two. The man who was caught up to paradise, that man he will boast about, because everything that happened to him was received. Paul distances himself from the experience, as if it happened to someone else. It was God’s gift, not his achievement.

But on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses. The man writing the letter, the one his readers know, the one with the scars and the tent-maker’s hands: about him Paul will boast only in what shows how weak he is. It is not false modesty. It is an accurate division. What was given to him is God’s to be proud of; what he actually is, is a clay pot. And the split explains something about how Christians should hold their own best moments. The times when God has plainly been at work in you are worth speaking about, and they are not your credentials, because you did not produce them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul had secret teaching that the church needs. Everything necessary for faith and life is revealed in Scripture.

Should I tell others about my experiences of God? Often, yes, with care. Telling what God has done for you can encourage others and give him glory, as the psalmists do again and again: come and hear, and I will tell what he has done for my soul (Psalm 66:16). But ask why you are telling it. Is it to point to God or to yourself? Will it help the hearer trust Christ, or make them feel they are missing something? Never use an experience to win an argument or to claim authority over someone else. And some experiences are best kept between you and the Lord, as Mary treasured things in her heart.

In a sentence. And he heard inexpressible things, things that no one is permitted to tell. Paul will boast about a man like that, but he will not boast about himself, except about his weaknesses.

On a Tuesday. If God gives you a special experience of his presence, treasure it humbly. You need not broadcast it. And if you find you want to know more than God has told you, about the future, about why something happened, about what heaven looks like, turn back to what he has revealed and live by that today.

For worship. There are words in heaven too holy for our ears, and the Word who spoke them came down to speak words we could bear. Paul heard things he could not repeat; we have been given the gospel, which he could and did repeat in every city. The God whose glory is beyond telling has told us the one thing we most needed to hear: that in Christ he has reconciled us to himself. Everything else can wait for the day we hear the rest in his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.

Though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth. A careful sentence, and the care is the point. First he protects the truthfulness of what he has said. He is not retracting the vision or hedging it. It happened. If he boasted of his revelations, every word would be accurate, unlike the rivals’ exaggerations.

But I refrain from it. The verb means to spare, to hold back. He chooses not to. And the reason he gives is one of the most quietly impressive things in the New Testament.

So that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me. Read that slowly. Paul is deliberately withholding true information about himself in order to keep people’s opinion of him accurate. He wants to be judged by what people can see in his life and hear in his teaching, not by a reputation built out of claimed experiences that cannot be checked. A healthy test for every leader. Consider how far that runs against the grain. All of us manage what people know about us, and the management almost always runs the other way: we put forward what is impressive and quietly leave out the rest. Paul has the most impressive item any Christian has ever had, and he is suppressing it precisely because it would inflate him beyond what a person could verify by watching.

Judge the visible man. Notice the standard he is willing to be judged by: what he sees in me or hears from me. That is a hard offer to make. It means no allowance for the private hours, the hidden devotion, the experiences nobody witnessed. Judge the visible man. Which supplies a test, and it is uncomfortable in an age built on presentation. Is the impression people have of you larger than the reality they could observe? Every one of us has some gap; the question is whether we are working to close it or to widen it. The gap is where disappointment lives, and it is the reason so many admired people are a grief to those who actually live with them.

The mercy of being what you appear. There is a mercy in Paul’s policy too, and it is worth seeing. A man who has arranged to be overestimated must then maintain the estimate, and the maintenance is exhausting and never finishes. Paul has spared himself all of it. He is exactly what he appears to be, which is why he can write a letter admitting he despaired of life, could not rest at Troas though a door was open, and left Damascus in a basket. None of it costs him anything, because nobody was ever asked to think otherwise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean experiences are irrelevant. It means character and teaching are the tests of ministry.

Is it dishonest to keep good things about myself hidden? No. Honesty forbids deceiving people, not keeping things private. You are not obliged to tell everyone everything, and Jesus told us to do our giving, praying and fasting in secret (Matthew 6:1–6). What would be dishonest is creating a false impression, making yourself look better than you are, or worse in order to be praised for humility. Paul’s aim is accuracy: he wants people to think of him exactly what is true and visible. That is a good aim for a Christian. Let your reputation be no larger than your life.

In a sentence. Even if he should choose to boast, he would not be a fool, because he would be speaking the truth. But he refrains, so no one will think more of him than is warranted by what he does or says.

On a Tuesday. Notice one way today in which you try to make yourself look better than the reality: an exaggeration, a carefully chosen photo, a hint about your devotional life. Close the gap, not by putting on more but by letting go of the image. You will find it a relief.

For worship. Christ is the one person whose reputation will never disappoint those who live closest to him. The disciples who saw him tired, hungry and weeping, who watched him at table and on the road for three years, came away worshipping. His glory was not a front; it was what he is. And he has promised to make his people the same: no longer actors managing an impression, but children being changed from one degree of glory to another, until what is seen and what is real are one.

verseByVerse.quote: So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.

So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations. Now the thorn, and the sentence is built with a repetition that cannot be accidental: the purpose clause appears twice, at both ends. To keep me from becoming conceited, and again, to keep me from becoming conceited. “Conceited” (hyperairomai) means lifted up too high, exalted above measure. Great revelations bring the danger of pride, and Paul bookends the verse with the reason, as though the danger were so real it needed saying on both sides of the affliction.

A thorn was given me in the flesh. What was it? The honest answer is that nobody knows, and the guessing has gone on for nineteen centuries. The word skolops means a sharpened stake or a splinter: something driven in. In the flesh suggests the body. The main proposals are a chronic illness of some kind; an eye complaint, since he tells the Galatians they would have torn out their eyes and given them to him, and he writes in large letters (Galatians 4:13–15; 6:11); recurring malaria, migraines or epilepsy; a speech impediment or some condition that made him hard to listen to; or the relentless human opposition that dogged him everywhere. The uncertainty is almost certainly deliberate. Had Paul named it, every sufferer with a different affliction would have been shut out of the passage. As it stands, whatever is driven into your flesh fits the gap.

Was given. Notice the verb. It is the divine passive: the giver is God. Paul does not say Satan gave it, though Satan sent it. He says it was given, and he knows from whose hand.

A messenger of Satan to harass me. Then the double description, and it is the theological heart of the verse. The word for messenger is angelos; the harassment is real and it comes from the enemy. Satan meant it for harm. “Harass” (kolaphizō) means to strike with the fist, the very word used when they struck Jesus at his trial (Matthew 26:67). It is in the present tense: an ongoing torment, blow after blow. Hold both together. One event, two agents, two entirely different purposes. Satan sends it to wreck a man. God permits it, and appoints it, to save him from something worse.

To keep me from becoming conceited. Repeated for emphasis. God used Satan’s weapon for Paul’s good. This is the shape of Job, where the accuser is on a leash and the leash is held (Job 1–2); and of Joseph, who told his brothers you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20); and supremely of the cross, where the worst thing anyone ever did was the thing by which God saved the world. Satan intended to hinder; God intended to humble. And note what God was protecting Paul from. Not failure. Not danger. Conceit. The apostle had been to the third heaven, and the risk attached to that was that he would become insufferable, and an insufferable Paul would have been no use to anybody. So the affliction is not the price of the revelation; it is the provision that made the revelation survivable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the author of evil. Satan is responsible for his evil intent. But God rules over even Satan’s actions for his people’s good (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20).

How can both God and Satan be behind the same thing? Because they are doing different things through it. Satan’s aim is to torment and destroy, and he is guilty for it. God’s aim is to humble, protect and strengthen, and he is righteous in it. God does not do evil, tempt anyone to sin, or delight in pain (James 1:13), but nothing happens outside his rule, and he can take what is meant for evil and turn it to good. That is why a Christian can resist the devil and still say of his suffering, this has come to me from my Father’s hand. You do not have to work out where one purpose ends and the other begins. You only need to know which one will win.

What if my thorn is something I brought on myself? Then confess the sin that caused it, and receive God’s forgiveness fully; the guilt is gone in Christ, even if the consequences remain. Paul’s thorn was not the result of his sin, but the promise of verse 9 is not limited to blameless suffering. A recovered addict with a damaged body, a man living with the results of a foolish decision, a woman bearing the scars of a past she regrets: God’s grace is sufficient for them too. He is able to use even the consequences of our sin to humble us, keep us close to him, and make us gentle with others who fall.

In a sentence. Or because of these surpassingly great revelations. Therefore, in order to keep Paul from becoming conceited, he was given a thorn in his flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment him.

On a Tuesday. What is your thorn? Ask God how he might be using it to keep you humble and dependent on him. That is a hard thought, and it is not one to say to anyone else; Paul says it only about himself. But if you carry something that will not go away, it may be worth holding: the thing you would most like removed may be the thing keeping you close to him and usable.

For worship. The God who rules this verse is not the anxious opponent of Satan, scrambling to repair what the enemy breaks. He is the Lord who holds the leash, who turns the devil’s fist into his own surgeon’s hand, and who brought the greatest good in history out of the greatest evil. On the cross Satan struck the Son of God with everything he had, and by that very blow his head was crushed. The God who did that can be trusted with your thorn.
verseByVerse.note: No one knows what the thorn was; suggestions include a chronic illness, poor eyesight, or persistent opposition.

parallels.desc: thorns in your sides

verseByVerse.quote: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.

Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this. One line, and it is the verse that keeps a great many Christians in the faith. Three times: not a passing mention in his devotions, but three sustained seasons of asking. The number is probably significant. The Lord himself prayed three times in Gethsemane about a cup he wanted removed, and submitted to the Father’s will (Mark 14:32–41; Matthew 26:39–44). “Pleaded” (parakaleō) is the great word of this letter, which has meant comfort throughout and here means to beg, to appeal. He is not making a polite request. He is imploring.

With the Lord. The Lord here is almost certainly Jesus, since the answer in verse 9 speaks of the power of Christ. Paul’s prayers are usually addressed to the Father, and it is worth noticing that here he prays directly to the Son, which tells you who he understood him to be.

That it should leave me. Specific, definite, unambiguous. He asked for healing or removal. He knew exactly what he wanted and he asked for exactly that. It was right to ask. And the answer was no.

Every condition was met. Every element that is supposed to guarantee an answered prayer is present here. The man praying is an apostle. The request is not selfish: a healthy Paul could serve more churches. There is no unconfessed sin, no lack of faith, no failure to persevere; he came back three times. And the thorn stayed. That has to be said plainly, because a great deal of teaching implies otherwise, and the people it damages are not the strong. There are believers who have been told that healing is theirs if they can muster the faith for it, and who have concluded, after years, that the fault is in them. Some have stopped praying. Some have stopped believing. This verse was written for them. One of the greatest Christians who ever lived prayed three times for the removal of an affliction and was told no, and the refusal is recorded in Scripture as a mercy rather than a failure.

He stopped at three. Notice also that Paul stopped at three. He did not conclude that persistence was the missing ingredient and press on to three hundred. He asked, he received an answer, and the answer settled it. There is a kind of prayer that will not accept a reply, and it is not greater faith; it is a refusal to let God be God. What changed was not the circumstance but the man, and what changed him was not the passage of time. It was a word, one sentence given in reply, which he carried for the rest of his life and which the church has been living on ever since.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul lacked faith. He prayed in faith, and God said no.

Should I stop praying for healing after three times? Not necessarily. Paul stopped because he received a clear answer, and we do not receive answers in his apostolic way. Jesus also told a parable about praying and not losing heart (Luke 18:1). So keep bringing your need to God for as long as it is on your heart, honestly and without guilt. But let your prayer change as Paul’s did. Ask not only for removal but for grace to bear it, for God to be glorified in it, and for the will to accept his answer, whatever it is. Over time many believers find that the prayer moves from take it away to be with me in it, and that is not defeat. It is the Gethsemane prayer: not my will, but yours.

In a sentence. Three times he pleaded with the Lord to take it away from him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your thorn to the Lord in prayer today, honestly and specifically, as Paul did. Say exactly what you want. And if the answer so far has been no, do not conclude that your faith is too small or that God has stopped listening. The apostle heard no, and it was the beginning of the best thing that ever happened to him.

For worship. The Lord to whom Paul prayed had prayed the same way. In the garden he fell on his face three times and asked for the cup to pass, and the Father said no, because if that cup passed from him it would come to us. The Son who was refused so that we could be spared does not despise anyone who pleads with him. He listens, and he answers with himself.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus too prayed three times in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

But he said to me. Here is the answer, and it is the summit of the letter. The verb is in the perfect tense: he has said, and it stands. Christ’s answer was not a passing comfort but a permanent word, as true on the day Paul wrote it down as on the day he first heard it, and as true now.

My grace is sufficient for you. Begin with the tense, because it is doing more work than any other word in the sentence. Not will be, when things get worse. Not has been, looking back. It is sufficient: present, continuous, already true in the moment the thorn is still going in. The word sufficient (arkeō) means enough, adequate to the need. It is not a promise of abundance or of relief. It is a promise that there will always be exactly as much as is required, and that the supply will not run out before the trouble does. Christ’s grace is all Paul needs to bear the thorn and serve faithfully. And notice what was not said. There is no explanation. The Lord does not tell Paul what the thorn is for beyond the one clause of verse 7, does not say how long, does not promise eventual removal. He gives him himself. That is the whole answer, and the answer is better than the request.

For my power is made perfect in weakness. Then the reason, and it turns the universe over. “Made perfect” (teleō) is from the root meaning to reach a goal, to be completed, fully displayed. Divine power does not merely cope with human weakness; it comes to its full expression there. Weakness is not the obstacle power has to work around. It is the place power was always heading for. Christ’s power is seen most clearly where human strength is weakest. This is the principle of the whole letter: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (4:7).

Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses. Then Paul’s response, and the word to watch is gladly. Not I will accept my weaknesses. Not I will endure them. I will boast all the more gladly. Paul does not just tolerate weakness; he boasts in it. Something has been so thoroughly reversed in him that the thing he begged to lose has become the thing he is pleased to have.

So that the power of Christ may rest upon me. The last phrase gives the reason, and it is worth ending on because it is a picture rather than an argument. “Rest upon” (episkēnoō) means to pitch a tent over, to dwell upon. It is built on the word for the tabernacle, where the glory settled in the wilderness, and it shares its root with John’s the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). Christ’s power settles on the weak. So the weakness is not merely tolerated. It is the ground the tent is pitched on. Where a man is emptied out, the glory of God comes down and settles, and stays. That is what the thorn was for, and it is what every unhealed affliction in the life of a believer is being turned to. He did not take it away. He came and lived on it.

Where Christians differ: healing and faith. Some teach that it is always God’s will to heal believers who have enough faith, and that remaining sick shows lack of faith. Verdict: Paul, the great apostle, prayed in faith three times for his thorn to be removed, and the Lord said no. God does heal in answer to prayer, and we should pray for healing (James 5:14–15). But he sometimes chooses not to, for purposes better than healing: humility, dependence, and the display of his power in weakness. Paul left Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness is good in itself, or that we should not seek relief. It means God’s grace is enough when relief does not come. This is not a call to cultivate weakness, to refuse medicine, or to make a virtue of incapacity. Paul prayed for removal, three times, and was right to. It means that when the weakness does not lift, you have not been shut out of God’s power. You have been placed exactly where it does its clearest work.

What is grace, in this verse? Here grace is not only God’s pardoning favour, though it is that, but his active help given moment by moment: the strength to keep going, the comfort that holds you up, the patience you did not have, the faith that does not fail. It is not a substance or a feeling but the Lord himself at work in you. That is why it is always sufficient: it is measured not by your need but by his fullness. You will rarely feel it in advance. Most believers find it given for the day, like manna, and only when they look back do they see how much was supplied.

How do I take hold of this grace when I feel nothing? You take hold of it by trusting the word, not by waiting for a feeling. Christ said it is sufficient; believe him and act on it. Pray honestly, even if all you can say is help. Keep using the ordinary means: Scripture, especially the psalms of lament; the Lord’s Supper; the company of believers who will pray with you. Do the next small duty in front of you and leave tomorrow’s for tomorrow. Get the medical and practical help you need, which is one of the ways God gives grace. And tell another believer, so you are not carrying it alone. Grace often arrives through their hands.

In a sentence. But he said to Paul, “My grace is all you need, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” So Paul will boast all the more gladly about his weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on him.

On a Tuesday. Write the sentence somewhere you will see it today: my grace is sufficient for you. Then name the weakness it is meant for, the illness, the grief, the limitation, the failure that keeps you humble. Do not ask for the grace to feel strong. Ask for the grace to do this day’s work in his strength, and watch for where his power shows up exactly where yours runs out.

For worship. Hear Christ say it to you, because he does: my grace is sufficient for you. It was spoken by the one who knows weakness from the inside, who was crucified in weakness and raised in power, and whose power reached its fullest expression on a cross where he could not move his hands. There has never been a thorn deeper than his crown, and there is no weakness he will not pitch his tent on. He did not take Paul’s thorn away. He came and lived on it, and he will do the same for every one of his people until the day weakness is swallowed up in glory.

parallels.desc: he gives power to the faint

verseByVerse.quote: For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

For the sake of Christ, then, I am content. The word to start with is content. The Greek, eudokeō, is stronger than the English: it means to take pleasure in, to be well pleased. It is the word the Father uses at the baptism: with whom I am well pleased (Matthew 3:17). Not resigned, but glad.

With weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. Then five things he is pleased with, and they are not a poetic list. Weaknesses: his own incapacity. Insults: the outrages done to him by people, including the men in Corinth calling him contemptible. Hardships: necessity, the grinding pressure of not enough. Persecutions: being hunted. Calamities: the word means being squeezed into a narrow place with no way out. Nobody enjoys any of these, and Paul is not claiming to. Notice the qualifier that governs the whole sentence: for the sake of Christ. He does not take pleasure in suffering. He takes pleasure in what the suffering is for and in who meets him inside it. Take Christ out of the sentence and it becomes something unhealthy; leave him in and it is the most liberated sentence in the letter.

For when I am weak, then I am strong. Then the paradox, stated as flatly as it can be. It is not a play on words.
