Both halves are literal, and the then is a hinge: not although I am weak, but when I am weak, at that moment, precisely there. The strength is not his own returning; it is Christ’s power resting on the empty ground of verse 9. When we are weak and know it, we depend on Christ, and his strength works through us. Self-reliance is real weakness; dependence on Christ is real strength.

A different account of usefulness. This is a genuinely different account of the Christian life from the one most of us carry about. We assume God uses us in proportion to what we bring: that the more competent, the more resourced, the more spiritually together we are, the more useful. This verse says the arithmetic runs the other way at exactly the point where our resources fail. It is worth testing against your own history rather than resisting it in the abstract. Think of the times you have been most obviously useful to another person. It is very rarely the season when you were flourishing. It is nearly always the time when you had been through the thing they are going through now, and had nothing to offer but that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should seek out weakness or suffering. It means they can embrace it when it comes. Christianity has repeatedly produced people who sought out affliction as though the pain itself were holy. It is not. Paul prayed to have his removed. What he learned was not to love the thorn but to love what the thorn made room for.

Does this mean I should not try to be competent or strong? No. Paul worked hard, planned carefully, argued brilliantly and used every gift God gave him. Competence is a gift, and laziness is not a spiritual weakness to boast of. The point is where your confidence rests. A skilled surgeon, a gifted teacher, a strong father can all be weak in this sense, if they know that every ability is on loan and that nothing of eternal worth will come from them without Christ. The danger is not strength but self-reliance. Use every gift, and then lean on him as though you had none.

In a sentence. That is why, for Christ’s sake, he delights in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when he is weak, then he is strong.

On a Tuesday. When you feel weak today, say it: when I am weak, then I am strong. Then lean on Christ for the thing in front of you. And look for one person who is going through something you have been through, and offer them what you learned in it. Your weakest season may become your most useful gift.

For worship. The whole letter has been circling this. The treasure is in clay so the power is plainly God’s (4:7). The captive is the one in the triumph (2:14). The Lord of glory became poor (8:9), and was crucified in weakness, and it is the one event in history that changed everything (13:4). God has chosen what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no one may boast before him. He is pleased with the weak who lean on his Son, because his Son is the one in whom he is well pleased.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — Signs of Apostleship and Pastoral Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he has made a fool of himself, but they drove him to it; they should have been speaking up for him, since he is in no way inferior to the super-apostles, even though he is nothing. The marks of a true apostle were done among them with great perseverance: signs, wonders and mighty works. The only way they have been treated worse than other churches is that he never burdened them, and he asks them, ironically, to forgive him that wrong. He is ready to come a third time and still will not be a burden, because he wants them, not their money; parents save for their children, not children for parents. He will gladly spend everything, himself included, for them, even if loving them more means being loved less. Some say he was cunning and tricked them, but did he or Titus or the brother he sent ever exploit them? Everything he has said has been spoken before God in Christ to build them up. He fears that when he comes he will find them not as he hopes, full of quarrelling, jealousy, anger, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder, and that God will humble him among them as he mourns over those who have not repented of their impurity and immorality.
verseByVerse.theology: The “signs of a true apostle” (v. 12) — signs, wonders, mighty works — are offered not as the primary credential of Paul’s apostleship but as evidence that the Corinthians have already received from him what a true apostle gives. His primary credential, as the entire letter has argued, is the cruciform pattern of his ministry. The miraculous signs are additional evidence, not the foundation. This ordering matters: making miraculous signs the primary criterion for apostolic authenticity is precisely the error of the super-apostles.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation’s governing board is reviewing the annual ministry assessment and focusing entirely on measurable outcomes — attendance, baptisms, giving — as indicators of pastoral effectiveness. This passage suggests a broader criterion: has the ministry demonstrated the signs of true apostolic work (transformed lives, gospel truth, pastoral care), and has the minister borne the cruciform character that authentic ministry requires? The absence of spectacular growth does not disqualify; the absence of gospel integrity does.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.

I have been a fool! You forced me to it. The fool’s speech ends, and Paul steps out of the character with obvious relief. Then he says whose fault it was. The Corinthians’ failure to defend Paul forced him to defend himself.

For I ought to have been commended by you. That is the real grievance of the whole four chapters. They should have spoken up for him. He founded that church, he was publicly humiliated in it, he was slandered by newcomers, and the people who owed him everything sat quietly. He should never have had to speak. Anyone who has been left undefended by people who knew better will recognise the note. It is not the attack that wounds most; it is the silence of the ones who could have spoken and did not.

For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. Then the two halves of the sentence, held together without embarrassment. Both are true and neither cancels the other. Measured against the men impressing Corinth, he is not behind by a step. Measured in himself, he is nothing (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). That is not self-hatred; it is the settled realism of a man who wrote that our sufficiency is from God (3:5) and that the treasure is in a clay pot. By God’s grace, not inferior; in himself, nothing. A Christian can hold a very high view of what God has done through him and a very low view of his own contribution at the same time, without either being false modesty.

The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience. Then the closest Paul comes to the credentials his rivals traded in. And look at the phrase attached: with utmost patience. “Patience” (hypomonē) is endurance, staying power under weight. The signs came wrapped in endurance. That is the qualifier his opponents could not match, and it is the one he puts first in the sentence. Power without patience is what they offered. Paul had both, and he lists the patience as the more significant of the two, because anyone can be impressive for an evening, and only a certain kind of man is still there eighteen months later, making tents. The marks of a true apostle include perseverance in suffering.

With signs and wonders and mighty works. Three words for miracles: signs, which point beyond themselves; wonders, which astonish; mighty works, which display power. So the miracles happened in Corinth (Romans 15:19). He does not deny them, and this is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that the apostles worked them. They were signs confirming his apostleship. But look at where he has placed the fact: at the end of four chapters of weakness, mentioned once, in a single line, after the beatings and the basket and the thorn.

Where Christians differ: the signs of an apostle today. Some argue that miracles should be normal in every church today. Verdict: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of an apostle: marks that distinguished true apostles from false. If they were common to all believers, they could not mark out apostles. This supports the view that the miraculous sign gifts were tied to the apostolic foundation of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; Ephesians 2:20) and are not the norm today. God remains free to do wonders.

Apostles were witnesses. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, brothers and sisters who love the Lord, believe such signs continue, and some speak of modern apostles. But an apostle in Paul’s sense had to be a witness of the risen Christ, appointed by him (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and Paul says he was the last of all to see him (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles were the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20). The more likely reading is that the apostolic office and its confirming signs ended with the apostles. God still answers prayer and may heal as he pleases; but the church today is led by elders and taught by the apostles’ words in Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean miracles alone prove truth. False prophets can do signs (Matthew 24:24). Doctrine and character must agree.

If the sign gifts have ceased, should I still pray for miracles? Yes. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped acting; it is the belief that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gifts of working miracles at will, as signs confirming new revelation. God is as powerful as ever and still answers prayer in ways that leave doctors puzzled. So pray boldly for the sick (James 5:14–15), for conversions, for deliverance from danger, and expect God to hear. Give him the glory when he answers. What we should not do is treat miracles as the proof of a ministry, or tell sufferers that their lack of healing shows lack of faith.

How should I treat Christians who believe the gifts continue? As brothers and sisters in Christ. This is an in-house difference among people who love the same Lord and the same gospel, and many charismatic believers put the rest of us to shame by their zeal in prayer and evangelism. Hold your convictions with charity. Discuss the question from Scripture, not from caricatures. Test every claimed word or sign by the Bible, as they themselves should. And reserve your warnings for teaching that adds to Scripture, promises health and wealth, or replaces the gospel with spectacle.

In a sentence. Paul has made a fool of himself, but you drove him to it. You ought to have commended him, for he is not in the least inferior to the super-apostles, even though he is nothing. The things that mark an apostle, signs, wonders and miracles, were done among you with great perseverance.

On a Tuesday. Speak up for faithful servants of Christ who are criticised unfairly. Think of someone, a pastor, a missionary, a fellow member, who is being talked about behind their back, and say a word in their defence when you next hear it. Silence is not neutral.

For worship. Every sign Paul did pointed away from himself to the risen Lord. Christ is the great sign and wonder of God, who healed the sick, raised the dead and stilled the storm, and whose greatest mighty work was done in weakness on a cross and in power at an empty tomb. The signs of the apostles confirmed his word once for all, and that word stands in our hands today. He who was not ashamed to call the weak his own is not ashamed to call us brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

For in what were you less favoured than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? The irony has one more turn in it. It is bitter and it is funny, and the sarcasm is aimed at an accusation so absurd that stating it plainly is the best refutation available. They received everything other churches did: the gospel, the founding, the teaching, the miracles. The single respect in which Corinth received less than any other church Paul served is that he refused to take their money.

Forgive me this wrong! Biting irony. He asks their pardon for it.

Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. Then the announcement. The first visit founded the church; the second was the painful one (2:1); this will be the third (13:1). And the policy has not changed and will not.

And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. Then the sentence that is the heart of pastoral ministry, and it should be written over every church door. One sentence, and it draws the line between a shepherd and a hireling. The false teachers wanted what the Corinthians had: their money, their allegiance, their admiration, the standing that came from leading a well-known church. Paul wanted the Corinthians. Not their money but them: their souls, their good. Not what could be got from them. Them. It is worth running as a test in both directions, because it exposes a great deal. Of anyone who ministers to you: does this person want you, or something you can supply? And of yourself, in whatever relationships you are the stronger party: is it the person you are after, or what they give you, the gratitude, the loyalty, the usefulness, the sense of being needed?

For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. Then the reason, and it changes the whole register. He has stopped arguing as an apostle and started speaking as a father. Paul is their spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:15). And the argument is simply how families work. A father does not present his children with an invoice. The flow of money in a household runs downhill, from the ones who have it to the ones who do not, and nobody regards it as a transaction. That is how Paul saw his relationship with this difficult, ungrateful, easily impressed congregation. Not a professional engagement with terms. A family, in which he was the one who paid.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children have no duty to care for ageing parents (1 Timothy 5:4). Paul is speaking of normal provision for children.

How do I know whether I want people or what they give me? Watch what happens when they stop giving it. If someone you serve stops thanking you, disagrees with you, or no longer needs you, do you still care for them, or do you lose interest? Do you rejoice when they grow beyond needing you, or feel threatened? Do you pray for them when no one will ever know? A parent who loves a child is glad to see him become independent; a parent who loves being needed resents it. Apply that to your ministry, your friendships and your family, and ask God to purify your love until it seeks them and not what is theirs.

In a sentence. How were you inferior to the other churches, except that Paul was never a burden to you? Forgive him this wrong! Now he is ready to visit you for the third time, and he will not be a burden to you, because what he wants is not your possessions but you. After all, children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

On a Tuesday. If you lead anyone, a home group, a class, a team, a family, ask yourself the question of this verse: do I seek what is theirs, or them? Do one thing this week for someone in your care that brings you nothing in return.

For worship. Thank God for pastors who seek you, not what is yours, because they learned it from him. That is exactly the position taken by the Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and who has never once sent anyone a bill. God does not want what is ours; everything is already his. He wants us. And the Son came to seek and to save the lost, not to collect from them, and paid for his children what they could never have paid for themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. Two sentences. The first is one of the great statements of Christian love; the second is one of the loneliest questions in the New Testament. The two verbs share a root, active and passive, and the difference between them is everything. To spend (dapanaō) is to lay out what you have: money, time, energy, effort. To be spent (ekdapanaomai) is to be laid out yourself: used up, utterly exhausted, consumed in the process. Anyone can spend for a while. Being spent is a different order of thing, and it is what actually happens to people who serve others for a long time. They do not merely give things away; they are gradually used up. The mother of a disabled child knows this. So does the man who has cared for his wife through a long decline, and the pastor in his twenty-fifth year.

Most gladly. The adverb is the astonishing part. It is a superlative. Not willingly, not without complaint. He is delighted to be used up for them. Like Christ, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20).

For your souls. Not for their approval, their project, or their good opinion. He is spending himself on what will still exist in a thousand years.

If I love you more, am I to be loved less? Then the question, and Paul lets it stand without answering it. It is heartbreaking. Something has gone wrong that everyone recognises. He has loved them more than any of the newcomers ever will, and it has cost him their affection. The men who exploited them are admired; the man who worked nights so as not to burden them is suspected. The more Paul loved them, the less they seemed to love him in return. Love does not always receive love back. It is a real pain and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But notice that the question does not become a threat or a withdrawal. He asks it, and then goes on loving them and announces he is coming again. Love that stops when it is not returned was something else all along.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul served in order to be loved. He loved regardless.

Is it wrong to want to be loved back? No. Paul plainly wanted it, and he says so; he asked them earlier to widen their hearts to him (6:13). Longing for love in return is human and good, and God made us for it. What would be wrong is making your love conditional on it, or punishing people when it does not come. Bring the ache to God honestly, as Paul brings it into the open here. Then go on loving, because your love is first a response to his. If you are pouring yourself out for someone who does not love you back, you are standing where your Lord stood, and he sees it.

How do I keep from burning out while being spent for others? Remember that Paul was spent for souls, not for every demand people made of him. He refused some things, rested at times, accepted help, and was sustained by the churches’ gifts and the company of friends like Titus. Being spent gladly is not the same as being consumed by guilt or by other people’s expectations. Keep a day of rest. Share the load; you are not the only servant God has. Let others care for you. And keep your own soul fed, because you cannot give what you do not receive. The Lord who spent himself also withdrew to lonely places and prayed.

In a sentence. So Paul will very gladly spend for you everything he has and expend himself as well. If he loves you more, will you love him less?

On a Tuesday. Spend yourself for others gladly, even if they do not love you back. Christ did. Think of the person you serve who gives you least in return, and ask God for the grace to say most gladly about them, and mean it.

For worship. There is only one place this pattern comes from. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The one who loved most was loved least, and was spent entirely, and did it gladly, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), for people who at the time were shouting for his death. He spent his glory, his comfort, his strength, his blood. Every servant of his who has loved and not been loved back is standing in a very old and very honourable place, and the Lord who stood there first will not let one drop of that love be wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?

But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. A new accusation, and it is the meanest one yet. The logic runs like this. Paul’s personal integrity about money could not be denied: he had never taken a penny and the whole province knew it. So the charge changed shape. Very well, he did not take it himself; that was the clever part. He was crafty and got the better of you by deceit, meaning that the Jerusalem collection was the real operation, and the money would be skimmed off through the men he sent.

Unfalsifiable suspicion. Notice what has happened. The very transparency Paul built, the delegates chosen by the churches, the several overseers, the refusal to handle funds alone (8:20–21), has been turned into evidence of a more sophisticated fraud. That is the nature of a certain kind of suspicion: it cannot be disproved. Honesty becomes proof of cunning, and precaution becomes proof of something to hide.

Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? Paul’s answer is not another protestation. It is a series of questions with names attached, and that is the only thing that works against such a charge. Paul invites them to check the record. Name one.

I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? They knew Titus. He had been among them; his conduct was a matter of public record and it was spotless. The answer expected is no. Titus’s conduct had been honest, as they knew.

Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps? Then the two closing questions, and they are quietly conclusive. The word for steps means footprints: walking in the same tracks. Paul and his co-workers behaved identically about money, with the same integrity, and everyone had watched them do it.

Answering a whispering campaign. That is the answer to a whispering campaign, and it is worth knowing, because whispering campaigns have not gone out of fashion. You cannot disprove an insinuation by denying it; denial only spreads it. What answers it is a public record of consistent behaviour, and other people who have been seen behaving the same way in the same room. Which is one more reason for the arrangements of chapter 8. Paul did not build that structure because he expected to be believed. He built it because he expected not to be, and when the accusation finally came, the answer was already in place and had witnesses.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not be accountable. Paul welcomes scrutiny.

How should a church handle money so that no one can suspect it? The way Paul did: never let one person handle funds alone. Have at least two unrelated people count every offering and sign for it. Keep clear records and let the members see them. Have the accounts checked by someone independent. Make sure those who decide on spending are accountable to others, and that no leader can quietly benefit. None of this implies that anyone is dishonest; it protects the honest from suspicion and the church from temptation. As Paul put it, we aim at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (8:21).

In a sentence. Be that as it may, Paul has not been a burden to you. Yet, crafty fellow that he is, he caught you by trickery! Did he exploit you through any of the men he sent to you? He urged Titus to go to you and sent our brother with him. Titus did not exploit you, did he? Did we not walk in the same footsteps by the same Spirit?

On a Tuesday. Ask God to keep you honest in all your dealings, especially with money: your tax return, your expenses claims, the change you were given by mistake. Then ask whether there is anywhere in your life where you would struggle to welcome scrutiny, and put that right.

For worship. Paul could appeal to Titus because both walked in the footsteps of another. Christ was accused of every kind of deceit, called a deceiver by the men who sealed his tomb, and not one charge would stick, because there was no deceit in his mouth. He is the faithful and true witness. And he leaves footprints for his servants to walk in, so that the honesty of ordinary believers becomes a quiet testimony to the honesty of their Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.

Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? Paul stops and reframes the entire four chapters. It is the obvious reading, and he knows it; he has spent four chapters answering charges, matching credentials, listing sufferings and refuting accusations. Anyone would call that a defence. The Corinthians might think Paul was trying to win their approval. He says it is not, or at least that they are not the court.

It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ. There is the correction. He has not been standing in the dock before the Corinthians. He has been speaking with God as the audience, and the Corinthians have merely been in the room. Paul’s court is God’s, not theirs (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). That single shift changes what all of it was. A man defending himself before people is managing an impression; everything he says is shaped by what will persuade them. A man speaking before God says what is true and lets the impression fall where it will, which is why these chapters contain so much that no advocate would ever have included. No one building a case mentions that he despaired of life, could not rest at Troas though a door was open, is unimpressive in person, and left Damascus in a basket. And it explains the freedom running under the bitterness. Paul is not frightened of losing the verdict, because the verdict is not theirs to give. He said it at 10:18: it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

And all for your upbuilding. Then the purpose, and it is the second half of the correction. Every word of it, the irony, the sarcasm, the catalogue of floggings, the fool’s speech he found so distasteful, was construction work on them. Not self-protection. He is back to the authority given for building up and not for destroying (10:8; 13:10). Even the sharpest chapter in the letter was aimed at making them stronger.

Beloved. And then the last word of the sentence, dropped in after everything. It is only the second time he has used it in the letter (7:1), and he saves it for here: after four chapters of conflict, addressed to the people who have doubted him, listened to his enemies, and left him to defend himself alone. That is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in, and he makes sure they cannot finish it without knowing so.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was unconcerned about what they thought. He cared, for their sake.

How do I live before God rather than before people? Start by remembering, often, that he is the one you will answer to, and that he already knows everything. Before you speak in a difficult conversation, ask what you would say if God were the only listener; he is the one who matters. When praise comes, give it to him quickly. When criticism comes, ask him whether it is true, rather than first asking how it makes you look. And let the purpose of your words be the good of the hearer, not your own defence. The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25).

In a sentence. Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? We have been speaking in the sight of God as those in Christ; and everything we do, dear friends, is for your strengthening.

On a Tuesday. Speak and act before God, for others’ good, not to win approval. Before a hard conversation today, pray this verse: Lord, let me speak in your sight, in Christ, for their upbuilding. Then notice how much less you need to win.

For worship. There is one court whose verdict counts, and for those in Christ it has already been given. God has justified us; who is to condemn? That is why Paul can speak so freely, and why every believer can. We are not on trial before people, and we are not on trial before God, because Christ stood trial for us and was condemned in our place. In his sight we are beloved, and that word, dropped into the end of a hard sentence, is the word the Father speaks over all his children for the sake of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish. The chapter ends in fear, and it is worth noticing what Paul is and is not afraid of. Twice he says I fear, and the word perhaps guards it. He is not predicting; he is dreading a possibility, that they will not yet have repented. That small word matters. He has not given up on them, and he will not describe their sin as settled before he has seen it.

And that you may find me not as you wish. If they are unrepentant, he will have to come with severity instead of gentleness, the rod rather than love in a spirit of gentleness (1 Corinthians 4:21). He would far rather not.

That perhaps there may be quarrelling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. Then the list of eight, and read as a group they are not the sins of a pagan city. They are the sins of a church. Quarrelling (eris), strife. Jealousy (zēlos), resentment of another’s good. Anger (thymoi), outbursts of temper. Hostility (eritheiai), selfish ambition and factions. Slander (katalaliai), speaking against people. Gossip (psithyrismoi), whisperings. Conceit (physiōseis), puffings-up. Disorder (akatastasiai), tumult. Every one of them is a relational sin, and every one is survivable indefinitely by a congregation that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Nobody is disciplined for gossip. Nobody leaves a church over conceit. And these eight are the exact photographic negative of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). Where the Spirit is not being followed, this list is what grows in the space.

I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you. Then verse 21, and it goes deeper. He is afraid that he will arrive and find the situation such that he is brought low in front of them. Their sin would humiliate Paul as their father. And notice the phrase my God: even the humbling would come from the hand of the God he belongs to.

And I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented. The verb is the strong one: to grieve as at a death (1 Corinthians 5:2). Not to discipline them, though he will; not to be angry, though he might be. To mourn.

Of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practised. The three sins named are the old Corinthian ones, the things the first letter dealt with (1 Corinthians 5–6). Some had never actually turned. The letter had been received, the crisis had been resolved, the church had come back to Paul, and underneath it, quietly, a number of people were still living exactly as they had been.

Corporate repentance is not personal repentance. That is a sober note for any church that has come through a good season. A congregation can be genuinely restored at the level of its relationships and still contain people for whom nothing has changed at all. Revival in the church does not automatically mean repentance in every pew.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the whole church was unrepentant. Many had repented (7:9–11). But not all.

Why does Paul put gossip in the same list as sexual immorality? Because both destroy, and both grieve God. We rank sins by how shocking they look, and gossip and conceit rarely shock anyone. God ranks them differently: Romans 1:29–30 puts gossips and slanderers in the same catalogue as murderers, and Proverbs says a whisperer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28). Sexual sin defiles the body and breaks covenants; gossip and slander poison a whole church and wreck reputations that took decades to build. Do not excuse the respectable sins because they are common. They are common because we excuse them.

What should I do if I recognise myself in this list? Repent specifically, not generally. Name the sin to God: not I have not been very loving, but I said that about her and it was not true, or not mine to say. Receive his forgiveness, which is complete in Christ (1 John 1:9). Then put it right with people where you can: apologise to the person you slandered, correct the story you spread, make peace with the one you have quarrelled with (Matthew 5:23–24). And starve the habit: stop listening to gossip, as well as spreading it. If sexual sin is involved, tell a mature believer and get help; this is a battle no one wins alone.

In a sentence. For Paul is afraid that when he comes he may not find you as he wants you to be, and you may not find him as you want him to be. He fears there may be discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder. He is afraid that when he comes again his God will humble him before you, and he will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual sin and debauchery in which they have indulged.

On a Tuesday. Look at the list of sins in these verses. Are any of them in your relationships at church? Repent and make peace. Pick the one that is most at home in you, very likely the quietest one, and ask God to root it out this week.

For worship. End where Paul does, on the word mourn. He is not looking forward to the confrontation and he is not sharpening his authority for it. The thought that keeps him awake is that he will have to weep. The apostle of the third heaven, who had been caught up into paradise, is afraid of arriving in a Greek port and finding people he loves unrepentant, and grieving over them as a father grieves. And that grief is a copy of a greater one. The Lord wept over Jerusalem, which would not come to him, and then went into it to die for sinners. He does not delight in the death of the wicked. He mourns over the unrepentant, and he still opens his arms to everyone who turns.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.<sup>2</sup>I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows.<sup>3</sup>And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—<sup>4</sup>and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter.<sup>5</sup>On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—<sup>6</sup>though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.<sup>7</sup>So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.<sup>8</sup>Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.<sup>9</sup>But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.<sup>10</sup>For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.<sup>11</sup>I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing.<sup>12</sup>The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.<sup>13</sup>For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong!<sup>14</sup>Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.<sup>15</sup>I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?<sup>16</sup>But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit.<sup>17</sup>Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?<sup>18</sup>I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?<sup>19</sup>Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.<sup>20</sup>For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder.<sup>21</sup>I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The letter ends with a warning and a blessing. Paul is about to make his third visit, and he will deal with unrepented sin properly, on the evidence of witnesses, as the law requires. The Corinthians have demanded proof that Christ speaks through him; they will have it. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will live with him by God’s power in dealing with them. But the real test is theirs: they must examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith, whether Christ is in them. Paul would rather appear to fail than see them do wrong; his authority is for building up, not tearing down, and he writes now so that he will not need to be severe when he arrives.

Then the tone softens into final appeals: rejoice, aim for restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. After greetings, the letter closes with the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. The letter that began with the God of all comfort ends with the triune God present with a troubled church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul announces his third visit. Any charge will be settled by two or three witnesses, and he warns those who sinned before, and everyone else, that this time he will not spare them. They wanted evidence that Christ speaks through him: Christ is not weak towards them but powerful among them. He was crucified in weakness yet lives by God’s power, and his servants, weak in him, will live with him by that same power in their dealings with the church. Paul turns the test round: they should examine themselves to see whether they are really in the faith, and recognise that Christ is in them, unless they fail the test. He hopes they will see that he has not failed. His prayer is that they do no wrong, not so that he looks good, but so that they do right even if he seems to have failed. He can do nothing against the truth, only for it. He is glad to be weak if they are strong, and prays for their restoration. That is why he writes before coming: so that he will not have to use his authority harshly, since the Lord gave it to him to build up, not to tear down.
verseByVerse.theology: The call to self-examination (v. 5) has been used in Reformed tradition as the basis for the practice of self-examination before the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11:28–31). Genuine self-examination is not the cultivation of paralyzing doubt but the honest assessment of the soul before God: am I in the faith? Is Christ in me? Is my trust in Christ or in my own religious performance? The examination that produces assurance is the examination that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the examination that finds sufficient personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prepares for a communion service and the pastor leads a five-minute self-examination period before the elements are distributed. Some members treat it as a routine; others spiral into anxiety. This passage clarifies the goal: not to find sufficient personal holiness to “qualify” for the table, but to find whether Christ is there — whether the faith that receives him is genuine. The person who comes to the table trusting Christ is examining themselves correctly; the person who comes evaluating their performance has missed the point of both the examination and the table.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 13 closes the letter with a final warning and a final blessing. First, Paul announces his third visit. He will act with justice, establishing every charge by witnesses, and will not spare the unrepentant. The Corinthians want proof that Christ speaks through him; they will get it. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will deal with them by that power (vv. 1–4). Second, he turns the test around: examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Paul hopes they will pass, and prays that they will do right, even if he seems weak, because his authority is for building up, not tearing down (vv. 5–10). Finally, he gives brief commands: rejoice, aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree, live in peace. He sends greetings, and ends with the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit (vv. 11–14). A letter that has gone through tears, floggings and a thorn that was never removed comes to rest in the triune God, pronounced over a whole difficult congregation.

This is the third time I am coming to you. The letter turns to business. Paul is coming, and he wants nobody surprised by what happens when he arrives. The first visit founded the church; the second was the painful visit (2:1); this is the third.

Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. He quotes the law (Deuteronomy 19:15). It is one of the oldest protections in Scripture: no one is to be condemned on one person’s word. The Lord himself built it into church discipline (Matthew 18:16), and Paul applies it to accusations against elders (1 Timothy 5:19). Why raise it here? Some have read Paul as saying his three visits are the three witnesses, which would be a strange use of the text. The straightforward reading is better: when he comes and deals with the unrepentant, it will be done properly. No summary judgment, no acting on rumour, no apostolic decree from the front. Evidence, witnesses, due process, for people who had been slandering him for a year. That is worth stopping on. Paul is about to exercise discipline in a church where he has been the injured party, and the first thing he establishes is the procedure that protects the accused. A man who wanted revenge would not begin there.

I warned those who sinned before and all the others. Then the warning, and notice how carefully he documents it. He warned them on the painful second visit. He is warning them now in this letter. This is the second warning, and he is counting them. Nobody will be able to say they did not know. That pattern is itself a mercy, and it is how God deals with people. Warnings come before judgment, repeatedly, and they come in time to be acted on. Nineveh was given forty days (Jonah 3:4). The generation of the flood had a hundred and twenty years and a man building a boat (Genesis 6:3; 1 Peter 3:20). Nobody in Scripture is ever ambushed by God.

If I come again I will not spare them. A clear final warning: he will exercise discipline. The verb is the one he used at 1:23, where he stayed away to spare them. So the sparing is over. He held off once; he will not hold off twice. And that answers the charge that has run through the whole letter, that Paul is fierce in his letters and weak in person. The truth was simpler. He had been patient, and they had mistaken patience for inability. It is a very old mistake, and Peter had to answer it about God himself: the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you (2 Peter 3:9). Delay is not weakness. It is room being given.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is eager to punish. He has given many warnings and much time.

What does church discipline actually involve? It is the church’s loving care for its members, which includes correcting those who fall into serious, unrepented sin. Most of it is quiet and private: a word between friends, a visit from an elder, an honest conversation (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Only when someone persistently refuses to repent of plain sin does it become public, and in the last resort the church may remove him from membership and the Lord’s Table (1 Corinthians 5:4–5, 13). The aim at every stage is restoration, not humiliation: to win the brother back. When it is done with patience, evidence and tears, as here, it is one of the ways Christ protects his flock and calls his wandering sheep home.

Why insist on witnesses when someone is accused? Because God hates false accusation and injustice, and because a single report, however sincere, can be mistaken, exaggerated or malicious. Requiring confirmation protects the innocent from rumour and the church from being manipulated. It does not mean that a lone victim of abuse should be ignored. Other evidence can confirm a charge, and patterns of behaviour often come to light when one person speaks. Serious allegations, especially of abuse or crime, must be taken seriously at once and reported to the proper authorities; the requirement of witnesses governs the church’s verdict, not whether it listens.

In a sentence. This will be Paul’s third visit to you. Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. He already gave you a warning when he was with you the second time. He now repeats it while absent: on his return he will not spare those who sinned earlier or any of the others.

On a Tuesday. Never act on rumour against a fellow believer. Insist on clear evidence and fair process, and refuse to pass on a story you cannot verify. And if God has been warning you about something, through Scripture, conscience or a friend, take the warning while it is still a warning.

For worship. The God who warns before he judges is the God who waited a hundred and twenty years while the ark was built, who sent Jonah to a city he meant to spare, and who sent his own Son to bear the judgment he had so long announced. His patience is not slackness. It is mercy holding the door open. And for those in Christ, the final verdict has already been given on better evidence than two or three witnesses: the testimony of the Father, the blood of the Son and the witness of the Spirit, that there is now no condemnation.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three

verseByVerse.quote: since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

Since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. Here is the demand behind everything. “Proof” (dokimē) means evidence, the result of a test. The Corinthians demanded evidence that Paul really spoke for Christ. And you can see what kind of demonstration they had in mind, because they had been getting it from somebody else: presence, force, the manner of a man who is plainly in charge. The super-apostles had it. Paul, working nights and declining their money, did not.

Standing inside the evidence. The tragedy in the sentence is that they were asking for proof from a man who had given them everything he had. The church itself was the proof (3:2); so were the scars. They were standing inside the evidence and asking to see some. People do this. A wife who has been loved faithfully for thirty years can still ask whether she is loved, because the thing she is looking for is a gesture rather than a life. The demand for proof is very often a sign that the actual evidence has stopped being looked at.

He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you. Then Paul’s answer, and it is a warning dressed as a correction. Notice the switch. They asked about Paul; he answers about Christ. You want to know whether Christ is speaking in me? Then understand what you are asking for. The Christ who deals with you through me is not weak. Christ himself has shown his power among them: in their conversion, in the gifts, in the miracles. They should not doubt Christ’s power in Paul’s ministry.

A domesticated Christ. There is a real danger being named. A church that has learned to disregard a gentle minister can slide, almost without noticing, into disregarding the Lord who sent him. The messenger’s mildness gets attributed to the message, and then to the one who gave it, and a congregation ends up with a tame Christ, endlessly patient in a way that means nothing much is at stake. Paul will not have it. The gentleness they have experienced is his; the power belongs to someone else, and it is not in short supply. And that is a searching thought for anyone who has grown comfortable. If your picture of Christ has quietly become someone who never presses, never confronts and never requires anything, ask where that picture came from. It did not come from the Gospels, where he cleared the temple with a whip and wept over a city that would not come to him (John 2:15; Luke 19:41). He is not weak in dealing with his people. He is patient, which is a different thing entirely.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s power is always visible as human strength. It is often displayed through weakness (12:9).

How does Christ show his power in a church today? Mostly in ways that do not look spectacular. Sinners are converted under ordinary preaching. Hardened people repent. Broken marriages are mended. Believers persevere through cancer, grief and persecution with a peace nobody can explain. Quarrelling members are reconciled. Children raised in the church come to faith. A small, unimpressive congregation keeps going for a hundred years and sends out missionaries. That is resurrection power, as real as any miracle, and it is happening wherever Christ’s word is faithfully preached. Learn to see it, and thank him for it.

In a sentence. Since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through Paul: he is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

On a Tuesday. Think of a way Christ has plainly worked in your church or your life in the past year, in a quiet way that nobody would put on a poster. Thank him for it. And if you have been waiting for some dramatic proof of his presence, look again at the evidence you are already standing in.

For worship. Thank Christ for his power at work in your church, often in quiet ways. He is the Lord who calmed the sea with a word and raised the dead with a shout, and who now works with the same power through jars of clay. He is never weak in dealing with his people. He is gentle with the bruised reed and fierce against everything that would destroy them, and his patience is the patience of the strong, who could end everything in a moment and chooses instead to wait and save.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.

For he was crucified in weakness. This is the theological floor under the whole letter, and it is laid in one sentence. Take the word at full strength. The crucifixion was not a strategic manoeuvre disguised as defeat; to every eye it was defeat. He did not come down. He was held by nails driven by men he had made, mocked by people whose next breath depended on him, and he died the way the powerless die: publicly, slowly, with nothing to show. The cross looked like utter weakness, yet the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25). Christ chose weakness.

But lives by the power of God. And then the sentence turns, and the turning is the gospel. The same body that hung there is alive. Not a memory kept warm by his followers; alive, by a power that reached into a sealed tomb. The resurrection displayed God’s power (Romans 1:4; Ephesians 1:19–20).

For we also are weak in him. Now watch Paul apply it to himself, and to every servant of Christ since. Paul shares Christ’s weakness, in suffering and humility. The pattern is not merely admired; it is shared. Paul’s weakness is not an unfortunate feature of his temperament. It is participation in the weakness of a crucified Lord.

But in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God. And he shares Christ’s resurrection power, which will be seen when he comes to deal with them. The power he will bring to Corinth is not his own recovered strength; it is resurrection power, belonging to Christ, exercised through a man who has none. The pattern of cross and resurrection shapes all Christian ministry. Which finally settles the question the Corinthians could not answer. They had been sorting people into strong and weak and had put Paul in the wrong column. He is telling them the columns do not work, because the one they worship is in both.

Weakness and power at once. It settles something for anyone who has felt disqualified by their own frailty. The Christian life is not weakness followed by strength, as though the weakness were a phase to get through. It is weakness and power at the same time, in the same person, as it was in Christ himself: crucified in weakness, but living by the power of God. Both halves are permanently true of him; the risen Lord still bears the wounds.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness and power are opposites to choose between. In Christ, they go together.

What does it mean to be weak in him? It means that your frailties, limits and sufferings, borne as a believer, are not outside your union with Christ but part of it. When you are worn out from serving, misunderstood for doing right, sick, grieving or simply ordinary, you are sharing in the pattern of his life on earth, and you are not further from him but closer. It does not mean every weakness is holy; sin is not weakness in him. But it does mean that what makes you feel least like a useful Christian may be exactly where his life is at work in you, and where you will most clearly live with him by the power of God.

In a sentence. For to be sure, he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by God’s power. Likewise, we are weak in him, yet by God’s power we will live with him in our dealing with you.

On a Tuesday. Your weakness is not the end of the story. In Christ, resurrection power follows. Name the weakness you are most ashamed of today, and bring it to the crucified and risen Lord, asking him to live in it by the power of God.

For worship. Stand back and look at what is being claimed. The centre of the universe is a man who was executed as a criminal and is alive. Everything in the Christian faith runs through that single fact: the forgiveness, the Spirit, the church, the hope of a body that will not fail. There has never been another event like it and there will not need to be. He was crucified in weakness. He lives by the power of God. Everything else in this letter, the clay pots, the thorn, the basket, the beatings, is that one pattern working itself out in the people who belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!

Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. They had been examining Paul for a year. He turns the instrument round. “Examine” (peirazō) means to put to the test, to put to the proof. In the faith means truly believing, united to Christ. And yourselves comes first in the Greek, in the emphatic position: yourselves examine.

Test yourselves. “Test” (dokimazō) is the word used of assaying metal: heating it to see whether the gold is gold. Again yourselves comes first. This verse has done a great deal of damage in the hands of people who have used it to manufacture doubt, so it needs handling with care, because the reader most likely to take it seriously is the one who least needs to.

Or do you not realise this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Start with what the test actually is. Paul supplies it in the same breath, and it is a single question. That is the whole examination. Not are you holy enough. Not is your faith strong enough. Not have you felt the right things. Is Christ there? The sign of a true believer is that Christ dwells in him by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). And notice the form of the question. It expects the answer yes. Paul is not suggesting they will probably fail; he is confident about them.

Unless indeed you fail to meet the test! He adds the failure clause as a sharp afterthought rather than an expectation. “Fail the test” (adokimos) is what an assayer says of metal that turns out not to be gold at all: disqualified, counterfeit. And there is a turn in the argument. If they find Christ is in them, then their faith came through Paul, which proves his apostleship. If not, they have bigger problems than Paul.

Where Christians differ: self-examination and assurance. Some say believers should never doubt their salvation; others make constant introspection the mark of true faith. Verdict: Self-examination is commanded, especially for those whose lives contradict their profession. Assurance rests first on God’s promises in Christ, confirmed by the inner witness of the Spirit and the fruit of a changed life (1 John; Westminster 18.2). Self-examination should lead not to endless morbid introspection but to looking at Christ, and to repentance where needed. Those who find Christ in them can rest assured.

How the test is run. Look for Christ, not for your performance. Do you love him at all? Do you want to be free of sin, even where you keep losing? Does the gospel still move you? Do you love his people, including the difficult ones? Is there anything in you that was not there before, that you did not put there? None of these is a measure of how well you are doing. Every one of them is a question about whether he is present.

The dead do not check their pulse. Here is the reassurance the anxious reader needs, said plainly. People who are entirely indifferent to Christ do not usually lie awake worrying whether he is in them. The very fear that you might fail this test, when it comes with a longing for Christ and a hatred of sin, is itself a sign of a heart God has made alive: the dead do not check their own pulse. If you are troubled by this verse in that way, it was not written to trouble you. It was written to the comfortable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on perfect performance. It means real faith shows itself, and should be checked.

Should I examine myself before the Lord’s Supper? Yes. The church has often applied this verse to the Lord’s Table, where Paul says, let a person examine himself, then, and so eat (1 Corinthians 11:28). The examination is not whether you are worthy enough to come; no one is. It is whether you are trusting Christ and willing to turn from your sin. Confess what you know is wrong, put away any grudge, and come. Those who find Christ in them come to the table; the examination is meant to bring them there, not to keep them away. The Supper is for sinners who need grace, not for saints who think they have outgrown it.

What if I examine myself and honestly do not find Christ? Then do not despair and do not wait. Come to him now. The test is not a final verdict but a summons. Christ invites everyone who is weary and burdened, and promises that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). You do not have to fix yourself first. Confess your sin, trust him as the one who died for sinners, and ask him to make his home in you. Then talk to a pastor or mature Christian who can walk with you. And if you are simply unsure, take the uncertainty to Christ rather than further into yourself. Assurance grows by looking at him.

In a sentence. Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realise that Christ Jesus is in you, unless, of course, you fail the test?

On a Tuesday. Take time to examine yourself before God, honestly and briefly. Ask the questions above. Repent of what you find that is wrong. Then stop looking at yourself and look at Christ, and thank him that he has come to live in you.

For worship. The examination, done properly, ends in relief rather than dread. You look inward, find very little to be proud of, and then find Christ there, not because you have kept hold of him but because he has taken up residence and has no intention of leaving. That is what the test is for. It sends you back to the only ground of assurance there has ever been, and it is not you. It is the Son of God, who loved you and gave himself for you, and now lives in you by his Spirit. If Christ is in you, rest in him. If not, come to him now; he is still receiving sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.

I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. Verse 6 sounds like the return of the argument. Paul hopes they will see that he is genuine: if you examine yourselves and find Christ in you, you will discover that the man who brought him to you is genuine after all. And then verse 7 does something extraordinary with it.

But we pray to God that you may not do wrong. That is what he actually wants. Not vindication, but their obedience. His real concern is their holiness, not his reputation.

Not that we may appear to have met the test. He is not praying for his own vindication. And he goes further, in a sentence that ought to be read twice by anyone in ministry.

But that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed. Follow what he is saying. If the Corinthians repent before he arrives, Paul will never get to demonstrate his authority. The showdown will not happen. He will have no need to show his authority in discipline, and may look weak again. His critics will go on saying he is all letters and no presence, and there will be nothing he can do about it, because the crisis that would have proved him will have evaporated. And he prays for exactly that outcome. He would rather be permanently misjudged than have them sin so that he can be proved right. He is happy to seem a failure, as long as they do right. That is selfless love.

How rare that is. Sit with it. Most of us, in a dispute, want two things: for the other person to do right, and for our position to be publicly established. We would not admit that the second matters much, but it does, and it shows up in a small reluctance to let the matter resolve quietly. There is a part of us that needs the wrong to be visible before it is put away. Paul cuts that off at the root. He puts their good so far ahead of his reputation that he prays away his own vindication. And notice where he is able to leave the matter, because it is the only place it can safely go. He does not need the record corrected, because the record is not kept by the Corinthians. It is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends (10:18). A man who genuinely believes that can afford to look like a failure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about the truth of his apostleship. He cared more about their good.

What if the person who wronged me changes but never admits I was right? Then thank God, and let it go. Their change is the thing that matters, and it is what you should have been praying for. You may long for an apology, and sometimes it is right to ask for one, especially where a wrong needs to be acknowledged for the sake of others. But do not make your peace depend on being vindicated. God knows who was right, and his opinion is the one that will stand. Holding out for a public admission often keeps a conflict alive long after the real problem is gone. Paul prayed for the outcome in which nobody would ever know he had been right.

In a sentence. And Paul trusts that you will discover that we have not failed the test. Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong, not so that people will see that we have stood the test, but so that you will do what is right even though we may seem to have failed.

On a Tuesday. Take any grievance you are currently carrying and put this to it. Ask honestly: if this were resolved tomorrow, quietly, with no one ever knowing you had been in the right, would you be glad? If the answer is no, or not entirely, then something other than the other person’s good is at work, and it is worth naming. Pray for their holiness, even if it means you look less impressive.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the supreme example of this verse. He was counted a failure, condemned as a blasphemer, and hung between criminals, so that we might be counted righteous. He did not need to be seen to pass the test; he needed us to be saved, and he was willing to seem to have failed for the joy set before him. And the Father vindicated him in his own time, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand. Those who follow him can afford to seem to fail, because their vindication is in the same safe hands.

verseByVerse.quote: For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. A short verse, and one of the most freeing sentences Paul ever wrote. The truth here means the gospel and God’s will. Read at the surface it is a statement about Paul’s own limits. His authority is not a possession he may use as he likes; it was given for one purpose and it does not function for any other. If the Corinthians are in the right, he cannot act against them: not may not, but cannot. The instrument does not work in that direction. If they are doing right, he has no grounds to discipline them.

The limits of church authority. That is the principle of all ministerial authority, and it is worth stating plainly, because its abuse is a running sore in the church. Church authority has limits: it cannot act against God’s truth. A minister’s authority is derived. It comes from the truth of the gospel, and it extends exactly as far as the gospel does and no further. The moment it is used to defend something the gospel does not teach, or to protect a man rather than serve a people, it has stopped being authority at all. There is no such thing as legitimate power in the church exercised against the truth. So the practical test for anyone under a leader is not does he have authority? Very possibly he does. It is what is he using it for? Authority spent on truth is real however gently it is exercised. Authority spent on anything else is a costume.

Nobody can do anything against the truth. But there is a larger reading in the sentence too, and Paul’s wording invites it. Not his opponents, not the super-apostles, not the men who have spent a year telling this church that its founder is a fraud. Take that as a plain statement about the world and it changes how a Christian holds a losing argument. The truth of God is not fragile. It has been attacked in every century by better minds than the ones currently attacking it, and it has outlived them all. It does not depend on being defended well, or on the reputation of the people who happen to be carrying it, or on whether this particular church in this particular year believes it. Which means the worst that can happen to a faithful person is that he is misunderstood for a while. The truth is not at risk. Gamaliel, of all people, saw it: if this undertaking is of man it will fail, but if it is of God you will not be able to overthrow it (Acts 5:38–39).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not sin. It means apostolic authority was given only to serve the truth.

What if my church leaders ask me to do something against Scripture? Then you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully but firmly. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and no church may bind it to anything contrary to his word (Westminster 20.2). Make sure first that the matter is really one of Scripture and not of your preference; most disagreements with leaders are about wisdom, and there you should be slow to resist and quick to trust. But if you are asked to sin, to keep silent about abuse, to deny what the Bible plainly teaches, or to give a leader the obedience due to Christ, decline graciously, explain why from Scripture, and seek counsel from other mature believers.

In a sentence. For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to bend the truth to win an argument, protect yourself or keep the peace, remember this verse: you cannot do anything against the truth that will last. And if you hold any authority, as a parent, a manager, an elder, ask whether you are using it for the truth or for yourself.

For worship. Nothing has ever been done against the truth. Every attempt has been absorbed and turned, and the greatest attempt of all, the one that killed the Son of God on a Friday, turned out on the Sunday to have been the truth’s own method all along. Christ is the truth. He stood before Pilate and said that he had come to bear witness to the truth, and the truth was crucified and rose. Ask God to make you someone who always stands for the truth, because the truth is a person, and he always wins.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.

For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. The word glad is not resignation. It means to rejoice. He has been arguing for four chapters that he is not weak, that he is not inferior to the super-apostles, that Christ is powerful in him. And here he says he is delighted to be the weak one, provided they are strong. Paul rejoices if he appears weak because they are strong in faith and holiness. Their strength is his joy.

That is what a father says. There is no competition in it at all. A parent who has spent himself raising children and watches them outgrow him does not feel diminished; the whole point was to be surpassed. Paul has been spending and being spent (12:15), and the only outcome he wants is a church standing on its own feet. It is worth measuring ourselves against, because the opposite instinct is very common in Christian work and rarely admitted. There is a way of helping people that keeps them slightly dependent: the counsellor whose people never quite graduate, the leader who cannot delegate, the parent who needs to be needed. It looks like devotion and it is a subtle form of self-service, and the sign is exactly this: whether you are genuinely glad when they no longer require you.

Your restoration is what we pray for. Then the word he uses for what he prays for. “Restoration” (katartisis) is a rich word: being put right, mended, equipped. It is used of mending nets; James and John were mending their nets when Jesus called them (Mark 1:19). It is used of setting a broken bone. It means putting something back into working order so that it can do what it was made for. Paul prays for the church to be made whole again. That is a better picture of what God does with a damaged church, or a damaged Christian, than most of the ones we carry. Not replacement. Not papering over. Mending: the patient work of joining what has come apart so the thing works again. A mended net still shows where it tore, and it holds fish.

Prayer and command. And it is the same word Paul will use as a command two verses later: aim for restoration. So he prays for the mending and then tells them to work at it, which is how Scripture almost always handles the relationship between God’s work and ours. He asks God for the very thing he then asks them to do, and neither request cancels the other.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wanted to be weak for its own sake. He wanted them strong.

How do I help someone without making them dependent on me? Aim from the start at their growth, not your role. Point them to Christ and to Scripture rather than to yourself. Teach them to pray and to read the Bible for themselves. Connect them to the wider church so that you are not their only support. Give them responsibility as soon as they can carry it, and let them make small mistakes. Celebrate when they no longer need you as much. And watch your own heart: if you feel a pang when someone you helped moves on, take it to God and ask him to make you glad. That gladness is the surest sign your help was love.

In a sentence. We are glad whenever we are weak but you are strong; and our prayer is that you may be fully restored.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s restoration and strength, even above your own reputation. Name one relationship in your church that is torn, and pray specifically for its mending. Then ask whether God wants you to be part of the answer.

For worship. God is the great mender. He restores the soul, binds up the broken-hearted, and mends nets that have been torn by storms and by fishermen’s carelessness. The Good Shepherd went down into weakness so that his sheep might be strong, and he is glad when they are. He does not keep his people dependent out of insecurity; he gives them his Spirit, makes them grow, and still delights to carry them. Every mended life in the church shows where it tore, and holds.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
