For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.

For this reason I write these things while I am away from you. Paul explains, at the end, why the letter exists. It is a piece of pastoral strategy and it is worth seeing clearly. He writes while he is away so that he will not have to be severe when he is present. The sharpness of the last four chapters is a deliberate attempt to make sharpness unnecessary later. Every hard sentence in this letter was written in the hope that it would spare them a harder conversation.

That when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority. “Severe” (apotomōs) means sharply, cuttingly, like a blade. He writes now to avoid severity later. That reverses the accusation of 10:10 completely. They had said he was bold at a distance and feeble in person. In fact he was bold at a distance so that he would not have to be severe in person, which is not cowardice but mercy, and it is a good deal harder to do than simply arriving and dealing with everyone.

Say it early. There is a lesson in the method for anyone who has to confront somebody. Say it early, and say it in a way that gives the other person room to move before you are face to face. A warning that arrives in time to be acted on is a kindness; the same words delivered at the confrontation are just a verdict. Paul has now warned them twice (v. 2), and each warning was an attempt to make the visit unnecessary.

That the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down. Then the phrase that governs everything. He has said it before (10:8), and he repeats it here at the close because it is the charter of all Christian authority. It was given: the Lord gave it. It has a stated purpose. And the purpose is construction, not destruction. Which supplies the plainest test there is for any exercise of power in a church. Not whether the person has the right; they may well. Ask what is being built. Discipline that aims at restoration is building; the same discipline aimed at establishing who is in charge is demolition, and the words used may be identical. The language reaches back a long way. God told Jeremiah he was appointed to pluck up and to break down, to build and to plant (Jeremiah 1:10; 24:6), and even there, the tearing down served the planting. Nothing in God’s hands is destroyed for its own sake.

What it does not mean. It does not mean authority never corrects. Sometimes building up requires tearing down what is false.

How should I receive correction? Quickly, humbly and gratefully, even when it hurts. Proverbs says whoever heeds reproof is honoured, and the wise love the one who rebukes them (Proverbs 9:8; 13:18). Listen to the whole of it before defending yourself. Ask whether it is true, even partly, rather than whether it was fairly delivered. Take it to God and ask him to show you what he wants you to learn. Thank the person, since it is rarely easy to say. And then act on it. Paul wrote this letter so that the Corinthians could change before he arrived; correction received in time is one of God’s great mercies.

In a sentence. This is why Paul writes these things when he is absent, that when he comes he may not have to be harsh in his use of authority, the authority the Lord gave him for building you up, not for tearing you down.

On a Tuesday. If you need to raise something difficult with someone, do it early and gently, while there is still room for them to move. And if someone has been trying to warn you, respond to correction quickly, before it has to become severe.

For worship. Thank God for leaders who correct in order to build up, because they reflect the Lord of the church. He is the wise master builder who tears down only to build, who disciplines those he loves for their good, that they may share his holiness. That is why an apostle who could have arrived and imposed order wrote a letter instead, and wept over it, and sent a friend across a sea with it, and waited. He was building, as his Lord is building, a temple of living stones that the gates of hell will not prevail against.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with brief appeals: rejoice, put things right, encourage one another, think alike, and live at peace, and the God of love and peace will be with them. They are to greet one another with a holy kiss, and he passes on greetings from all the believers with him. The final words are a blessing naming the Lord Jesus Christ, God the Father and the Holy Spirit together: may the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit be with them all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction is not a formula but a theology: it presents the three persons in distinct but coordinated action, each contributing uniquely to the believer’s life. The order (Christ, Father, Spirit) is unusual — the more common Pauline order puts the Father first — possibly because the letter’s concerns have centred on the grace of Christ (the atonement of ch. 5, the self-giving of ch. 8). The coordinated action of all three persons in the single benediction is an implicit trinitarian claim: to receive grace, love, and fellowship from these three distinct persons is to receive from one God in three persons.

Koinōnia of the Holy Spirit — three possible meanings, all theologically valid: (1) the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers; (2) participation in the Spirit — sharing in the Spirit’s life; (3) the Spirit as the one who communicates fellowship with the Father and Son. These are not mutually exclusive; the Spirit’s work achieves all three simultaneously. Those who are indwelt by the Spirit share in the divine koinōnia — the mutual love and life of the Trinity — and that sharing is expressed in genuine community with one another.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that closes every service with this benediction has been pronouncing it for decades as a familiar liturgical ending. A new pastor stops before pronouncing it and asks the congregation: do you know what you are about to receive? Each phrase is unpacked slowly — the grace that flows from Christ’s cross, the love that originated in the Father’s heart before creation, the fellowship that the Spirit creates both with God and among the gathered community. The familiar words suddenly land with the weight they have always carried. The benediction is not a farewell; it is a sending into the world with the fullness of the Triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.

Finally, brothers, rejoice. The tone changes entirely, and the first word out of him is brothers. After a whole letter of defence, irony and warning, that is what he calls them. Then five commands, fired off quickly, and each one answers something that had gone wrong in that church. “Rejoice” (chairō) can also mean farewell, the ordinary word of greeting and parting. Both senses are probably here: goodbye, and be glad in the Lord. But given the letter it closes, take it as the command: rejoice. Said to a congregation that has been quarrelling, suspicious and divided, by a man who has been flogged five times.

Aim for restoration. The same word he prayed for in verse 9: katartizō, be mended. What he asked God to do he now tells them to work at. Mend the nets. Set the bone. Work toward putting things right.

Comfort one another. Or, as it can also be translated, listen to my appeal. Either way, the word is parakaleō, the great word of the letter one last time, from chapter 1, where God is the God of all comfort, who comforts us so that we may be able to comfort others (1:3–4). The letter that opened with comfort coming down from God closes with comfort moving sideways between believers. That is where it was always meant to end up.

Agree with one another. Literally, think the same thing: be of one mind (Philippians 2:2). Not uniformity of opinion; Paul, of all people, was not asking for that. It is the shared mind of people pulling in one direction, which is exactly what a church loses first when it starts sorting itself into parties.

Live in peace. The plainest of the five, and the hardest. End the quarrels (12:20).

And the God of love and peace will be with you. Then the promise, and notice that it comes last rather than first. The order matters. He does not say God will be with you and then you will manage these things. He gives the five commands and attaches the promise to them. Not because obedience earns God’s presence, but because a church living in mutual comfort and peace is a church where his presence is known and felt, and a quarrelling one is not, whatever is true of it in principle. And the title is chosen for them: the God of love and peace, the only time this exact title appears in the New Testament. Both nouns are precisely what that congregation lacked. Whatever a church is short of, Paul has a habit of naming God by it at the end of a letter, because the supply was never going to come from inside the room. As they live in love and peace, they will know the God who is love and peace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s presence is earned. It means a church living in peace experiences his presence.

How can I rejoice when my church is a mess? By rejoicing in the Lord rather than in the church’s condition (Philippians 4:4). Paul commands joy to a church that has broken his heart, because the grounds of joy are not in Corinth: they are in Christ, who has not changed, who is still building his church, and who will present her spotless in the end. Rejoice that the gospel is still preached, that sinners are still forgiven, that God is still patient. Thank him for the people in your church who are faithful. Then do your part in the mending. Joy is not pretending things are fine; it is knowing that the Lord is greater than the mess.

Does agreeing with one another mean I must never disagree? No. It means pulling in the same direction, with the same aim, under the same Lord. Christians will differ on many matters of judgment, and Paul himself disagreed sharply with Barnabas (Acts 15:39). What he forbids is factions, rivalry and the refusal to seek common ground. So disagree honestly and kindly, keep the gospel at the centre, do not let disagreement curdle into contempt, and be willing to give way on what is not essential for the sake of peace. As far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18).

In a sentence. Finally, brothers and sisters, rejoice! Strive for full restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.

On a Tuesday. Pick one of these commands and do it today: rejoice, mend a relationship, encourage someone, agree, make peace. If there is someone in your church you have not spoken to properly since a disagreement, make the first move this week.

For worship. The God of love and peace is not a distant reward for peaceful people; he is the one who made peace by the blood of his Son’s cross, when we were his enemies. He is love, and he so loved the world that he gave. He is peace, and he has reconciled us to himself and given us the ministry of reconciliation. Wherever his people comfort one another and live at peace, they are showing the world a small likeness of the God who dwells among them, and he delights to be with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. Two short lines, and it would be easy to skip them. They are doing more than they look. Paul gives this instruction in four letters (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26), so it was not a throwaway. In that world a kiss on the cheek was the ordinary greeting between family members and close friends: the equivalent of a handshake or an embrace now, and carrying the same social information. This person is one of mine. In the church it expressed love, reconciliation and family belonging.

Across every line. What makes it worth a command is who was doing it to whom. In a Corinthian gathering the kiss crossed every line the city cared about. A slave greeted his owner. A labourer greeted a householder. A Jew greeted a Greek. Outside that room none of those things happened, and inside it they happened weekly, in public, as a matter of course. And Paul is telling this particular church to do it: the one that had been sorting itself into factions, taking each other to court, and humiliating the poor at the Lord’s Table. After all the conflict, it is a pointed command. It is very difficult to greet someone as family in front of the congregation while carrying a grudge against them, which is presumably part of the point.

Holy. The word holy is the guard on it. The gesture was to be genuinely a family greeting and nothing else, pure and without any other intent, a caution that was evidently needed then and is needed now.

All the saints greet you. Paul is writing from Macedonia, and he sends greetings from believers the Corinthians have never met: the churches of Philippi and Thessalonica, poor and afflicted, the ones who had funded his work in Corinth. The wider church cares about them. It is a small line and it does something large. It reminds a troubled congregation, at the very end, that they are not alone and not the whole story. There are Christians across the sea who pray for them, whose names they do not know. The church has never been the size of the room you are standing in.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a literal kiss is required in every culture. It means warm, pure, family affection. Cultures differ, and the form is not the command; a church that shakes hands or embraces is not disobeying. But the substance is not optional, and it is easily lost. A congregation can hold sound doctrine and never once make warm, public, unembarrassed contact across the lines its society draws, and something the New Testament assumed would be visible every week has quietly disappeared.

What does a holy kiss look like in my church? Whatever form of warm greeting your culture uses between family members, given to fellow believers, especially to those you would not naturally greet. A firm handshake and a real conversation with the visitor nobody knows. An embrace for the widow who sits alone. A greeting for the member of a different class, race or generation. A smile and a word for the person you clashed with at the last meeting. Respect people’s comfort, and keep every gesture appropriate and above reproach, especially with children and between men and women. The holy kiss is family affection made visible; make sure no one leaves your church on a Sunday feeling like a stranger.

In a sentence. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All God’s people here send their greetings.

On a Tuesday. Greet your fellow believers warmly this Sunday, especially anyone you have been at odds with. And pray this week for a church in another country by name, remembering that they belong to the same family.

For worship. The family in which slave and master greeted one another as brothers was created by the Son of God, who was not ashamed to call us brothers. He welcomed tax collectors and touched lepers. He let a sinful woman kiss his feet. He was betrayed with a kiss and did not turn away the traitor’s face. And he has made one new family out of every tribe and language, whose members greet one another across every line the world draws, because they have all been received by him.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. The letter ends here, and it is the fullest benediction in the New Testament: three persons, three gifts, one sentence. Paul closes his letters with grace, always. Here alone he opens the blessing out into all three persons, and it is worth asking why this letter. Because every one of the three has been the subject of it. Grace was what he was told was sufficient. Love was what he was accused of lacking. Fellowship was what had broken down between him and them. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is named first, which is unusual; the Father normally comes first in Paul. But grace has been the pressure point of the whole letter, and this church knows what he means by it: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (8:9); my grace is sufficient for you (12:9). It is the free, undeserved favour shown in Christ to people who have earned the opposite, and it is the door everything else comes through. Grace comes first because it is through Christ that we come to know the Father’s love.

And the love of God. The Father’s love, the source of everything (John 3:16; Romans 5:8). It stands behind the grace rather than being produced by it. This is important and often muddled: Christ did not persuade a reluctant Father to love us. The love came first and sent him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10).

And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) means sharing, communion, having something in common. It means at least two things and probably both: our fellowship with the Spirit, the one who gives us a share in God himself; and the fellowship among believers that the Spirit creates, making a collection of unrelated people into a body. Both are true, and the second was precisely what this church needed.

Be with you all. Then the last three words, and they are the most striking in the sentence. All of them. The ones who had stayed loyal, and the ones who had listened to his enemies. The man who had insulted him publicly. The people who had let it happen and said nothing. Those who had not yet repented, whom he expected to have to mourn over. Paul has one blessing and he does not divide it. The letter ends with blessing for everyone.

The Trinity. This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is one of the clearest witnesses to the Trinity in Scripture. Each person is distinct, each gives a distinct blessing, and they are named side by side as equal sources of divine blessing. Written about twenty-five years after the resurrection, it shows that the early church worshipped one God in three persons. It has been used as a benediction in Christian worship ever since.

What it does not mean. It does not mean each blessing belongs to one person only. Grace, love and fellowship come from the one God. But each is especially associated with one person.

Why does the Trinity matter for ordinary Christians? Because it is the shape of our salvation and of our prayers. The Father planned it and sent the Son in love; the Son accomplished it by his grace, living, dying and rising for us; the Spirit applies it, uniting us to Christ and to one another. If God were not three persons, there would be no one to send and no one to be sent, no Son to stand in our place before the Father, and no Spirit to bring us home. We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. And because God has always been a fellowship of love within himself, love is not something he needed us for; it is what he is, and what he shares with us freely.

What is a benediction, and does it actually do anything? A benediction is a word of blessing spoken over God’s people in his name, as the priests blessed Israel with the LORD bless you and keep you (Numbers 6:24–26). It is not magic, and it does not work apart from faith. But it is more than a polite wish. It is a declaration of what God gives in Christ, spoken by his word to his people, and God is pleased to use his word. That is why many churches end worship with this verse. When you hear it, do not reach for your coat. Receive it, believe it, and go out under it.

In a sentence. May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

On a Tuesday. Pray this blessing over yourself, your family and your church today, slowly, one phrase at a time. Then think of someone you find difficult in your church, and pray it over them by name. Paul did not divide the blessing, and neither should you.

For worship. And there is where the letter comes to rest. It began with a man who had despaired of life itself and found God to be the Father of mercies; it has gone through tears and floggings, a thorn that was never removed, a church that broke his heart and mended, and an apostle lowered out of a window in a basket. It ends with the triune God pronounced over the whole difficult congregation without distinction. The grace of the Son, who became poor. The love of the Father, who did not spare him. The fellowship of the Spirit, who makes it ours. Three, and one, and given away freely to people who could never have earned any of it, which is what he has been like from the beginning, and what he will be found to be when everything currently visible has finished happening.
verseByVerse.note: This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is still widely used to close Christian worship.

parallels.desc: the priestly blessing

13.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>2</sup>I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—<sup>3</sup>since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.<sup>4</sup>For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.<sup>5</sup>Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!<sup>6</sup>I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test.<sup>7</sup>But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.<sup>8</sup>For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.<sup>9</sup>For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.<sup>10</sup>For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.<sup>11</sup>Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.<sup>12</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>13</sup>All the saints greet you.<sup>14</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
